name: Vimta Labs
business: Contract testing laboratory and CRO. It built, operates and will eventually transfer the National Food Laboratory at JNPT/Nhava Sheva under a PPP agreement with FSSAI, and its Hyderabad lab is a National Reference Laboratory for water and beverages testing. Does GLP/GCP preclinical and BA/BE work accepted for US, EU, Japan and South American regulatory submissions, serving pharma sponsors and food importers/exporters. Exports 37.5% of revenue (verified: Rs 1,528 mn of Rs 4,073 mn).
moat_note: Vimta itself makes no 'only/largest in India' claim; the moat is regulator-conferred and is the strongest single moat data point in the whole cohort — a national regulator has delegated statutory laboratory infrastructure to a listed private company, confirmed by FSSAI's own press releases rather than by Vimta's marketing. Certifications are the deepest accreditation stack found anywhere in this screen: NABL ISO/IEC 17025, NABCB ISO 17065, BIS, TEC (telecom), QCI/NABET, MoEF recognition, ISO 45001, CE-marking capability, plus GLP/GCP and BA/BE capability. Switching costs are accreditation-based and genuinely hard: a pharma sponsor's regulatory dossier names the testing lab, so moving mid-programme means re-filing. The NFL/JNPT concession puts Vimta inside the food import/export clearance chain at India's largest container port — but it is FSSAI's third National Food Laboratory and importers are not restricted to it, so this is privileged access, not a toll gate.
pricing_power_note: Pricing power — strong. OPM 25% (FY21) to 29% to 30% to 33% to 35% to 35% (FY26). Four years of expansion through wage and input inflation, then a two-year plateau, with PAT margin 15% to 19%. 'This is the cleanest margin series in the cohort and the only name where margin, revenue and ROCE all point the same way.'
import_substitution: None stated — this screen was run on monopoly and pricing power, not import substitution. (The nearest adjacent point is that the FSSAI concession places Vimta inside the food import/export clearance chain at JNPT, which is access, not import replacement.)
why_obscure: Not obscure: 50,190 holders, well over the 25,000 v3 limit — 'It is not undiscovered.' It is included on moat quality, not on being undiscovered.
risk_note: On a consolidated basis it is materially worse than the standalone numbers the screen picks up — ROCE 17.6%, ROE 13.5%, P/E 45.7; the note says use consolidated if you are sizing a position. Alongside that, promoter holding is only 35.7% and slipping every quarter.
v3_gates: Fails two — 50,190 holders (well over 25,000) and promoter 35.66% (under 45%). Included despite that because the moat is the best-evidenced in the set.
penalty_detail: Promoter 35.7% and slipping every quarter (-3)
The FSSAI concession is a finite-term BOT-style contract whose tenor and renewal terms I could not verify (-2)
warnings: Consolidated economics are materially worse than standalone (ROCE 17.6%, ROE 13.5%, P/E 45.7).
Promoter holding is 35.7% and falling every quarter.
The FSSAI/NFL concession is a finite-term BOT-style contract with unverified tenor and renewal terms.
DII holding collapsed from 1.50% to 0.37% for reasons the author could not establish.
The NFL is FSSAI's third National Food Laboratory and importers are not restricted to it — privileged access, not a toll gate.
coverage gate: 50,190 shareholders — 10,190 over the 40,000 limit, as of 2026-08-23
promoter 35.7% — 4.3pp below the 40% gate, as of 2026-08-23
verify_comment: The PPP/National Reference Laboratory status is independently verified — confirmed by FSSAI's own press releases, not company marketing — and exports of 37.5% were verified from the accounts (Rs 1,528 mn of Rs 4,073 mn). What could not be verified is the tenor and renewal terms of the FSSAI BOT-style concession, and the reason for the DII exit.
watch_note: Watch. DII holding collapsed from 1.50% to 0.37% while FIIs went 2.74% to 4.41%. Domestic institutions have been net sellers and I do not know why.
data_note: From the v4 moat & monopoly screen (19 Aug 2026), which was NOT gated on size or obscurity — it was run on exclusivity claims and pricing power. Its score comes from a different 100-point rubric and is not directly comparable with a v3 score.  v3 gates: Fails two — 50,190 holders (well over 25,000) and promoter 35.66% (under 45%). Included despite that because the moat is the best-evidenced in the set.

name: Sika Interplant Systems Ltd.
business: Bengaluru-based engineering company (operating as Sika Aerospace & Defence) providing engineered projects, interconnect solutions, electrical module integration, MRO services, landing-gear/hydraulics manufacturing and value-added distribution for the aerospace, defence & space and automotive sectors in India.
import_substitution: Aerospace/defence interconnect systems, electrical harness/module integration and landing-gear/hydraulics MRO were historically serviced by foreign OEMs and their India distributors; Sika has built a domestic engineering and manufacturing base (including landing-gear and hydraulics work) to indigenise these systems for Indian aerospace/defence primes, reducing dependence on imported sub-systems and MRO support.
moat_note: Aerospace/defence-grade quality certifications (AS9100-type) and years of qualification with prime contractors create high switching costs; specialised landing-gear/hydraulics manufacturing capability is rare among small Indian suppliers.
why_obscure: Small free float, thin institutional ownership (only 3.25% FII, 0.04% DII) and a complex multi-segment (engineering + distribution + MRO) business model that doesn't fit neatly into standard defence-stock screens.
risk_note: Extremely rich valuation (67x P/E) after very strong 3-year growth (52% sales CAGR) — execution/order-book risk if defence capex slows; part of the business is distribution/MRO rather than pure high-margin manufacturing.
liquidity_note: This is the most established, widest-held name in the group (26,959 shareholders vs low hundreds/thousands for the SME peers), so liquidity is meaningfully better than the rest of this list, though exact daily traded value was not independently obtained.
penalty_detail: P/E 67 - price has run far ahead of earnings (-3)

no FII/DII on the register yet (-3)

Business mixes higher-margin manufacturing with lower-margin distribution/MRO, so headline margins can overstate the pure-manufacturing economics

name: Accent Microcell Ltd.
business: EXCiPACT and US-DMF certified manufacturer of 22+ grades of Microcrystalline Cellulose (MCC), a critical pharmaceutical excipient used as a tablet binder/diluent, serving 200+ customers in India and internationally across generics, nutraceuticals and food applications.
import_substitution: Yes — MCC, an essential tableting excipient, has historically been imported into India from global majors (e.g., FMC Corp, US) and China-based producers; Accent's US-DMF-filed, EXCiPACT-certified domestic MCC production directly displaces these imports for Indian generic formulators seeking excipient supply security and cost savings.
moat_note: A DMF filing plus EXCiPACT quality certification for a commodity-adjacent excipient is a genuine regulatory barrier — most global/regulated-market excipient buyers require DMF-backed validated suppliers, a bar few Indian MCC makers clear at scale.
why_obscure: A Rs 1,400cr excipient (not finished-drug or classic API) manufacturer that is routinely missed by pharma-stock screens focused on formulations or bulk drugs.
risk_note: Promoter holding declined year-on-year (55.09% to 53.02%); commodity excipient pricing faces margin pressure risk from Chinese MCC imports if trade dynamics shift; P/E of 32x is rich for a largely commodity-adjacent business.
penalty_detail: very thin shareholder base (-2)
cwip_note: Very large and sharply rising capex — CWIP ₹2cr → ₹13cr → ₹102cr, now ~1.9x the existing net block, for the new MCC Unit-3 / Phase-1 build.
guidance_quote: Management expects a 15–20% CAGR for the next 3–5 years; growth in H1 will be muted as current capacity is optimally utilised and Phase-1 capacity only comes online in Q3.
guidance_source: H2/FY26 earnings call (May 2026), relayed via secondary research note — not verified against a primary transcript
data_note: Guidance is second-hand and is a 3–5yr CAGR, not an FY27 number. Treat with caution.

name: Simplex Castings Ltd.
business: Nagpur-based manufacturer of grey cast iron, alloy cast iron and stainless-steel engineering castings; a one-stop shop covering castings, fabrication, forging, machining, assembly, equipment building, in-house testing and EPC/turnkey execution for heavy engineering customers.
import_substitution: Complex heavy castings (pump/valve bodies, compressor components, process-equipment shells) for capital-goods OEMs that historically sourced large single-piece castings from Europe/China; domestic full-service casting-to-machined-assembly capability reduces need for imported finished castings and rework.
moat_note: Full in-house chain from melting/casting through machining, fabrication and testing (own EPC division) is unusual among small foundries and lets it bid for complete equipment packages rather than just raw castings, raising switching costs for OEM customers.
why_obscure: Sub-Rs 500cr market cap foundry with no analyst coverage; overshadowed by larger listed foundries (Nelcast, Steelcast, Ramkrishna Forgings) that dominate screener searches for 'castings'.
risk_note: Cyclical order-driven business tied to capex of steel/power/cement OEM customers; promoter holding has been trimmed slightly YoY (52.36% to 50.36%); working-capital intensive project business.
penalty_detail: very thin shareholder base (-2)
cwip_note: Heavy and rising capex — CWIP ₹12.4cr → ₹29.6cr, now roughly equal to the entire ₹30.7cr net block, for the new dedicated railway plant and defence casting capability.
guidance_quote: “We are targeting a revenue milestone of ₹500 Cr by end of FY28” — slide headed ‘Targeted Revenue Growth Aspiration’ showing FY26 ₹203cr → FY28E ₹500cr.
guidance_source: Investor presentation, 29 May 2026; reiterated in the Q1FY27 deck, 13 Aug 2026
data_note: The % is the implied 2-yr CAGR from management's own two figures, not a stated percentage. Management calls it an ‘aspiration’.

name: Modison Ltd.
business: ISO-accredited manufacturer, in technical collaboration with DODUCO KG (Germany), of silver electrical contact materials and finished contacts — including silver-tungsten, silver-cadmium-oxide and silver-tin-oxide contacts — for low, medium, high and extra-high voltage switchgear.
import_substitution: Silver-based electrical contacts for switchgear were historically imported or supplied by a handful of global specialists (Doduco, Umicore, Tanaka); Modison's decades-old Doduco technology tie-up localised this precious-metal contact manufacturing in India, and it is described as one of very few companies globally (and effectively the only major Indian one) making the full range of silver electrical contact materials, directly displacing imports for Indian switchgear OEMs (Siemens, ABB, Schneider India plants, L&T, etc.).
moat_note: Precious-metal metallurgy know-how (silver-alloy sintering/brazing) via an exclusive German technology partnership, combined with switchgear-OEM qualification cycles, creates a genuine near-monopoly domestic position — one prior analysis explicitly called it 'a monopolistic business.'
why_obscure: Despite a near-monopoly domestic position and 32% ROE, virtually no FII/DII holding and no sell-side coverage — a textbook case of a strong import-substitution business hiding in plain sight.
risk_note: High-value silver as raw material creates working-capital and margin volatility with silver price swings; still substantially exposed to switchgear-industry capex cycles.
penalty_detail: no FII/DII on the register yet (-3)
cwip_note: Capex cycle winding down — CWIP falling ₹10cr → ₹4cr → ₹3cr as spend is capitalised into a net block that grew to ₹94cr.
data_note: A search hit projecting 20–35% sales growth turned out to be Modine Manufacturing (US), not Modison — discarded. Q1FY27 coverage states no guidance was given.

name: Fluidomat Ltd.
business: India's pioneer (since 1971) manufacturer of fixed-speed and variable-speed hydraulic fluid couplings up to 3500 KW, used to smoothly transmit power and protect industrial drives (conveyors, crushers, mills, fans, pumps) from shock loads and overloads.
import_substitution: Fluid couplings for heavy industrial drives were historically sourced from European majors (Voith, Fluidomat's own licensor lineage); Fluidomat is one of very few Indian manufacturers making the full range domestically, reducing reliance on imported Voith/Transfluid-type couplings for cement, steel, mining and power-plant conveyor drives.
moat_note: Deep application engineering know-how built since 1971, wide range of standard + custom coupling sizes, and an installed base across cement/steel/mining creates high switching cost; scale is small so it stays under the radar of MNC competitors.
why_obscure: Sub-Rs 500 cr market cap, virtually no FII/DII holding, thinly traded niche industrial component maker not covered by any broking house.
risk_note: Highly cyclical demand tied to core-sector capex (cement, steel, mining); small size limits liquidity and pricing power vs global majors.
penalty_detail: no FII/DII on the register yet (-3)
cwip_note: Small but rising capex — CWIP ₹0 → ₹2cr → ₹4cr, now ~36% of an ₹11cr net block, a meaningful addition relative to size.
data_note: Screener ticker 404s; resolved via BSE 522017. Mar-26 PAT of ₹10.27cr is a sharp outlier — likely a year-end/other-income item, unverified.

name: CFF Fluid Control Ltd.
business: Incorporated in 2012; manufactures, overhauls, repairs and maintains shipboard machinery and systems for submarines and surface ships of the Indian Navy — spanning sonar, weapon-handling, fluid-control and electro-mechanical systems, from indigenous design through testing, refits and lifecycle support.
import_substitution: Critical submarine/naval shipboard fluid-control and weapon-handling systems were historically imported (from Russia, France and other OEM-source countries under licence); CFF is one of a small number of Indian private manufacturers indigenising design, manufacture and lifecycle support of these systems under India's defence 'Atmanirbhar' push, directly displacing imported naval equipment and spares.
moat_note: Defence-sector security clearances, naval type-approval and years of qualification on submarine-class systems create an extremely high barrier to entry; being one of very few private players trusted with submarine-system MRO is a durable moat.
why_obscure: Recently listed (2023 IPO) with tiny free float and near-zero FII holding; genuine strategic defence-import-substitution story overlooked because of its small size and niche naval focus.
risk_note: Richly valued at 54x P/E; single-customer (Indian Navy/MoD) concentration means order lumpiness and budget-cycle dependency; promoter holding has fallen from 73.3% to 68.1% over the past year.
penalty_detail: very thin shareholder base (-2)
no FII/DII on the register yet (-3)

name: Devson Catalyst Ltd.
business: Manufactures catalysts (chloride guards, sulphur guards, Claus/hydrotreating/reforming catalysts), adsorbents (activated alumina, molecular sieves) and ceramic/alumina bed-support media for oil & gas refining, petrochemicals, steel, fertilizer and emission-control customers; exports to 30+ countries.
import_substitution: Markets itself as 'India's Leading Indigenous Manufacturer of Catalysts & Adsorbents' in the guard-bed catalyst / adsorbent / support-media niche of the refinery catalyst value chain, a segment still substantially import-supplied by majors (Clariant, Axens, Haldor Topsoe, BASF, Chinese producers); core high-end reforming/hydrocracking catalysts remain imported, but Devson displaces imports in guard-bed and support-media applications for refiners and fertilizer plants — the company does not disclose specific substitution volumes.
moat_note: Ceramic/alumina catalyst and adsorbent manufacturing requires tight process control and multi-year technical qualification with refiners (IOCL/BPCL/HPCL-type customers) and petrochemical/fertilizer plants — a genuine customer-qualification barrier for new entrants.
why_obscure: SME-platform IPO with just 731 shareholders; effectively unknown outside refinery and petrochemical procurement circles.

name: International Conveyors Ltd.
business: India's only listed player in PVC (fire-resistant, anti-static) conveyor belting — a critical consumable for underground coal mining and bulk transport of coal, potash and salt — ISO 9001:2015 certified, associated with the Coal India ecosystem.
import_substitution: Fire-resistant PVC conveyor belting for underground coal mines was historically dominated by imported/MNC belting (e.g. European suppliers) given the stringent DGMS safety certification required; ICL is positioned as India's sole listed domestic manufacturer meeting these underground-mining safety standards, displacing imported belting for Coal India and other mining customers.
moat_note: DGMS (Directorate General of Mines Safety) approval for underground fire-resistant belting is a slow, safety-critical certification barrier; being the only listed domestic player in this niche gives ICL pricing power with a captive Coal India-linked customer base.
why_obscure: Sub-Rs 500 cr, low share price (~Rs 75) niche mining-consumable supplier with negligible FII/DII holding and almost no broker coverage.
risk_note: Revenue heavily tied to Coal India capex/production cycles (3yr sales growth is slightly negative); single-customer-type concentration risk in coal mining.
penalty_detail: no FII/DII on the register yet (-3)
cwip_note: No CWIP in FY24–FY26; effectively zero capex pipeline on a small ₹15cr net block — this is an investment-portfolio-driven company, not a capex story.
pat_turn_note: PAT back to +₹120cr in Jun 2026 after Sep 2025 −₹17cr.
data_note: Earnings are extremely volatile because they are driven by mark-to-market on the investment book, not operations. The Jun-26 swing is not an operating turnaround.

name: Sharvaya Metals Ltd.
business: Manufactures and exports aluminium alloyed ingots, billets, slabs, sheets and circles, with recent diversification into EV battery-pack housings, for cookware, automotive, LED-lighting, EV, construction, aerospace and defence customers. Recently listed via SME IPO (2025) and moved to mainboard.
import_substitution: EV battery-housing aluminium alloys and aerospace/defence-grade sheet stock in India have historically depended on imported billet/alloy feedstock or specialty alloys sourced from established global aluminium majors; Sharvaya's backward-integrated alloying (recycled + primary aluminium blending to custom alloy specs) targets the segment of EV OEMs and defence-adjacent fabricators looking to localise alloy sourcing under PLI/Make-in-India push, rather than importing pre-alloyed billet.
moat_note: Real but modest barrier: alloy-chemistry control (trace-element specification for EV thermal/structural housings) and OEM qualification cycles matter, but the core process (melting/casting/rolling) is capital-moderate and replicable, so the moat is more about established customer qualification than a hard technology lock.
why_obscure: Freshly listed microcap (2025 IPO) with under 500 shareholders and effectively zero analyst coverage; too new and too small to appear on any conventional materials or EV-supply-chain screener.
risk_note: Very limited operating history as a listed entity — most growth/margin figures not yet available on standard data feeds; aluminium scrap/LME price volatility is a direct margin risk; customer concentration risk typical of a newly scaled alloy producer.
penalty_detail: only 472 shareholders - effectively no secondary market (-7)
cwip_note: First CWIP in three years — ₹2cr appears in Mar-26 against zero in FY24 and FY25, ~15% of net block.
data_note: Resolved via BSE 544506. Latest half (₹2cr) is a sharp fall from ₹9cr — worth checking against the filing.

name: Steelcast
business: Steel foundry making castings for global mining and earthmoving OEMs, plus railway and aerospace-qualified work. Exports are 60.2% of revenue and 78.3% of FY26 revenue comes from three customer groups, the largest at 37.6%. FY26 PAT Rs 86.9 cr (+20%); it is committing Rs 120 cr to add 30% capacity while running at 63% utilisation.
moat_note: Steelcast makes no monopoly claim, 'and that is to its credit'. What it has instead is externally conferred: Caterpillar SQEP Bronze for Excellence in Quality, AAR (Association of American Railroads) accreditation, Ministry of Railways Class A approved foundry, EN 9100:2018 (aerospace) via TUV NORD, first Indian steel foundry to get ISO 9002, a NABL lab, and AEO T1 customs status. 'Those are qualifications a competitor cannot buy, and they took twenty years.' The switching cost is embedded in that customer- and regulator-conferred approval stack rather than in any stated market share.
pricing_power_note: Pricing power — strong, 'and the test is the interesting part.' OPM 20% to 21% to 24% to 29% to 28% to 27% (FY21-FY26). Critically, margin expanded from 24% to 29% and then held 27-29% through a revenue decline from Rs 477 cr (FY23) to Rs 373 cr (FY25). 'Margin defended through a volume downcycle is the single most informative pricing-power signal in this data set, and only three companies here pass it.'
import_substitution: None stated — this screen was run on monopoly and pricing power, not import substitution. (Steelcast is an exporter, 60.2% of revenue.)
why_obscure: Low profile on the shareholder-base measure — only 16,225 holders and 2.84% institutional holding, so it screens as Tier 1; it fails the v3 screen only on market cap.
risk_note: Customer concentration: 78.3% of FY26 revenue from three customer groups, the largest at 37.6%, so 'one lost relationship is a third of the business' — and this is still a foundry selling into the global mining and earthmoving capex cycle, at P/E 40 and P/B 9.2.
v3_gates: Fails only on market cap — Rs 3,620 cr against the Rs 3,000 cr Tier 1 ceiling (2.84% institutional holding, so Tier 1). Everything else passes: 16,225 holders, promoter exactly 45.00% (knife-edge — one small sale breaks the gate), ROCE 32.3%, ROE 24.0%.

P/E 40 and P/B 9.2 for a cyclical foundry (-2)

name: Prevest Denpro Ltd.
business: Incorporated in 2000, develops and manufactures dental materials for diagnosis, prevention and treatment of dental conditions — over 100 SKUs spanning restorative materials, endodontic solutions, preventive-care products, orthodontic adhesives and impression materials. Heavily export-oriented, selling to 80+ countries.
import_substitution: India's dental consumables/materials market (composites, glass-ionomer cements, endodontic sealers, impression materials) has long been dominated by imported brands (3M, Dentsply Sirona, GC, Ivoclar, etc.); Prevest Denpro manufactures CE-marked dental materials domestically, substituting imports both in India and via direct exports that displace the same global majors in other markets.
moat_note: Dental material formulations require CE marking for EU/export markets and CDSCO clearance domestically, plus years of clinical trust with practicing dentists before adoption; debt-free balance sheet and a 34% OPM suggest real pricing power in a replacement-driven, fragmented consumables category with high switching friction once a dentist standardizes on a material.
why_obscure: Export-oriented dental materials manufacturer with no consumer-facing brand visibility in India; essentially unfollowed by domestic retail investors and brokers despite a debt-free, high-margin, export-driven business.
risk_note: Narrow niche (dental consumables only) with exposure to a handful of large global dental-materials majors as competitors; 3-year sales/profit CAGR not disclosed on screener, limiting growth-trend visibility; export concentration creates currency and geopolitical/tariff exposure.
penalty_detail: only 1,975 shareholders - severe illiquidity (-5)
cwip_note: No CWIP in FY24–FY26 — growth is coming from higher utilisation of existing lines (management cited ~67–68% utilisation on traditional capacity), not new capacity.
data_note: Sep 2024 quarter not returned by the source. FY26 call (29 Jun 2026): management gave qualitative commentary and a ₹125cr full-capacity figure but no quantified growth guidance.

name: Spunweb Nonwoven Ltd.
business: One of the larger manufacturers of polypropylene spunbond nonwoven fabrics in India (installed capacity ~32,640 MTPA as of FY24), based in Wankaner, Gujarat. Fabric is sold into hygiene (diaper/sanitary-pad top-sheets), healthcare (surgical gowns/drapes), packaging, agriculture (crop-cover/mulch fabric), construction and home-furnishing end markets. Small SME-turned-mainboard listing (IPO July 2025) still largely undiscovered by institutional research.
import_substitution: Indian hygiene and medical-nonwoven converters have historically imported specialty spunbond/SMS grades (barrier fabrics, hydrophilic top-sheet grades) from China, Korea and the Middle East because domestic capacity was thin outside a handful of large players (e.g. the erstwhile Reliance/large integrated producers). Spunweb's capacity expansion targets this gap for standard-to-mid-spec spunbond grades used in diapers, agri-mulch and geotextile-adjacent applications, letting converters source locally instead of importing baseline PP nonwoven rolls.
moat_note: Moderate barrier: nonwoven spunbond lines are capital-intensive (continuous polymer extrusion + calendering) and require a qualification cycle with hygiene/FMCG converters on GSM consistency and hydrophilicity, but the base PP-spunbond segment (vs. meltblown/SMS) is not deeply differentiated technology, so pricing power is limited to capacity discipline and customer stickiness rather than a hard technical moat.
why_obscure: Listed via NSE mainboard IPO only in July 2025 from an SME base; sub-Rs 250 cr market cap, ~1,000 shareholders, and no visible broker coverage — falls well outside any commonly followed textiles or specialty-chemicals screener list.
risk_note: PP granule (crude-oil linked) input-cost volatility can compress OPM quickly; single-plant concentration risk in Wankaner; nonwoven spunbond is a commodity-adjacent, capacity-driven business prone to margin compression if larger integrated players (Reliance, large petrochem groups) add capacity.
liquidity_note: SME-turned-mainboard listing (Jul-2025) with ~972-1,000 shareholders and a sub-Rs250cr market cap; exact daily traded value not confirmed but the small float makes sub-Rs25-lakh/day turnover likely on non-news days.

import-substitution thesis weak on independent check (-5)

name: Krishna Defence and Allied Industries Limited
business: Ahmedabad-based maker of steel bulb bars and special-alloy ballast bricks for naval warship hulls, super-alloy weld consumables (wire, flux, electrodes), and homeland-security hardware such as vehicle barriers and tyre killers. Two ISO 9001:2015 plants in Gujarat at Kalol and Halol. Named defence customers include the Ministry of Defence, Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Goa Shipyard. A separate legacy stream makes stainless dairy equipment (bulk milk coolers, a patented robotic milk collection unit) and bulk kitchen equipment supplied to Hatsun Agro, Aavin, Verka and the Akshaya Patra Foundation.
import_substitution: Steel bulb bars for naval warship hull framing — previously imported; the company indigenised them in 2006 and was recognised by DRDO's Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory for the import-substitution effort. Origin country of the prior imports is not disclosed in any source I could reach.
moat_note: Warship-grade bulb bar and ballast supply requires DMRL/Navy material qualification and yard-level vendor registration at MDL, GRSE and Goa Shipyard; each hull section spec is approved lot-by-lot, so a new entrant faces a multi-year re-qualification cycle. The 30.7% ROCE on a near-debt-free balance sheet is consistent with a conferred, not commodity, position.
why_obscure: Migrated up from the SME platform, no BSE line, sub-19,000 shareholders and no institutional research coverage. Screens badly on name because roughly half the revenue is dairy and kitchen equipment, so sector filters mis-bucket it as a consumer engineering company.
risk_note: Defence revenue is concentrated in three PSU shipyards (MDL, GRSE, Goa Shipyard) whose bulb-bar offtake is tied to the naval order pipeline; a slip in warship build schedules hits the entire high-margin segment at once, with the low-margin dairy business unable to absorb it.
liquidity_note: NSE-only mainboard line at a ₹1,611 cr cap with 37% public float. Tradeable in small size but there is no BSE counter, so a single-exchange outage or a delivery-heavy day moves the price; not an institutional-size position.
cwip_note: CWIP of ₹3 cr against a ₹34 cr net block is routine maintenance capex, not a step-change expansion — this is not a heavy-capex story.
score_rationale: Regulator- and yard-conferred qualification on warship bulb bars backed by 30.7% ROCE and a debt-free balance sheet puts this at the top of the batch on moat and financials. Held back only by an already-visible re-rating — 18,720 shareholders is no longer truly obscure and the P/E of 37 prices in the defence narrative.

Defence offtake concentrated in three PSU shipyards
3Y sales growth of 57% is off a very small base and unlikely to repeat
P/E 37 leaves no margin for an order-flow slip

name: Control Print
business: Makes coding and marking systems (industrial printers) and the consumables, spares and service that go with them. 22,000-23,000 installed printers with 2,500-3,000 added a year, supported by 350+ engineers covering 1,700+ towns and 2,700+ pin codes. Over 60% of consolidated revenue is recurring consumables, spares and service. Overseas units include Markprint BV, Codeology UK and CP Italy; exports are only 2.85% of standalone revenue.
moat_note: Company-stated, quantified and self-limiting: 'The Coding and Marking Industry in India today stands at approx Rs 2,000-2,200 crore. Control Print has an overall market share of 18-20% of the organized players. The industry is dominated in India by 4 key players including Control Print (the only Indian company); these 4 contribute nearly 80%.' The note calls this 'not a monopoly claim, and it is more credible because it isn't — the company has quantified its own limits, which almost nobody else in this cohort does.' The real moat is the annuity, not the share: installed printers generate cash over 7-8 years because they are integrated into a production line, backed by service density the MNCs cannot match, and demand is partly regulatory because coding is legally mandated on many product categories. No third-party certifications are cited; the credit reference is CRISIL A/Stable.
pricing_power_note: Pricing power — strong. OPM 25% to 24% to 26% to 25% to 24% to 25% (FY21-FY26). 'Six years inside a two-point band, including through the 2021-22 input spike. The most stable margin series in the cohort.'
import_substitution: Not framed as import substitution, but the company describes itself as 'the only Indian company' among the four players that contribute nearly 80% of the Indian coding-and-marking market — i.e. the sole domestic player against three MNCs, with service density in 1,700+ towns as the differentiator.
why_obscure: Not fully undiscovered — 28,042 holders against the 25,000 Tier 1 limit, a narrow fail. The apparent cheapness (standalone P/E 12.8) is itself a coverage artefact: the note says '12.8x is the ex-subsidiary core, not the price you actually pay' (consolidated P/E 23.6).
risk_note: The loss-making European subsidiaries: consolidated FY26 PAT fell 56%, from Rs 100 cr to Rs 44 cr, consolidated ROE is 9.52%, and capital is leaving the good domestic business for Markprint BV, Codeology UK and CP Italy. 'You are paying 23.6x consolidated for a domestic core that earns 22.6% ROCE, wrapped around loss-making European units... The whole case rests on those units being fixed or written off.'
v3_gates: Fails narrowly on holders — 28,042 against a 25,000 Tier 1 limit. Passes market cap, promoter (52.99%), ROCE and ROE.

name: Axtel Industries Ltd.
business: Manufactures custom-designed food processing plants and machinery, offering engineered process systems covering the entire food-processing value chain from raw-ingredient handling to final processing stages.
import_substitution: Custom food-processing plant machinery (dairy, edible-oil, and general food process lines) in India has traditionally leaned on European (German/Danish) process-equipment specialists for hygienic, food-grade engineering; a domestic custom-engineering food-machinery builder substitutes such imports for India's expanding processed-food sector, particularly for mid-size plants.
moat_note: Engineering-to-order food-plant design requires food-safety/hygienic-design expertise (CIP-ability, food-grade materials) and repeat relationships with FMCG/food processors, creating moderate switching costs once qualified as a plant builder.
why_obscure: Sub-Rs 700cr food-processing-machinery maker with no analyst coverage, entirely overshadowed in any food-equipment search by larger names; shareholder base (18,789) is close to the 25,000 gate limit and worth monitoring.

why_obscure: Small free float and ~6,900 shareholders with no sell-side coverage; rides India's smart-meter theme without being a headline 'smart meter stock'.

name: OCCL Ltd (ex-Oriental Carbon)
business: Makes insoluble sulphur, the curing agent used in tyre vulcanisation, with capacity of 39,500 MTPA. It is a preferred or second-preferred supplier to most global tyre makers; exports are 48.1% of revenue (FY25 annual report). FY26 sales Rs 506 cr and PAT Rs 48 cr. The company was demerged from Oriental Carbon & Chemicals in 2024, so it has only two years of standalone listed financials.
moat_note: Verified by ICRA's rating rationale, which states explicitly that OCCL is the sole manufacturer of insoluble sulphur in India, holds 55-60% of the Indian market and roughly 10% of the global market. The note stresses that 'OCCL's own annual report is vaguer than ICRA — the hard numbers come from the credit analyst, not the company, which is the right way round.' Certifications: IATF 16949:2016 (the one that matters for automotive), ISO 9001/14001/45001, ISO 20400, Responsible Care, EcoVadis Gold. Switching costs are real: insoluble sulphur is under 1% of tyre cost but determines cure behaviour and blooming, so a tyre maker must re-run compound trials and re-homologate the tyre to switch supplier — 'a genuine moat, on a single, mature molecule, sold to one end-industry.'
pricing_power_note: Pricing power — moderate, and structurally impaired. The predecessor entity ran 30-36% OPM from FY17 to FY21. 'That regime broke in FY22 on sulphur, energy and Chinese competition, and has not returned': FY25 17%, FY26 18%, TTM 20.7%, Q1 FY27 28.1%. 'The recovery is real but from a permanently lower base.'
import_substitution: Yes — ICRA verifies OCCL as the sole manufacturer of insoluble sulphur in India, supplying 55-60% of Indian demand from 39,500 MTPA of domestic capacity. The note cautions that the 55-60% figure is ICRA's domestic market share, not an export percentage, and that 'the two are frequently conflated.'
why_obscure: Only two years of standalone listed financials after the 2024 demerger, so screener history is misleading and long-run comparables do not exist; 19,549 holders and 5.02% institutional holding keep it Tier 1.
risk_note: The 30%+ margin regime is gone and has not returned, and on top of that FY26 operating cash flow fell 84% year on year despite PAT more than doubling — a working-capital build the note flags as needing checking in the cash-flow statement.
v3_gates: Passes every one. Rs 823 cr, 19,549 holders, promoter 51.76%, ROCE 13.0%, ROE 12.2%, institutional 5.02% so Tier 1. 'This is the single best candidate for merging into the main v3 list.'

name: 3B BlackBio Dx Ltd.
industry: In-vitro Diagnostics - PCR/molecular diagnostic kits and reagents (legacy agrochemical formulations arm)
business: Formerly Kilpest India, the company manufactures PCR-based molecular diagnostic kits, PCR enzymes and reagents under the TRUPCR brand from Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, through its subsidiary 3B BlackBio Biotech India, and owns Belgian rapid-diagnostics maker Coris BioConcept. Assay menu spans oncology, HLA/transplant, HPV, infectious disease and food-borne pathogen panels sold to hospital labs, standalone pathology chains and research institutes; the May-2026 investor presentation puts FY26 molecular-diagnostics revenue at Rs 131.1 cr across 1,000+ customers, of which Coris contributed Rs 35.9 cr. A legacy agrochemical formulation business (the original Kilpest line) still sits inside the group, which is why several databases still classify the stock under agrochemicals. It is a genuine manufacturer with its own kit production and enzyme capability, not a repackager.
import_substitution: Named: TRUPCR real-time PCR kits (oncology, HLA/transplant, HPV, infectious disease) displace imported IVD kits from Qiagen (Germany), Roche Diagnostics (Switzerland) and Thermo Fisher/Applied Biosystems (USA), which historically supplied Indian molecular labs. Coris BioConcept adds CE-IVD rapid tests made in Belgium (that leg is an export, not an import substitution).
moat_note: CE-IVD marking on the Coris and TRUPCR portfolios plus CDSCO IVD manufacturing licence and ICMR validation of assays; once a hospital lab validates a PCR assay dossier and writes it into its NABL scope, switching kit vendors forces re-validation of the whole assay - real clinical-dossier lock-in, and the 25.5% ROCE and 40% OPM are consistent with it.
why_obscure: Renamed from Kilpest India, an obscure Bhopal agrochemical microcap, only in 2022; most screeners and index providers still tag it under agrochemicals rather than healthcare. No sell-side coverage, no earnings call - only a BSE investor presentation - and the COVID-era revenue spike (FY21 MDx sales of Rs 214 cr) makes the base optics look like decay rather than a rebuilt business.
risk_note: FY26 profit is materially flattered by a one-time event management itself flags: the Coris 'HAT order', within Coris sales of Rs 35.9 cr and Coris profit of Rs 8.76 cr, described in the presentation as 'a one-time event'. Coris is ~27% of FY26 MDx revenue; if the HAT order does not repeat, FY27 group revenue can fall by roughly a quarter and the Rs 22.4 cr Dec-2025 quarter (already down to Rs 9.8 cr by Mar-2026 and Rs 9.0 cr by Jun-2026) shows the swing is already underway.
liquidity_note: Mainboard (BSE 532067 / NSE 3BBLACKBIO), Rs 982 cr market cap with a 59% non-promoter float and 11,049 holders - by far the most liquid name in this batch, though still a microcap where a large ticket moves the price.
cwip_note: No CWIP in Mar 2024, Mar 2025 or Mar 2026. Net block still jumped from Rs 7 cr to Rs 28 cr in FY26, so capex was capitalised straight through rather than parked in CWIP - this is not a heavy-CWIP candidate.
score_rationale: Regulator-conferred CE-IVD/CDSCO barrier with clinical dossier lock-in and 25.5% ROCE earns 18/25 on moat; a clearly named import displacement (Qiagen/Roche/Thermo PCR kits) earns 16/20. Promoter at only 40.95% and drifting down caps promoter score at 8. FII 2.5% + DII 2.15% sits squarely in the 2-15% sweet spot (12). 11,049 holders with zero broker coverage gives 9 on obscurity, and ROE 19.8% with a debt-free balance sheet and 31% 3Y profit CAGR gives 9 on financials. Total 72.
warnings: Promoter holding 40.95% is only 95 bps above the 40% gate and has fallen 33 bps YoY - one more small sale breaches the screen.
FY26 earnings include a management-flagged one-time Coris 'HAT order'; the last two quarters have already halved from the Dec-2025 peak.

name: Alpex Solar Ltd.
industry: Solar PV Modules, Aluminium Frames & Solar Pumps
business: Incorporated 2008, Alpex manufactures crystalline PV modules at Greater Noida (UP) and has backward-integrated into solar module aluminium frames — the extruded/anodised frame is one of the few module BOM items it actually makes rather than buys. It also makes solar water pumps (26,000+ pumps installed to FY26 under PM-KUSUM) and runs a small EPC/IPP arm. A TOPCon solar cell line is under construction, which is what the CWIP line represents. Customer base is largely government solar-pump tenders (state nodal agencies under PM-KUSUM) and domestic module distributors; screener/company disclosure does not name individual private offtakers, so no named customer is asserted here.
import_substitution: Solar module aluminium frames (previously imported from China, and to a lesser extent Vietnam) are made in-house today; TOPCon solar cells — currently imported almost entirely from China — are the target of the cell line under construction. Caveat: until that line commissions, the cells inside Alpex modules are imported, so today the company is a module assembler plus a genuine frame manufacturer.
moat_note: ALMM List-I listing for modules is the regulator-conferred barrier (mandatory for government and PM-KUSUM offtake) plus BIS IS 14286 certification; PM-KUSUM empanelment with state nodal agencies is a separate multi-year qualification. Backward integration into frames raises switching cost modestly. None of this is a fortress — ALMM List-I now has dozens of names.
why_obscure: Only 8,517 shareholders and no mainstream sell-side coverage; the company has no earnings-call transcript in the filings database at all, so the only public information is the results filing and the annual report. Listed via SME route and migrated, so it sits outside most institutional screens.
risk_note: Borrowings went from Rs 49 cr (Mar 2024) to Rs 537 cr (Mar 2026) to fund a cell line while CWIP (Rs 175 cr) now exceeds the entire existing net block (Rs 168 cr) — the balance sheet is being doubled on an unproven asset just as ALMM List-II raises domestic cell supply and compresses cell margins. A one-year delay in commissioning against ~Rs 537 cr of debt at a 14% OPM business is the single biggest risk.
liquidity_note: Mainboard-migrated microcap at Rs 2,117 cr; daily traded value is adequate for retail-size positions but the 8,517-holder register means the free float is genuinely thin — a Rs 1 cr order will move the price.
cwip_note: CWIP Mar 2024 Rs 0 cr -> Mar 2025 Rs 23 cr -> Mar 2026 Rs 175 cr. At 104% of net block this is the heaviest CWIP-to-net-block ratio in this batch; it is the TOPCon cell line plus frame capacity.
score_rationale: Moat 16: ALMM List-I plus BIS plus PM-KUSUM empanelment is a real regulator-conferred gate backed by 43.5% ROCE, but the ALMM module list is crowded so it is not a 20+. Import-sub 15: aluminium frames vs China is a NAMED, in-production substitution; the cell substitution is future, not present. Promoter 11: 65.9% is in the sweet spot but a 2.86pp fall in one year is a real discount. Institutional 10: FII 3.13% is genuine, DII 0.40% is not. Undercovered 11: 8,517 holders and zero transcripts, but the stock is no longer unknown after a 125% 3Y sales CAGR. Financials 9: 52% ROE and 276% 3Y profit CAGR, docked for D/E rising to ~0.96.

name: Pix Transmissions Ltd.
business: Leading Indian manufacturer of rubber belts and mechanical power-transmission products — industrial, agricultural, lawn & garden, and automotive belts — over 80% sold under its own PIX brand, primarily into after-sales/replacement markets globally.
import_substitution: Industrial and automotive rubber power-transmission belts were historically sourced from global brands (Gates, ContiTech, Optibelt); PIX has built its own globally-recognised export brand selling into 100+ countries' after-markets, competing head-on with and displacing these imported/MNC belt brands both in India and abroad.

why_obscure: High absolute share price (~Rs 1,940) and minimal FII/DII holding relative to its genuine global-brand franchise keep it under-owned by institutions.
risk_note: Modest 3-year sales growth (6%) despite strong brand and margin profile suggests demand/capacity constraints; rubber input-cost (natural rubber, crude derivatives) volatility is a recurring margin risk.

name: Digilogic Systems Ltd.
industry: Automated Test Equipment, Radar & EW Simulators
business: Founded 2011 in Hyderabad, Digilogic designs, builds, integrates and life-cycle-supports Automated Test Equipment (ATE) for defence and aerospace, along with radar and electronic-warfare simulators, application software and embedded signal-processing solutions. It operates two facilities, in Hyderabad and Bengaluru, and serves the DRDO/DPSU ecosystem. Revenue went ₹51.71cr (FY24) to ₹72.19cr (FY25); FY26 OPM is 20% and 3-year profit CAGR is 67%. It listed on BSE SME on 28 January 2026 at ₹104 after an ₹81cr issue, of which ₹51.68cr is earmarked for a new facility. Promoters are the Jetty family, whose stake went from 88.5% pre-issue to 64.26%.
import_substitution: ATE racks, radar target simulators and EW threat simulators for Indian defence programmes have historically been bought from US and European vendors — National Instruments/Emerson and Teradyne on the ATE side, Rohde & Schwarz and Astronics on the RF/simulator side — with long lead times and ITAR/export-licence friction on anything defence-specific. Digilogic builds these indigenously in Hyderabad and Bengaluru for Indian defence customers. The displaced category and origin countries are clear; no filing names a specific foreign product line displaced or quantifies the import value.
moat_note: Programme-level qualification. An ATE set or an EW simulator is specified against one weapon or radar programme, validated with the customer's own hardware, and then becomes the accepted test asset for that programme's entire production and depot-maintenance life — switching means requalifying the test regime itself, so incumbency is very sticky. Backed by 18.7% ROCE and 20% OPM, this is a customer-conferred barrier rather than a claimed one, though at ₹72cr of revenue the company is a long way from proving it at scale.
why_obscure: Genuinely obscure. Only 976 shareholders on record, listed on BSE SME barely seven months ago, no sell-side coverage at all, and a ~₹2.5 lakh minimum lot that excludes ordinary retail. It does not appear in the Trendlyne document corpus, so even filings-based screens miss it.
risk_note: Concentration plus a lock-in cliff. DIIs hold 17.39% and FIIs 2.40% against a public float of just 14.97%, so nearly 20% of the register sits with anchor investors from a January-2026 IPO whose lock-in unwinds through 2026 — into a book with only 976 holders. Separately, ₹51.68cr of the ₹81cr raise is going into a new facility against an existing net block of only ₹9cr, a roughly 6x asset-base expansion that must be filled by a customer base of essentially one buyer.
liquidity_note: BSE SME platform, trading in a 1,200-share lot — about ₹2.46 lakh per lot at ₹205. This is the binding constraint: minimum ticket size alone rules out most participants, daily traded value is thin, and there is no NSE listing.
warnings: BSE SME listing with a ~₹2.46 lakh minimum lot — severe liquidity constraint.
Only two half-yearly profit data points exist since the January 2026 listing.
Combined FII+DII of 19.8% against a 14.97% public float means anchor lock-in expiry could overwhelm the float.
₹51.68cr of IPO capex against a ₹9cr existing net block is a ~6x asset-base expansion with no disclosed order book to underwrite it.
3-year sales CAGR of only 11% sits oddly against a 67% profit CAGR — margin expansion, not volume growth, drove earnings.
P/E of 58 on a company with under ₹100cr of revenue and a single end-customer ecosystem.
No management guidance, no earnings calls and no analyst coverage.

name: Tipco Engineering India Ltd.
business: Manufactures industrial process equipment for grinding, dispersion, mixing and homogenisation, supplying process machinery to the paints, coatings, chemicals, printing, packaging, metal and infrastructure industries.

name: Resonance Specialties Ltd.
business: Manufactures pyridine, picoline, cyanopyridine and their derivatives (Boisar/Vapi, Maharashtra); supplies pharma bulk-drug, agrochemical, dye and rubber-chemical intermediate customers domestically and via export supply agreements with multinationals.
import_substitution: Global pyridine/picoline derivatives supply is concentrated among a handful of producers (Jubilant Ingrevia, US-based Vertellus, and Chinese manufacturers); Resonance is one of very few Indian vapor-phase pyridine producers, giving domestic pharma/agrochem intermediate buyers a domestic alternative to Chinese imports — the company does not itself disclose specific substitution volumes.
moat_note: Vapor-phase catalytic pyridine/picoline synthesis is hazardous, high-temperature chemistry requiring specialized reactor design and emission control; few global producers; multi-year customer qualification cycles for pharma/agro intermediates raise switching costs.
why_obscure: Zero sell-side coverage, zero FII holding, ~11,000 shareholders on a Rs 198 cr market cap chemical-intermediate maker most investors have never heard of.
risk_note: Static promoter holding (no visible insider buying) despite otherwise decent growth, thin institutional interest, customer concentration typical of intermediate suppliers, cyclicality tied to agrochem/pharma capex cycles.
cwip_note: CWIP jumped ₹0 → ₹1cr → ₹4cr over FY24–FY26 and is ~19% of net block — the largest capex build in over a decade.
data_note: Resolved via BSE 524218. PAT accelerating sharply — Jun 2026 a record ₹5.74cr. No guidance statement in the FY26 annual report.

name: Mayur Uniquoters Ltd.
business: Manufactures PVC and PU coated textile fabrics (artificial leather) at Jaitpura and Dhodsar, Rajasthan, with a dedicated PU line built to serve global automotive OEMs. Roughly half of profit comes from the auto seat-cover and interiors segment, supplying Tier-1s and OEM programmes for Ford, General Motors, Chrysler/Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz and BMW; the balance goes to footwear (Bata, Liberty, Relaxo-type accounts), furnishings and fashion accessories. Subsidiary Mayur Tecfab runs the retail furnishing brand 'Texture and Hues'. FY26 standalone revenue about Rs 1,030 cr with 25% operating margin and effectively zero debt.
import_substitution: Replaces Chinese and Korean PVC/PU synthetic leather that historically supplied Indian footwear and auto-interior converters; on the export side Mayur is one of very few non-Chinese sources qualified on US/European OEM seat-cover programmes, so it displaces Chinese coated fabric inside those supply chains rather than inside India.
moat_note: Automotive coated-fabric approval is the real barrier: each OEM seat programme requires PPAP/IATF-16949 documented qualification, abrasion/fogging/UV testing to the OEM's own spec, and multi-year audits, and the fabric is designed into a vehicle platform for its life. That is why one Indian coated-fabric maker earns 25% ROCE while dozens of PVC-leather job shops earn nothing. Backward integration into knitted substrate and in-house PU chemistry adds switching cost.
why_obscure: Only one small brokerage (Monarch Networth) hosts the call; the company is filed under 'textiles' in most screens, so auto-ancillary investors never see it and textile investors dismiss it as leather cloth. No index membership, no ADR, promoter runs it conservatively with no equity issuance in over a decade.
risk_note: Customer concentration in a handful of US/European auto seat programmes: a single OEM platform loss or a US tariff action on Indian coated fabric could remove a double-digit share of PAT, and Q2 FY27 (Sep 2026) results are not yet out to show whether the Jun 2026 dip from Rs 61 cr to Rs 59 cr is the start of destocking.
liquidity_note: Mainboard NSE+BSE with Rs 3,291 cr market cap and 38,037 holders - by far the most tradeable name in this batch, though 58.8% promoter plus 7.3% institutional leaves a thinner true float than the headline. Exact daily traded value not verified.
cwip_note: CWIP Mar 2024 Rs 1 cr, Mar 2025 Rs 1 cr, Mar 2026 Rs 3 cr against Rs 213 cr net block - this is NOT a capex story. Growth so far has come from filling existing PU/PVC lines; management said on the Q4 FY26 call it has 'ordered one line' which has not yet shown up as CWIP.
guidance_quote: We have ordered one line, which will increase the capacity. And we are in sync, what we had said in the past. Until there is a very big challenge from an external factor, we see our growth trajectory in the similar level as given in the past.
guidance_source: Mayur Uniquoters Q4 & FY26 earnings call, 20 May 2026 (transcript filed 23 May 2026)
score_rationale: Highest moat score in this sweep and the only name where a customer-conferred barrier (auto OEM PPAP/IATF qualification) is backed by genuinely high ROCE of 24.7%. Promoter at 58.8% sits in the ideal band. Institutional score is strong because both FII (3.68%) and DII (3.65%) are present in the 2-15% window. It loses heavily on obscurity - 38,037 holders and an active concall make it the best-followed name here, and it barely squeaks under the 40,000-holder gate.

name: Fabtech Technologies Cleanrooms Ltd.
business: Manufactures and installs pre-engineered/pre-fabricated modular cleanroom panels, doors, wall and ceiling systems for pharmaceutical, healthcare, biotech and hospital sterile facilities, covering design, engineering, manufacturing, quality assurance, installation and validation.

name: Teamtech Formwork Solutions Ltd.
business: Designs and manufactures aluminium monolithic formwork systems - the reusable wall-and-slab shuttering sets used to cast high-rise concrete structures - and also leases formwork sets to contractors. Revenue mixes system sale, rental and the engineering/shop-drawing service that goes with each project. Customers are residential high-rise developers and EPC contractors; the company does not disclose named marquee clients in its filings, so no customer names are asserted here. Listed on NSE Emerge in 2025.
import_substitution: Aluminium monolithic formwork systems, historically imported into India from Malaysia (MFE Formwork), South Korea (Kumkang Kind) and China; a domestic designer-manufacturer displaces those imported system sets and their imported spares.
moat_note: Not regulator-conferred. The barrier is proprietary panel-system design plus the shop-drawing/BIM engineering that must be redone for every tower, and an owned rental fleet that lets it serve contractors who cannot fund a purchase. A 41% ROCE on a 33% OPM says the barrier is currently real; it is contestable by any competent extruder with design staff.
why_obscure: NSE SME board, listed only in 2025, 880 shareholders, reports interim numbers sparsely (screener carries just one interim column), and formwork sits in nobody's coverage universe - it is neither cement nor real estate.
risk_note: Demand is a pure derivative of high-rise/affordable-housing launch volume; on a ~Rs 12 cr PAT base priced at 31x, one slow launch cycle in one metro is a de-rate. The rental model also ties up capital in a fleet that is illiquid if utilisation drops, while CWIP of Rs 8 cr against a Rs 19 cr net block means capacity is being added ahead of contracted demand.
liquidity_note: NSE SME - lot-size trading, thin order book, wide spreads. Institutional holding of 12.6% combined (FII 2.63% + DII 9.97%) means a meaningful share of the float is locked, further reducing tradeable volume.
cwip_note: CWIP has gone 0 -> 2 -> 8 cr across Mar 2024/25/26 against a Rs 19 cr net block. At 42% of net block this is the heaviest relative build in this batch and points to a capacity/fleet doubling.
score_rationale: Best-scoring name here. Import substitution is named and specific (Malaysian/Korean aluminium formwork). Institutional score is high because both FII (2.63%) and DII (9.97%) sit inside the 2-15% band - unusual for an SME. Moat capped at 14 because nothing regulatory protects it despite the 41% ROCE. Promoter 59.67% sits in the sweet spot with no visible pledge. Undercovered at 880 holders. Financials 9 - ROE 42%, D/E 0.52, 58% 3Y profit CAGR - docked one point because the earnings base is only four years old.

name: Sacheerome Ltd.
business: Creates and manufactures fragrance and flavour compounds sold as an ingredient to FMCG makers - personal wash, hair oil, detergent, agarbatti, deodorant, oral care and food brands. Incorporated 2009; manufacturing and creative/evaluation labs at Noida with a large new site under construction. It is purely a B2B ingredient supplier - it owns no consumer brand of its own, the value it adds is the perfumer-created formulation plus compounding, and its 24% OPM is unusually high for an Indian ingredient house.
import_substitution: Replaces imported fragrance compounds supplied into India by Givaudan (Switzerland), Firmenich/dsm-firmenich (Switzerland), IFF (USA) and Symrise (Germany) - the four MNCs that historically controlled compound supply to Indian FMCG. Sacheerome supplies the same brief at Indian cost.
moat_note: Formulation lock-in: once a fragrance is approved into an FMCG SKU the brand will not re-open the brief because consumers recognise the scent, so revenue per approved code is annuity-like. Barrier is perfumer talent plus a captive library of accords, not capital - evidenced by a 24% OPM and 35.7% ROCE in a supposedly commoditised category.
why_obscure: NSE Emerge SME listed 2025, reports only half-yearly, 1,158 shareholders, no sell-side coverage and no earnings call. Screener does not even render its financials on the consolidated page - most screeners therefore miss it entirely.
risk_note: Customer concentration in a B2B ingredient model plus a capex bet that is 2.5x the existing asset base: CWIP of Rs 57 cr against a net block of only Rs 23 cr. If the new capacity commissions into a slower FMCG cycle, depreciation and fixed cost land on a base where FY26 PAT was only Rs 28 cr.
liquidity_note: NSE Emerge SME board - lot-size trading, thin daily traded value, and a 1,158-holder register means exit in size is not realistic; treat as a multi-year illiquid position.
cwip_note: CWIP has gone 8 -> 28 -> 57 Rs cr over Mar24/Mar25/Mar26 while net block is only Rs 23 cr - a 248% CWIP-to-net-block ratio. This is the single largest capex cycle in the name's history and nothing has yet been capitalised.
score_rationale: Highest-quality name in the sweep: 35.7% ROCE, debt-free, 68% 3Y profit CAGR, formulation-driven customer lock-in and a genuine named import-substitution story against Givaudan/Firmenich/IFF. Marked down on promoter (71.5% is above the 55-70 sweep spot, low float) and institutional (6.5% combined, DII only).

CWIP at 248% of net block; execution and absorption risk on the new plant

name: Rappid Valves (India) Ltd.
business: Incorporated 2002; manufactures industrial valve solutions — ball, gate, globe, butterfly, check, double-block-and-bleed, filter and marine valves — in ferrous and non-ferrous materials, sizes 15mm to 600mm.
import_substitution: Mid-size and large-bore industrial valves for process industries (oil & gas, marine, water) in India have long relied on imports from Italy, Germany and China for pressure/temperature-critical applications; a domestic manufacturer spanning ball/gate/globe/butterfly/marine valve types across a wide size range displaces multiple import categories at once.
moat_note: Breadth across valve types and sizes plus marine-grade certification is a meaningful barrier versus single-product valve shops, and valve businesses typically carry an aftermarket spares/replacement annuity tied to the installed base.

name: Aztec Fluids & Machinery Ltd.
business: Provider of coding and marking solutions in India; manufactures/supplies equipment for printing variable information (batch codes, expiry dates, barcodes) onto products and packaging, along with printers, consumables and spares.
import_substitution: Industrial coding-and-marking machinery (continuous inkjet, laser and thermal transfer printers used on packaging lines) in India is dominated by multinational imports/local-assembled units from Videojet, Markem-Imaje and Domino; a domestic coding-and-marking equipment and consumables supplier substitutes imported machines and, more importantly, the recurring imported-ink/consumables annuity for FMCG and pharma packaging lines.
moat_note: Coding/marking is a classic razor-and-blade business — the installed printer base drives a recurring consumables (ink, solvent, ribbon) revenue stream — and regulatory-grade traceability requirements (pharma serialization) raise switching costs once a line is qualified on a given system.
why_obscure: Sub-Rs 150cr niche coding/marking equipment maker misclassified even on data platforms (listed under 'Computer Hardware' industry rather than machinery), with only 738 shareholders and zero analyst coverage.
risk_note: Misclassified industry tagging suggests the company is unlikely to appear in most sector-based investor screens, which explains part of its obscurity but also means less scrutiny of disclosures; debt-to-equity not disclosed.

name: Jay Bee Laminations Ltd.

import_substitution: India has no meaningful domestic CRGO steel-melting capacity, so the raw electrical steel itself stays imported (Japan/Korea/China/Russia) — but Jay Bee's precision core-cutting/lamination-assembly plant substitutes the FINISHED, ready-to-wind transformer cores that many small and mid-sized transformer makers used to import directly from China/Korea
moat_note: Precision slitting/cutting tolerances and burr-free lamination quality needed to hit transformer core-loss specs; long-standing approved-supplier relationships with transformer OEMs
why_obscure: Sub-Rs200cr niche CRGO lamination converter with no sell-side coverage, easily overlooked next to large transformer OEMs
risk_note: Thin 6% OPM signals commodity-like margins and direct exposure to CRGO steel import price/currency swings it cannot fully pass through
penalty_detail: only 2,491 shareholders - severe illiquidity (-5)

name: Kothari Petrochemicals
business: Single-product maker of polyisobutylene (PIB), with capacity raised to 48,000 MTPA. The plant sits at Manali, Chennai, taking C4/isobutylene feedstock by pipeline from the adjacent CPCL refinery and from RIL. PIB grades are specified into lubricant-additive, adhesive and paint formulations. Exports 26.9%; PAT rose every year from Rs 33 cr to Rs 72 cr.
moat_note: Verified by ICRA (2025): 'the largest manufacturer of poly iso-butylene (PIB) in the country,' capacity raised to 48,000 MTPA. 'Independent, current, and from a credit analyst — the strongest attribution in the chemicals half of this screen. Note it says largest, not sole, and no percentage is given.' The real moat is location: a new entrant needs both refinery-adjacent feedstock access (pipeline C4/isobutylene from CPCL and RIL) and a licence. Requalification is slow because PIB grades are specified into lubricant-additive, adhesive and paint formulations. No certification stack is cited — the FY25 annual report is notably thin.
pricing_power_note: Pricing power — strong on the record. OPM 13% to 12% to 16% to 14% to 16% (FY22-FY26). 'Margins expanded through the 2022-23 crude spike, which is the test.' PAT rose every single year: Rs 33 to 39 to 64 to 66 to 72 cr.
import_substitution: Not framed as import substitution: ICRA calls Kothari the largest PIB manufacturer in the country, 'largest, not sole', with no percentage given. The domestic barrier described is refinery-adjacent feedstock access plus a licence, not replacement of imports.
why_obscure: Yes — 'Why the market isn't paying up. 11x for 28.6% ROCE usually means doubt. Here the doubt is feedstock durability and the HR-PIB question. The FY25 annual report is notably thin — no capacity, no market share, no customers, no export geographies — so ICRA is doing all the verification work.' Zero FII and 0.10% DII, so no institutional footprint.
risk_note: The HR-PIB question combined with total concentration: the FY25 annual report contains no mention of a highly-reactive PIB programme while global lubricant-additive demand migrates to HR-PIB, so if Kothari is conventional-PIB-only it is on the wrong side of a product shift — in a business that is single product, single plant, single city with no diversification whatsoever.
v3_gates: Passes as Tier 2. Rs 794 cr, 39,301 holders (under the 40,000 Tier 2 limit, but by only 699), promoter 72.22%, ROCE 28.6%, ROE 21.4%, institutional 0.10% so no Tier 1 footprint.

name: Munish Forge Ltd.
business: 40+ year forging and casting manufacturer supplying forged and cast components to Defence, Oil & Gas, Automobile, Construction and Infrastructure customers, recently expanding into Railways.
import_substitution: Forged components for defence and oil & gas end-uses in India have historically drawn on imported forgings for critical-grade alloy parts; domestic forge shops with defence/oil-gas qualification displace such imports as indigenisation programs (Make in India defence sourcing) expand.
moat_note: Multi-decade forging know-how and existing qualification across defence and oil & gas customers (both demanding rigorous vendor approval processes) is a real barrier to new entrants, though the forging business itself is capital- rather than IP-intensive.
why_obscure: Micro-cap forge shop (527 shareholders) with no coverage, easily confused with and dwarfed by listed forging majors like Ramkrishna Forgings, Bharat Forge and MM Forgings.

name: Euro Panel Products Ltd.
business: Mumbai-based manufacturer of Aluminium Composite Panels (ACP) under the 'Eurobond' brand, including standard and fire-retardant (FR) core ACP for building facades, cladding and signage; ranked among the top handful of organised Indian ACP producers, with export reach as well.
import_substitution: Aluminium composite panels — especially fire-retardant/FR-core and A2-fire-rated grades now mandated by tightening fire-safety codes post high-rise fire incidents — were long dominated by Chinese and Middle-Eastern imports (cheap PE-core and even mis-labelled FR panels). Euro Panel/Eurobond is one of a small set of domestic manufacturers building genuine FR-core capacity, directly displacing imported ACP rolls/panels for Indian facade contractors who need certified, code-compliant material with shorter lead times than importing from China.
moat_note: Barrier is a mix of capital intensity (continuous lamination/coil-coating lines) and code-compliance/testing certification (fire rating, weatherability) that Chinese imports increasingly struggle to match post-regulation; brand recognition among facade contractors (Eurobond name) adds a modest distribution moat.
why_obscure: A sub-Rs 500 cr market cap building-materials name with no sell-side coverage; usually overshadowed in investor attention by paints/tiles majors, despite EUROBOND being a recognised brand within the facade-contractor trade.
risk_note: Aluminium/PE-resin input cost volatility; cyclicality tied to commercial real-estate and infra construction activity; competitive intensity from both larger domestic groups (e.g. Alstone, Viva) and residual grey-market Chinese imports on the non-FR commodity end.
penalty_detail: very thin shareholder base (-2)
cwip_note: Big capex cycle already capitalised — CWIP peaked at ₹32cr in Mar 2024 then dropped to nil as net block jumped ₹32cr → ₹80cr; only ₹3cr fresh CWIP now.
data_note: Jun 2026 PAT fell ~16% YoY after a record Mar 2026 quarter. Q1FY27 revenue ₹119.8cr (+14% YoY) but no guidance given.

name: Menon Bearings Ltd.
business: Kolhapur-based manufacturer of critical engine components — bimetal bearings, bushes and thrust washers for high-stress heavy-duty diesel engines — operating across Bimetal, Alkop (aluminium die-casting) and Braking Systems segments, marketed as one of India's largest engine-bearing companies.
import_substitution: Precision engine bearings/bushes for heavy-duty diesel applications were historically an import-heavy category dominated by global bearing majors (Federal-Mogul/Tenneco, MAHLE); Menon markets itself as India's largest engine-bearings company, supplying domestic and export OEMs and displacing imported bimetal bearings for diesel engine manufacturers.
moat_note: Bimetal-bearing metallurgy and precision-tolerance machining for engine applications require long OEM-qualification cycles; scale as India's largest listed player in the category gives cost and relationship advantages.
why_obscure: No FII/DII holding despite being a scale leader in its niche; auto-ancillary bearings segment gets overshadowed by larger listed peers (NRB Bearings, Timken).
risk_note: 3-year sales and profit growth are both flat (0%), signalling stagnation despite strong current-year ROCE/ROE; richly valued at 38x P/E for a no-growth business.
penalty_detail: no FII/DII on the register yet (-3)

name: SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd.
business: Hyderabad-based bulk-drug maker built originally on ranitidine, where it was among the world's largest producers, and since rebuilt around anti-platelet, anti-ulcer and CNS APIs plus a growing contract-development book run through subsidiary VKT Pharma. Operates multiple USFDA-inspected API units in and around Bachupally and Kandivalasa, Andhra Pradesh/Telangana. Customers are regulated-market generic formulators; the CDMO arm serves innovator and mid-size pharma clients under confidentiality.

moat_note: USFDA-inspected plants with a stack of US DMFs and EU filings per molecule — a customer who has validated an SMS DMF into an approved ANDA cannot switch source without a prior-approval supplement, which is the actual lock-in.

name: Shree Refrigerations Ltd.
business: Karad (Maharashtra) manufacturer of marine-grade and defence HVAC, chilling plants, AC plants and refrigeration systems, supplying the Indian Navy, defence PSUs and shipyards for warships and submarines. FY26 standalone revenue was ₹153.6cr (up ~55% YoY) with ₹21.4cr PAT; the closing unexecuted order book at 31 Mar 2026 was ₹270.8cr, about 1.8x revenue. The company inaugurated a new defence and marine HVAC&R plant at Karad during FY26 and is entering data-centre cooling with a reference installation in FY27. IPO of ₹95cr fresh issue completed in FY26.
import_substitution: Marine-grade chillers, AC plants and refrigeration units for warships and submarines were historically imported from European marine HVAC&R OEMs (German, Italian and French naval suppliers) or supplied through foreign shipbuilding packages. Shree now builds these to Navy specification in India under the indigenisation mandate, and each unit requires design approval and type testing by the Navy before it can go on a platform — a genuine substitution of an imported, sanction-exposed subsystem.
moat_note: Naval design approval and type testing is the barrier: management said H1FY26 revenue was muted precisely because it spent the half doing design approvals and type testing on new orders. Once a chiller or AC plant type is approved for a warship class, it carries through the class and into decades of spares and AMC — spares and services were 30% of revenue in FY25. A new entrant faces a multi-year, non-purchasable approval cycle. ROCE of only 13.5% caps the score, reflecting a still-brutal 370-day working capital cycle.
why_obscure: Listed only in FY26 with a ₹95cr IPO, 4,461 shareholders, no sell-side broker coverage, and no NSE line — a BSE-only ticker that most screens never surface. FII holding is a rounding error at 0.12%.
risk_note: Working capital is the business risk: the cycle is still 370 days after improving from 570, against ₹153cr of revenue — a 40% CAGR guidance means funding a growing receivable book, and the ₹95cr IPO cash is the only buffer. Management also conceded that 'unprecedented commodity price rise' will hit EBITDA margins; EBITDA margin already fell from 27.3% (FY25) to 21.4% (FY26).
liquidity_note: BSE-only listing with roughly 4,461 shareholders and a ~1-year trading history — free float is small and traded value is thin for a ₹1,318cr market cap; no NSE line means no index or NSE-only institutional flow.

name: Admach Systems Ltd.
business: Customised machine builder for the Indian and global engineering industry; designs, manufactures and supplies Special Purpose Machines (SPMs), automation systems, assembly and packaging machines, robotic material-handling systems, and non-destructive testing (NDT) equipment.

name: Bharat Rasayan Ltd.
business: Manufactures agrochemical technicals — synthetic pyrethroids such as lambda-cyhalothrin, cypermethrin and bifenthrin, plus organophosphates — and is backward integrated into the key intermediate meta-phenoxy benzaldehyde (MPBD). Plants are at Dahej in Gujarat and Rohtak in Haryana. It sells technical-grade actives business-to-business to multinational and domestic formulators rather than to farmers, so it carries none of the channel-stuffing risk of branded agrochem peers. Effectively debt-free with D/E of 0.001.
import_substitution: Substitutes Chinese-origin pyrethroid technicals — lambda-cyhalothrin, bifenthrin, cypermethrin — and, more importantly, the upstream intermediate meta-phenoxy benzaldehyde (MPBD), which India otherwise imports almost entirely from China. Backward integration into MPBD is the specific import-substitution asset here.
moat_note: CIB&RC technical registrations per molecule (multi-year, data-intensive to obtain) combined with in-house MPBD capacity that few Indian pyrethroid makers hold — this is a cost moat layered on a regulatory one, though it is contestable as Chinese capacity restarts.
why_obscure: Delisted from analyst attention after years of flat topline; 74.99% promoter holding leaves a 22% float, no earnings calls, and the market reads it as an ex-growth agrochem supplier rather than an intermediates play.
risk_note: Chinese pyrethroid price deflation — three years of 0% sales growth is the direct evidence that pricing power in these actives has already gone, and a further leg down compresses the 16% OPM fast.
liquidity_note: Mainboard, but a Rs 1,278 price on a 22.6% float makes it genuinely illiquid; expect single-digit-crore daily turnover and wide spreads on size.
cwip_note: CWIP has tripled across three years — Rs 6 cr, Rs 15 cr, Rs 46 cr — reaching ~19% of net block, the first meaningful capex the company has run in years and funded entirely from internal accrual.
score_rationale: Named-molecule import substitution (MPBD, lambda-cyhalothrin vs China) plus 17.4% ROCE on a debt-free balance sheet and a tripling CWIP earn a solid mid-60s score. Capped on moat because agrochem technicals are contestable and the 0% 3Y sales growth proves it, and promoter scores below peak because 74.99% is above the 55-70% sweet spot and leaves too little float.
