name: Schneider Electric President Systems Ltd.
industry: Industrial Machinery / Data-centre & IT Enclosure Systems
business: Thirty-year-old designer and manufacturer of standard and customised 19-inch enclosure systems - server racks, network cabinets, card frames, components and accessories - for IT/networking, ITES, telecom, general and industrial electronics customers, plus trading of electrical equipment. Now majority-owned (74.12%) by Schneider Electric, which plugs the product into the APC/Schneider secure-power and data-centre channel. Sells through a nationwide distribution, installation and service network. FY26 revenue was roughly Rs 390 cr across the four quarters with 13% operating margin.
import_substitution: Solid and named: 19-inch data-centre server racks and network enclosures were historically imported into India as finished cabinets from Rittal (Germany) and from Chinese cabinet OEMs. SEPSL fabricates these domestically at Indian plants and supplies them into the same hyperscale, colocation and telecom projects, with Schneider's global specification behind them.
moat_note: The barrier is qualification rather than licensing: data-centre racks must pass seismic, EIA-310/IEC dimensional, thermal-containment and load certifications before a colocation operator will spec them, and once a data-centre estate is standardised on a rack platform the whole hot/cold-aisle containment, PDU and cable-management ecosystem is locked to it - re-specifying mid-build is not done. Schneider's 74% ownership converts that into channel access no independent Indian fabricator has. 23.9% ROCE on a genuine Rs 33 cr manufacturing asset base, not an accounting artefact.
why_obscure: BSE-only line with just 2,141 registered shareholders and effectively zero institutional ownership (DII 0.25%, FII nil). It carries an industrial-machinery sector tag rather than a data-centre one, so it does not surface in AI/data-centre screens, and there is no analyst coverage - a targeted document search returned no company filings, presentations or calls at all.
risk_note: Quarterly PAT has halved from the Rs 15.84 cr peak (Mar 2025) to Rs 4.47 cr (Jun 2026) - four consecutive quarters of deterioration - while the stock still trades at 71x earnings; a Rs 2,465 cr valuation on trailing PAT of roughly Rs 34 cr assumes a data-centre-order recovery that the P&L is not showing. Underneath that, 3Y sales CAGR is only 5%: the 32% profit CAGR came from margin expansion, not volume, and sheet-steel and copper input costs are the direct swing factor on a fabrication business with 13% operating margins.
liquidity_note: BSE mainboard but with only 2,141 shareholders and a 25.6% free float on a Rs 2,465 cr cap, the tradeable value is small and the register is closely held post the Schneider transaction. Daily turnover is thin for the market cap; expect wide spreads.
cwip_note: CWIP Rs 1 cr (Mar 2024), Rs 2 cr (Mar 2025), Rs 3 cr (Mar 2026) against a Rs 33 cr net block - a steady, modest 9% of net block. Consistent maintenance-plus-debottlenecking capex, not a step-change expansion; there is no evidence here of a capacity build ahead of the Indian data-centre cycle.

Import-sub 14/20: a named imported product (19-inch data-centre server racks) with named origins (Rittal, Germany; Chinese cabinet OEMs) - held just under 15 because a meaningful share of enclosure content and all the active power/cooling kit is still imported, and the company also trades bought-in electrical equipment. Institutional 3/15: DII 0.25%, FII nil - effectively no institutions. Undercovered 13/15: 2,141 holders and zero coverage, but an MNC parent means it is not truly unknown. Financials 8/10: ROE 17.7%, essentially debt-free (Rs 1 cr borrowings vs Rs 238 cr equity), 32% 3Y profit CAGR, but only 5% sales CAGR and four quarters of falling PAT.

name: Premier Polyfilm Ltd.
industry: PVC sheeting, vinyl flooring and artificial leather cloth
business: Incorporated 1992, manufactures flexible PVC flooring film and sheets, PVC sheeting and artificial leather cloth by the calendering route, with in-house coating, printing, lamination and embossing. Its own quarterly filing states it operates a single business segment - manufacture and sale of flexible PVC flooring film and sheets - so the artificial-leather-cloth line rides the same calender assets. ISO 9001:2015 certified. FY26 revenue about Rs 341 cr with 16% operating margin, 30.8% ROCE and effectively no net debt (Rs 136.6 cr reserves at Jun 2026 against a Rs 10.6 cr paid-up capital). Q1 FY27 total income Rs 100.7 cr, PAT Rs 9.08 cr.
import_substitution: Flexible PVC flooring and artificial leather cloth compete directly against Chinese calendered PVC flooring and leather cloth, which dominates the low and mid segments of the Indian market and the export channels Premier serves. This is a genuine but generic substitution - the imported product and origin are identifiable, but there is no protected specification, quota or standard behind it.
moat_note: Modest and hard to locate on paper. What exists is a fully integrated calendering line (calender plus coating plus printing plus lamination plus embossing under one roof, which most Indian PVC sheeting units do not have), an ISO 9001:2015 quality system, and a long-standing export distribution network. There is no OEM panel, no technical approval, no BIS mandate. The 30.8% ROCE is the strongest single financial number in this sweep and is not explained by any disclosed barrier - most likely a very low asset base (Rs 60 cr net block on Rs 341 cr revenue) doing the work rather than pricing power.
why_obscure: Classified under plastics/furnishing rather than textiles, so it is missed by both screens. No earnings call, no investor presentation - a document search returned only its bare quarterly results filing. Its 23,612 shareholders are almost entirely retail with no institution above 1.02%, and the sub-Rs 100 share price attracts the kind of holder who does not generate research demand.
risk_note: The valuation now embeds the peak of a margin cycle. Sales have grown only 6% CAGR over three years while profit grew 40% - the entire story is margin, and PVC calendering margin is a resin-and-plasticiser spread that mean-reverts. At a 27.4x P/E - roughly double the multiple of every other name in this batch - a return to the 10-11% operating margin of the FY22-FY23 period would cut PAT by a third and leave the stock on 40x. Cardiac capacity was expanded 25 to 45 beds and a Philips Azurion cath lab was commissioned in March 2026; a GE Healthcare dual-detector SPECT gamma camera was installed for nuclear medicine.
import_substitution: None - domestic services play. Asarfi is a buyer of imported medical capital equipment (Philips Azurion cath lab, GE Healthcare SPECT gamma camera), the opposite of an import substituter.
moat_note: Regional scarcity plus catchment lock-in rather than a licence. Being one of only three dedicated cancer hospitals in the state of Jharkhand means radiation-oncology patients from ten neighbouring districts have no local alternative; oncology also requires AERB licensing for radiation equipment and a nuclear-medicine authorisation, which are real regulatory gates. Cancer-unit ARPOB of Rs 37,428 versus Rs 23,020 for the general unit shows the oncology franchise carries the pricing. Weakness: everything sits in one district, and a competing chain entering Dhanbad would contest it directly.
why_obscure: BSE SME with 1,399 shareholders and zero FII holding. It voluntarily reports quarterly despite SME rules requiring only half-yearly, but the concalls are hosted by a small broker (Hem Securities) and attended largely by individual investors, so there is no institutional research trail. Eastern-India single-district hospitals are outside the coverage map of every healthcare analyst who follows Apollo/Max/Medanta.
risk_note: The FY27 revenue target of Rs 260 cr requires +50% on FY26's Rs 173.5 cr and depends on the cancer unit going from 65 to 150 beds by end-FY27 plus a bone-marrow-transplant unit - and the cancer unit is only at 42% occupancy today. Adding 85 beds into a unit already less than half full is the classic hospital gestation trap: depreciation and staffing land immediately while occupancy ramps over years. If occupancy stays near 42%, FY27 EBITDA margin goes the wrong way rather than to the guided 22-25%.
liquidity_note: BSE SME, Rs 438 cr cap, 35.87% public float (roughly Rs 157 cr) across just 1,399 holders. Better float percentage than the other SME names here but still SME-lot trading with episodic volume clustered around results and the concall. Institutional participation is 2.97% DII and nil FII.
cwip_note: CWIP is negligible at Rs 2 cr against Rs 108 cr net block (Rs 0 cr in Mar 2024, Rs 2 cr in Mar 2025 and Mar 2026) - the Rs 260 cr FY27 revenue target and the 65-to-150 cancer-bed expansion are NOT yet showing up as capital work in progress on the balance sheet. Management stated the expansion is planned from internal accruals with no debt decision taken. That gap between a +50% revenue target and near-zero CWIP is the single most important thing to monitor at the Sep 2026 result.
guidance_quote: Q (Gaurav Sanghvi): 'what could be a top-line target for FY27 as you have mentioned it will be INR 260 crores. So, are you confident to achieving that top-line amount?' A (Harendra Singh, CFO): 'Yes, sir; we are working hard and we should be able to achieve it.' On margins: 'we are trying to [manage] case mix and margins in such a way that EBITDA achieves 23% to 25%. This year we have achieved 20% EBITDA. We definitely would like to push it to at least 22% next year.' Vision 2028 roadmap: 500+ beds, ~Rs 400 cr revenue, 23-25% EBITDA margin.

Moat 17 - one of only three dedicated cancer hospitals in Jharkhand with AERB-licensed radiation and nuclear-medicine capability is close to regulator-conferred, but a single district and only 42% oncology occupancy keep it under 20. Import-sub 2, correctly near zero. Promoter 14 is the highest in the batch: 61.17% sits squarely in the 55-70% peak band, unchanged YoY, no disclosed pledge. Institutional only 6 (nil FII, 2.97% DII). Undercovered 14 on 1,399 holders with only broker-hosted retail calls. name: Veljan Denison Limited
business: Hyderabad fluid-power manufacturer making hydraulic pumps, motors, valves and custom-built power packs and manifold blocks, from plants in and around Hyderabad. The company states its solution expertise covers shipbuilding, energy, mobile and industrial segments. It began in 1974 as a collaboration with the Denison division (USA), passed through Sweden's Hägglunds ownership, became independent in 1994 and was renamed Veljan Denison in 2010; the wider Veljan group traces to Veljan Hydrair, founded 1965.
import_substitution: Domestically manufactures Denison-lineage hydraulic pumps, motors and valves that would otherwise be sourced from Bosch Rexroth (Germany), Parker/Denison (USA) or Eaton — a genuine displacement of imported fluid-power hardware, but I could not confirm a single named part number or a stated origin country from company sources.
moat_note: Inherited Denison pump and motor designs give it drop-in interchangeability with an installed base of legacy Denison-fitted equipment, which is a real switching-cost barrier for spares and refits. Beyond that installed base it competes head-on with Rexroth and Parker on new builds, so the barrier is genuine but contestable — reflected in a 14.9% ROCE rather than a 25%+ one.
why_obscure: BSE-dominant line with only 25.02% float and 4,549 shareholders, effectively zero institutional holding (FII and DII 0.01% each), no earnings calls, and an industry tag of 'Auto Parts & Equipment' that buries it beneath the auto-ancillary universe. The Denison name reads as a foreign MNC subsidiary, so domestic screens skip it.
risk_note: Promoter holding at 74.98% sits a whisker under the 75% maximum permitted — the company has no headroom to raise equity without the promoter's stake falling, so any capacity expansion must be debt- or cash-funded, and the sub-2bps of institutional interest means there is no natural buyer if the promoter ever needed to sell down.
liquidity_note: BSE line with 25.02% public float, 4,549 shareholders and no institutional participation. At a ₹1,300 share price this trades in tiny volumes; realistic exit is measured in weeks and the quoted price is not a clearing price for size.
cwip_note: CWIP has run down from ₹15 cr to ₹3 cr to ₹2 cr across the three years screener returned — the capex cycle here is finished, not starting.
score_rationale: Genuinely under-followed — 4,549 shareholders and effectively zero institutions — with a defensible Denison installed-base position in fluid power and shipbuilding named as a served segment. Capped by contestable economics: 14.9% ROCE and 10.8% ROE against Rexroth and Parker, flat 11% 3Y sales growth, and a quarterly profit line that has gone sideways at ₹5–7 cr for eight straight quarters.

name: NILE Ltd.
business: Hyderabad-based producer of refined lead and specialty lead alloys made from recycled lead-acid battery scrap, supplying the Indian battery industry. Operates licensed hazardous-waste smelting and refining capacity and has been diversifying into lithium-ion battery packs through a subsidiary (the FY26 consolidated accounts now carry a non-controlling interest, indicating the new venture is separately held). Named customers were not disclosed in the sources reviewed.
import_substitution: Replaces imported refined lead and lead alloys — India is structurally short of primary lead and historically imports refined lead ingots and alloy grades; domestic secondary refining substitutes those tonnes. No single origin country is named in the sources reviewed.
moat_note: Licence-gated: secondary lead smelting requires CPCB/state pollution-control registration under the Hazardous Waste and Battery Waste Management Rules, and the tightening Battery Waste Management/EPR regime is actively squeezing unregistered informal smelters out — a regulator-conferred advantage that shows up as 25.3% ROCE on a 7% OPM commodity conversion business.
why_obscure: A 10,700-name register, no broker coverage found, and a lead-recycling label that reads as commodity metals rather than the energy-transition materials play it is becoming.
risk_note: Lead price and spread volatility — a 7% OPM conversion business has almost no buffer, and the entire ROCE advantage evaporates if LME lead moves against the scrap-purchase cycle.
liquidity_note: Mainboard, ~10,700 shareholders and a ₹1,569 share price on a ₹471 cr market cap — thinly traded, but genuinely more accessible than the SME names here.

Promoter 50.39% is only just above the gate and public float 49.16% is the widest here — 10/15. Institutional 4/15: FII+DII combined 0.43%, effectively zero. Financials 9/10 — near debt-free, 35% 3Y profit CAGR, 9.7x P/E.

name: EPW India Ltd.
business: IT electronics refurbisher running an end-to-end reverse supply chain: sources used laptops, desktops, Chromebooks, monitors and peripherals, refurbishes them in-house through a 15-20 day test-repair-clean-reimage cycle, and resells through B2B channels and direct-to-consumer via company-owned retail stores and its own website. Operates a single 4,500 sq ft refurbishment facility with 32 technicians. Founded by Mohd. Fasi Uddin, Mohd. Zaki Uddin and Yousuf Uddin; listed on NSE SME on 30 December 2025 at Rs 97 per share. Revenue scaled Rs 19 cr (FY24) to Rs 53 cr (FY25) to Rs 107 cr (FY26); FY25 mix was roughly 54% consumer, 45% business.
import_substitution: Generic rather than named: every refurbished laptop sold displaces a new imported unit (India imports essentially all finished notebooks, predominantly from China under the IT hardware import-authorisation regime). But the company substitutes no specific product line from a specific supplier - it extends the life of already-imported devices rather than manufacturing a replacement.
moat_note: Weak. The only formal requirement is CPCB/SPCB authorisation as a refurbisher-dismantler under the E-Waste Rules, which is inexpensive and widely held. Real differentiation would have to come from sourcing access to corporate off-lease fleets and from warranty/brand trust in the D2C channel, neither of which EPW has demonstrated at scale. Larger, better-capitalised competitors (GNG Electronics/Electronics Bazaar, Newjaisa) are chasing the same supply.
why_obscure: Listed on NSE SME only eight months ago with 421 registered shareholders. Half-yearly reporting means three disclosure points exist in total, there is no concall, and a targeted document search returned no EPW filings at all.
risk_note: State it plainly: the 44.5% ROCE is an artefact of a Rs 3 cr fixed-asset base - the entire operation is one 4,500 sq ft room with 32 technicians turning Rs 107 cr of revenue, so the return ratios measure working-capital velocity, not a defended franchise, and they will compress the moment the company adds capacity. The concrete danger is inventory and sourcing: revenue doubled twice in two years (Rs 19 cr to Rs 53 cr to Rs 107 cr) on a business whose input is scarce, price-volatile second-hand hardware, and Rs 10 cr of borrowings now sit against Rs 43 cr of net worth funding that stock. A single mis-timed bulk purchase of off-lease inventory at the wrong price, or an OEM price cut on new laptops, writes down the entire float.
liquidity_note: NSE SME with 421 shareholders and eight months of trading history. Lot-size dealing, negligible daily value, and the 8.9% combined FII+DII line is anchor-investor stock from the December 2025 IPO that is only just out of lock-in. Expect no exit liquidity.
cwip_note: CWIP nil across Mar 2024, Mar 2025 and Mar 2026; fixed assets went Rs 0 cr / Rs 0 cr / Rs 3 cr. There is no capex programme - growth to date has been funded entirely into working capital, which is the opposite of the heavy-CWIP profile and is itself the risk.

name: Creative Graphics Solutions India Ltd.
business: Incorporated 2014; makes digital and conventional flexographic printing plates, letterpress plates, metal-back plates and coating plates — the imaged photopolymer plates that flexible-packaging and label converters mount on press. Seven plants: Noida, Vasai (Mumbai), Chennai, Baddi (HP), Hyderabad, Ahmedabad and Pune. Runs DuPont, Kodak and Esko imaging equipment imported from Germany and Canada, with long-term supply agreements with Performance Specialty Products (DuPont group), Miraclon India and Cookson India. Named customers include ITC, Tata Consumer, Mars, CavinKare, Haldiram, Dabur India, KRBL, Himalaya and Hamdard. Exports to Africa, Thailand, Qatar, Kuwait and Nepal.
import_substitution: None — domestic demand play. The photopolymer plate raw material and the imaging hardware are themselves imported (DuPont/Kodak/Esko); the company localises the plate-making service, not the input.
moat_note: Barrier is brand-owner artwork governance, not technology: a plate carries an FMCG's approved colour standard and SKU artwork, so plates for ITC or Dabur are re-qualified against a signed-off colour target and cannot be swapped supplier mid-SKU without re-approval. Seven regional sites give same-day turnaround that a single-site rival cannot match on a repeat-order business. It remains a service converting business at 10% OPM, so this is a real but contestable moat.
why_obscure: NSE Emerge SME with 1,847 shareholders, half-yearly reporting, and no listed pure-play comparable in India — the company itself notes no other listed Indian company offers exclusively flexographic plates, so it sits in no screener peer set and gets no sell-side coverage.
risk_note: Margin and earnings are already rolling over: H2 FY26 PAT fell to Rs 7 cr from Rs 12 cr in each of the prior two half-years, and OPM is down to 10%. This is on Rs 95 cr of borrowings against Rs 125 cr of equity (D/E 0.76) for a business with only Rs 76 cr of net block — leverage is funding working capital and acquisitions rather than plant.
liquidity_note: NSE Emerge SME, lot-size trading, 1,847 shareholders. Rs 336 cr market cap is large for the Emerge board but traded value is thin and there is no institutional bid beyond 1.07% DII.
cwip_note: Zero CWIP in each of Mar 2024, Mar 2025 and Mar 2026 — the seven-site network was built by acquisition and equipment purchase rather than greenfield construction, so no capex signal here.
score_rationale: The only listed Indian pure-play in flexo plates, with a verifiable blue-chip FMCG customer list (ITC, Tata Consumer, Mars, Dabur), 57%/30% three-year growth and 1,847 shareholders — a genuinely under-followed franchise. Scored down on the most recent half, where PAT halved and OPM compressed to 10% while D/E sits at 0.76 on a business with no capex to show for the debt.

name: Pyramid Technoplast Ltd.
business: Incorporated 1997; pan-India industrial packaging company making HM-HDPE polymer drums, barrels, jerry cans and IBC (intermediate bulk) containers, plus MS drums, for chemical, agrochemical, specialty chemical and pharmaceutical customers. FY26 revenue Rs 681 cr against Rs 591 cr in FY25 and Rs 532 cr in FY24. Plants are sited next to customer chemical clusters; specific plant list and customer names are not asserted here as they were not confirmed in this pass.
import_substitution: None — domestic demand play. Empty drums and IBCs are almost never imported because the freight economics of shipping air make it uncompetitive.
moat_note: The real barrier is UN certification for hazardous-goods packaging plus per-customer, per-chemical compatibility approval — a drum qualified for a specific agrochemical at a specific plant is not casually re-sourced. Layered on that is a geographic moat: drums are freight-uneconomic beyond roughly a 300 km radius, so proximity to Bharuch/Dahej-type chemical clusters is the franchise. But at 8% OPM and 12.3% ROCE, pricing power is clearly limited.
why_obscure: IPO'd only in August 2023 into a sector the market codes as commodity plastic converting; 25,684 shareholders but almost no sell-side following, and the small-format investor calls (via a boutique IR firm) are not widely transcribed.
risk_note: ROCE of 12.3% only just clears the screen and OPM has compressed to 8%, while borrowings ran up to Rs 184 cr against Rs 277 cr of net worth after a debt-funded capex cycle (CWIP peaked at Rs 45 cr in FY25). name: Eco Recycling Ltd.
business: India's first e-waste recycler (operating since 2005, listed on BSE), running an end-to-end service chain of reverse logistics, certified data destruction, IT Asset Disposition (ITAD), e-waste and lamp recycling, precious-metal and critical-mineral recovery, and EPR/CSR implementation via its 'Recycling on Wheels' mobile units. Installed capacity is 31,200 MTPA of e-waste plus 6,000 MTPA of lithium-ion battery recycling; the company reports 45,000+ tonnes recycled and 500+ clients spanning MNCs, PSUs, NBFCs, banks and government bodies, with recycling technology sourced from the US, Europe and Japan. FY26 consolidated revenue was Rs 48.2 cr with PAT of Rs 22.9 cr.
import_substitution: Partial and generic: precious-metal and critical-mineral recovery from scrap displaces some imported refined metal input, but no single named imported product or origin country is substituted.
moat_note: The barrier is regulator-conferred: CPCB/State Pollution Control Board authorisation as a registered e-waste recycler under the E-Waste (Management) Rules, which is slow to obtain and site-specific, combined with the EPR credit regime that forces producers to route waste through authorised recyclers. Certified data-destruction (NAID-style) credentials create genuine switching costs with BFSI and MNC clients who cannot risk a data leak. 30% ROCE against that licensed position is the right kind of evidence.
why_obscure: BSE-only listing (no NSE line), no sell-side coverage, and a Rs 48 cr revenue base that is too small for institutional mandates - FII plus DII together hold 0.44%. The narrative is also easy to confuse with the several newer e-waste SME IPOs.
risk_note: Revenue is only Rs 48 cr against a Rs 896 cr market cap - 37x earnings on a business whose quarterly revenue swung from Rs 5.9 cr (Dec 2025) to Rs 18.6 cr (Mar 2026), a 3x range inside two quarters. That lumpiness is because a large share of income is EPR/credit and one-off ITAD contracts rather than steady tonnage, so a single delayed corporate contract can halve a quarter. The 60% OPM is unusually high for physical recycling and depends on scrap-to-metal spreads the company does not control.
liquidity_note: BSE mainboard but thin - the 37,205 shareholder base is largely retail and daily traded value is modest. Better than the SME names here, but this is not a stock you can move size in.

name: S P Apparels Ltd.
business: Founded 1989 and headquartered near Tirupur, Tamil Nadu, S P Apparels is a vertically integrated manufacturer and exporter of knitted garments for infants and children - it runs spinning, knitting, processing, printing, embroidery and garmenting in-house, which is unusual in Tirupur where most exporters are cut-and-sew only. Structure is three arms: the core garmenting division including the Young Brand acquisition and a Sri Lankan facility, the SPUK retail/sourcing arm in the UK, and a domestic Retail Ventures business. Management's FY27 revenue split guidance is Rs 1,800 cr garmenting, Rs 150 cr SPUK and Rs 80-90 cr Retail Ventures. Long-standing UK and European retail customers on multi-year vendor panels; the stated path to Rs 2,500 cr revenue runs through filling out to 9,000-10,000 machines.
import_substitution: None - domestic demand play is also the wrong label. This is an export manufacturer, so there is no imported product being replaced in India. Its competitive frame is other supplying countries: management explicitly frames the opportunity as competing against duty-free Bangladesh and Sri Lanka while India pays duty, offset by rupee depreciation. Scored at the floor accordingly.
moat_note: Brand vendor-panel qualification is the only barrier and it is a real one: infantwear and childrenswear carry the strictest chemical, mechanical-safety (drawstrings, small parts) and social-compliance audit regimes in apparel, and a vendor is onboarded over 18-24 months and audited continuously. Vertical integration from yarn to garment gives traceability that GOTS/organic-cotton programmes require, which single-process Tirupur units cannot offer. But Tirupur has hundreds of exporters and several are also panel-qualified - this is contestable, and 14.0% ROCE on 13% operating margin says so.
why_obscure: It is the least obscure name here and is scored down for it - the company runs regular earnings calls with buy-side participation (Equitree Capital, Eco Quantum, Trinetra), DIIs hold 16.15%, and it has 17,353 shareholders. It stays a second-tier name mainly because Indian apparel exporters are structurally out of favour and because the SPUK and Retail Ventures arms muddy the multiple.
risk_note: Management is guiding to Rs 2,000 cr of FY27 consolidated revenue at 14% EBITDA margin - roughly 25% growth - and the two levers cited on the call are rupee depreciation and India's duty disadvantage narrowing versus Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. Both are exogenous. Quarterly PAT has already been erratic (Rs 35 cr in Sep 2025 down to Rs 19 cr in Mar 2026) and Q1 FY27 at Rs 25 cr is not tracking a 25% year. If the rupee strengthens or an EU/UK duty realignment favours Bangladesh again, the guidance misses on a 22.8x P/E with D/E at 0.45. name: Sattva Engineering Construction Ltd.
business: Chennai-based ISO-certified EPC contractor established 2005, specialising in water infrastructure for the Government of Tamil Nadu and its urban local bodies. Scope covers water supply schemes (underground and overhead tanks, distribution networks), underground sewerage systems, sewage treatment plants, water treatment plants, and electromechanical plus SCADA works, frequently bundled with multi-year operations and maintenance. Also does industrial and residential construction. FY26 sales Rs 143 cr. Individual ULB clients are not named on the screener page and are not asserted here.
import_substitution: None - domestic services play. Sattva installs pumps, membranes and SCADA hardware sourced from third parties; it substitutes no imported product itself.
moat_note: Weakest moat in this batch and scored accordingly. What exists is pre-qualification: TNUIFSL/CMWSSB and ULB water tenders require registered contractor class, past-completion certificates for comparable-value schemes, and bonded performance capacity, which keeps out new entrants below a threshold. The embedded O&M tails inside the EPC contracts create some annuity. But this is competitive-bid contracting against a single state customer - price, not capability, decides most awards, and pre-qualification is achievable by any established regional contractor.
why_obscure: 784 shareholders, NSE SME, half-yearly reporting, no analyst coverage and no earnings call in the filings database. The whole listed water-EPC narrative belongs to VA Tech Wabag, EMS and Enviro Infra; a Rs 148 cr Tamil-Nadu-only contractor is below every screen's floor.
risk_note: Government-tender receivable risk, quantified: debtor days are 126 on FY26 sales of Rs 143 cr, implying roughly Rs 49 cr of receivables against a Rs 47 cr net worth - i.e. more than the entire equity base is sitting in ULB receivables. name: Gujarat Kidney and Super Speciality Ltd.
business: Formerly Vihaan Medicare, GKSL is a regional healthcare operator in central Gujarat running a chain of mid-sized multi-speciality hospitals focused on secondary and tertiary care, with its origin and clinical identity in nephrology, dialysis and renal transplant. Listed on BSE in 2025; the FY26 balance sheet shows Rs 108.58 cr parked in investments and Rs 41.72 cr in bank balances against total assets of Rs 266 cr, i.e. more than half the balance sheet is undeployed IPO proceeds.

A renal transplant programme requires state Authorisation Committee clearance under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act plus a registered transplant centre licence, and dialysis units need continuous water-quality and infection-control compliance - these are genuine regulatory gates. Dialysis is also the stickiest revenue line in healthcare: a patient on maintenance haemodialysis attends thrice weekly for years, so a filled chair is an annuity. Offsetting this: central Gujarat is a competitive market and 172 debtor days points to heavy government-scheme and TPA dependence, which is a price-taking mix.
why_obscure: Listed 2025 with 18,301 holders and no sell-side initiation; a document search for management guidance returns only its filed balance sheet, meaning there is no concall and no investor presentation in the database at all. Every rupee of that cash must be deployed into beds that take 3-4 years to reach breakeven occupancy. Meanwhile 172 debtor days on ~Rs 101 cr of revenue implies about Rs 48 cr locked in government-scheme and insurer receivables - trade receivables actually rose from Rs 12.80 cr to Rs 18.88 cr on the standalone balance sheet even as the consolidated figure implies far more.

name: Jyoti Resins & Adhesives
business: Wood adhesives sold retail under the Euro 7000 brand, 100% domestic.
moat_note: There is no monopoly claim and you should not treat this as one. The company's own words: Euro 7000 is "the second largest (No. 2) selling wood adhesive brand in India in the retail segment." Notably the FY26 presentation softened this to "amongst the top selling" — a self-downgrade worth watching. The genuine mechanism is the carpenter loyalty programme — 3.5 lakh carpenters, 2 lakh active, no-expiry points, 54 branches, 13,000 retailers — real, but replicable with money, and Pidilite is 30x larger running the same playbook.
pricing_power_note: OPM 10% → 13% → 23% → 33% → 32% → 27%: the expansion was VAM input deflation, and the 600bp FY26 contraction plus TTM PAT of −11% shows costs are not being passed through.

risk_note: The margin expansion was input deflation, not pricing power — VAM is crude-linked, wholly imported, management confirmed backward integration is "not workable" at their volume, and the 600bp FY26 contraction shows costs are not being passed through.

name: AMIC Forging Ltd.
business: Kolkata-based (Garstin Place) maker of steel forgings and machined heavy precision parts - forged rounds, shafts, blanks and engineered spares in carbon steel, alloy steel, stainless steel, nickel alloys and tool alloys, produced to international standards. Output goes into steel plants, power, cement, defence and general heavy engineering as replacement and OEM spares. FY26 revenue was Rs.141.8 cr with a 30% operating margin - unusually high for a forger, implying a spares/short-run mix rather than volume automotive work. Named customers are not disclosed in filings.
import_substitution: Heavy forged rounds, shafts and engineered spares in nickel alloys and tool alloys - grades Indian heavy-industry users have typically sourced from Chinese and European forge shops. The category is nameable but AMIC does not disclose specific imported part numbers or origin countries it displaces, so this is a partial rather than a documented substitution case.
moat_note: The barrier is metallurgical capability at heavy section sizes plus per-customer part qualification for critical spares - a steel plant will not swap a forged shaft supplier casually. But AMIC does not disclose ASME, PED, API or nuclear approvals, so the barrier is customer-conferred and contestable, not regulator-locked.
why_obscure: BSE SME board, 2,686 shareholders, half-yearly reporting only, and no sell-side coverage - remarkable for a Rs.2,287 cr market cap, which is unusually large for an SME-platform name.
risk_note: 80.9x P/E on a Rs.142 cr revenue forger whose FY26 PAT (Rs.28.3 cr) actually fell versus FY25 (Rs.35.6 cr) - and FY25 was flattered by Rs.20.7 cr of other income including a Rs.18.9 cr investment gain. Underlying operating earnings are much smaller than the headline suggests.

name: IFB Agro Industries Ltd.
business: Two segments: (1) spirits — a West Bengal distillery producing Extra Neutral Alcohol, Ordinary Denatured Spirit and country liquor (IML) under own brands, with a newly commissioned 25 KLPD ethanol plant whose ethanol sales begin in FY27 once OMC tenders are floated; and (2) marine products — shrimp processing plus an aqua-feed business acquired at Rajahmundry, Andhra Pradesh (effective 1 Aug 2025) and a capex-light value-added shrimp venture in Vietnam whose first shipment went out in April 2026. FY26 gross revenue ₹1,911.57cr, up 24.25%; net debt zero at 31 Mar 2026.
import_substitution: None — domestic demand play. ENA/country liquor is a state-licensed domestic market and the marine arm is an exporter, not an import substituter.
moat_note: State excise licensing: a West Bengal distillery licence, IML bottling licences and brand registrations are the barrier, and they are non-replicable by a new entrant. The same regulator is also the risk — the Chairman's FY26 letter records production stoppages and district-level excise interference dating to 2020, so the licence is a two-edged moat, not a clean one.
why_obscure: IFB-group orphan: a spirits business bolted to a shrimp business, no analyst coverage, 13,369 holders, and a governance narrative dominated by a decade-long dispute with the West Bengal excise department that most investors will not underwrite.
risk_note: West Bengal ENA/ethanol margin compression is already underway and is structural, not cyclical: the FY26 annual report states several new dual-ENA ethanol distilleries have been commissioned in the state, forcing 'stiff price cut of the ENA and Ordinary Denatured Spirit', while DDGS and CO2 by-product prices fell on excess supply — and the December 2025 excise-duty increase pushed IML consumers into smaller pack sizes. Distillery segment result was ₹116.9cr for FY26; a further ENA price cut of a few rupees a litre takes a double-digit percentage out of it.
liquidity_note: Mainboard NSE/BSE, ₹944cr cap, 33% public float — tradeable in modest size but with wide intraday spreads; not a name to build a large position in quickly.

Growth capital is going into acquisitions (aqua feed) rather than CWIP, and management says 2-3 further projects in glycerine and bio-gas are under evaluation with at least one to be closed by Q3 FY27.

name: Marine Electricals (India) Ltd.
business: An integrated electrical-automation and ICT solutions provider originally built around marine electricals — main and emergency switchboards, integrated power management systems, bridge navigation and control systems — where it is a tier-1 supplier to the Indian Navy, Goa Shipyard and Cochin Shipyard and claims roughly 50% share of the Indian marine electrical segment. Over the last two years the industrial arm has overtaken marine: it now supplies power distribution and LV/MV switchgear packages to hyperscale data centres, winning ₹141.74cr and ₹27.21cr orders from Princeton Digital Group among others. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue was ₹263.46cr, up 53% YoY, with PAT of ₹17.51cr up 51%. The board approved a direct BSE main-board listing in August 2026.
import_substitution: Marine main switchboards, emergency switchboards and integrated platform management systems for Indian naval and commercial shipbuilding were historically sourced from European marine-electrical houses — Siemens, Schneider, ABB Marine and Norwegian/German specialists — because they carried classification-society and naval type approvals Indian firms lacked. Marine Electricals now holds those approvals domestically and supplies Indian yards directly. No filing names a specific displaced foreign OEM or the import value replaced, so the origin link is inferred from the customer set rather than disclosed.
moat_note: Naval type-approval plus classification-society certification for shipboard switchgear: a switchboard for a warship must pass shock, vibration and EMI qualification per naval standards alongside a specific hull programme, so once designed into a class of ships the supplier is effectively locked in for the build and the refit cycle. The moat is genuine on the marine side but does not extend to the fast-growing data-centre power business, where it competes with much larger switchgear players on price.
why_obscure: Not obscure — well covered. 89,030 shareholders, near-daily coverage of order wins in the retail financial press, and a ₹5,198cr market cap on the NSE main board.
risk_note: Mix drift into a lower-moat business at an 80x multiple. The industry/data-centre segment now generates more revenue than marine, but that segment carries no naval qualification barrier and OPM is already only 11%; a single large data-centre order deferral would hit a company trading at 80x earnings with 13.2% ROE, and the ₹141.74cr Princeton Digital order alone is over half a quarter's revenue.
liquidity_note: NSE main board only at present — the company migrated up from SME and the board has only just approved a direct BSE main-board listing (Aug 2026). At ₹5,198cr with 30.87% public float and 89,030 holders, NSE liquidity is ample.
warnings: P/E of 80 against 13.2% ROE and 11% OPM leaves no margin for execution error.

name: Everest Organics Ltd.
business: Telangana-based bulk-drug and intermediate maker operating from Aroor village, Sadasivpet in Sangareddy district. Historically built on ranitidine hydrochloride, the book has been rebuilt around the sartan antihypertensive family (losartan, telmisartan), metformin and contract intermediates. It is a single-site producer selling API and advanced intermediates to Indian formulators and export customers; no marquee customer names are disclosed in its filings.
import_substitution: Substitutes Chinese-origin sartan APIs and, critically, their tetrazole intermediates — the losartan/telmisartan chain where Chinese and a handful of Indian producers dominate after the 2018-19 NDMA-driven consolidation of global sartan supply.
moat_note: Thin and contestable: WHO-GMP certification and DMF filings on its sartan molecules, but no USFDA, no EDQM CEP, and a 12.0% ROCE that only just clears the hurdle — this is a capacity story, not a regulatory-barrier story.
why_obscure: BSE-only, Rs 299 cr cap, 7,827 shareholders, no NSE line, no analyst coverage and no investor communication of any kind — it is close to the definition of an unfollowed microcap.
risk_note: Single-site, single-therapeutic-chain concentration with a 53.8x P/E on a Rs 7 cr annual profit base — any regulatory action at Sadasivpet or a sartan price reset removes the entire earnings case, and the promoter has been selling.
liquidity_note: BSE-only microcap with a 40% public float and no institutional presence; daily traded value is very low and exit on size is not realistic.
cwip_note: CWIP of Rs 21 cr against a Rs 48 cr net block is the heaviest ratio in this sweep at ~44%, but it has sat flat at Rs 21-23 cr for three years — a stalled project, not an accelerating one, which is a yellow flag rather than a green one.

name: Shri Techtex Ltd.
business: NSE SME incorporated in 2011, manufacturing polypropylene non-woven fabric in a range of widths and GSM from a 41,548 sq m facility at Simaj, Dholka taluka, Ahmedabad district, Gujarat, with roughly 3,600 MT/year of installed non-woven capacity. It also provides job-work conversion. End markets are agriculture (crop cover, mulch), healthcare and hygiene, home furnishing and industrial packaging. Domestic customers sit in Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal; exports go to the USA, Taiwan, Canada, Denmark and China. Announced expansion into PP tufted fabric (artificial grass, 30 lakh sq m/year) and PP multifilament yarn (1,200 MT/year). FY26 net profit Rs 19 cr on a Rs 118 cr equity base with essentially no debt.
import_substitution: PP spunbond non-woven for hygiene, agro-textile and packaging use has historically been imported from China, and domestic capacity like this replaces some of it. The claim is materially weakened by the fact that Shri Techtex itself exports to China, Taiwan and Denmark - it is competing in a globally traded commodity fabric, not sheltering behind an import gap. The announced PP tufted artificial-grass line is the cleaner substitution: Indian artificial turf is overwhelmingly imported from China.
moat_note: Weak, and the sector deserves the low score. PP spunbond non-woven is a machine-bought converting business - buy a Reifenhauser or Chinese spunbond line, buy resin, run it - with no customer qualification gate, no BIS mandate and no switching cost. The company's own description explicitly includes 'job work services', which is the lowest-moat activity in this theme. The 28% operating margin and 22.8% ROCE are striking for such a business and probably reflect an unusually favourable job-work-plus-agro mix rather than a durable barrier; treat them as data to be explained, not proof of a moat.
why_obscure: 837 shareholders - the lowest count in this sweep by an order of magnitude. NSE SME platform only, no BSE line, no analyst coverage, no earnings call, and a document search returned zero indexed filings. It reports half-yearly, so it disappears from any quarterly-momentum screen. It also pays no dividend despite consistent profits, which keeps income-oriented retail away.
risk_note: Single plant, single polymer, single product family, and a 28% operating margin in a commodity fabric that has no defensible reason to hold. If the margin normalises toward the 10-14% typical of Indian non-woven converters, FY26 PAT of Rs 19 cr becomes roughly Rs 8-9 cr and the 7.6x P/E becomes 16x on an SME with 837 holders and no exit liquidity. The announced diversification into artificial grass and multifilament yarn is an unrelated capital commitment into two more commodity markets.
liquidity_note: NSE SME with a Rs 146 cr market cap, 29.21% public float and 837 registered holders - this is the hardest name in the batch to enter or exit. SME trading is in fixed lot sizes with minimal depth and frequent circuit-limit days; a single institutional-sized order would move the price several percent. name: Esconet Technologies Ltd.
industry: HPC/AI server systems, data-centre build and IT infrastructure integration
business: New Delhi based IT infrastructure and data-centre systems integrator that designs, builds and services high-performance computing clusters, AI/GPU compute, enterprise storage, private cloud and data-centre facilities for government departments, PSUs, research institutions and enterprises. name: Rajputana Industries Ltd.
industry: Other Non-Ferrous Metals - Copper/Brass/Aluminium Semis from Scrap
business: Rajputana Industries manufactures non-ferrous semi-finished products - copper, aluminium, brass and assorted alloys in the form of wire rod, strip and profile - made predominantly from recycled scrap, from facilities in Rajasthan. It is a conversion business: buy scrap, refine, cast, roll or draw, sell semis into electrical, transformer and general engineering channels. Named customers are not disclosed in filings and none are asserted here.
import_substitution: Weak. Copper and brass semis are overwhelmingly domestically supplied in India already; there is no specific named imported product with an identified origin country that this company is displacing.
moat_note: Minimal. A 4.0% operating margin is the number that settles it: this is scrap-in, semis-out conversion with no proprietary alloy, no customer qualification of consequence and no captive resource. The rubric's floor band for beneficiation/smelting on bought-in input applies directly.
why_obscure: NSE SME with 870 shareholders - among the smallest registers of any listed Indian manufacturer at this market cap. No coverage, no call, no presentation, and a Rs 148 cr market cap that is below most institutional minimums by an order of magnitude.
risk_note: The 4.0% operating margin is the whole risk. On roughly Rs 700-900 cr of metal throughput, a two-percentage-point adverse move in the copper scrap-to-semis spread - well inside normal LME volatility - takes operating profit to roughly zero, and there is Rs 63 cr of borrowing sitting behind it. Additionally, Rs 13 cr of CWIP against Rs 56 cr of net block means the reported 19.7% ROCE is calculated on a capital base that is about to grow by ~23% before the associated revenue arrives, so ROCE will mechanically fall.
liquidity_note: NSE SME (Emerge), Rs 148 cr market cap, 870 shareholders. This is the thinnest name in the batch - realistically a watch-list entry rather than a position for anything but the smallest book.

name: Haldyn Glass Ltd.
business: Haldyn Glass melts and moulds container glass - flint and amber bottles and jars for liquor, pharmaceuticals, food and cosmetics - from a single integrated furnace complex at Gavasad, Padra taluka, Vadodara district, Gujarat. A subsidiary, Haldyn Corporation, adds closures and decorating, so the group can ship a filled-ready pack rather than only the bottle. The company does not publish a named customer list in its filings, so no customer names are asserted here; end-users are Indian liquor, pharma and FMCG fillers within economic freight distance of Gujarat.
import_substitution: None - domestic demand play. Container glass has a value-to-weight ratio that makes imports uneconomic beyond a few hundred kilometres; there is no named imported product being displaced.
moat_note: Physical, not proprietary: a continuous glass furnace runs a 10-12 year campaign and cannot be idled, so incumbency plus a freight radius of roughly 500-700 km is the barrier. Pharma and liquor fillers also qualify a glass source and re-qualification is slow. This is real but contestable - AGI Greenpac, Hindusthan National Glass successors and regional furnaces can and do compete on the same customers.
why_obscure: No earnings call, no investor presentation cadence, no sell-side coverage. Free float is under 39% and effectively smaller, and the stock trades mostly on BSE with modest daily turnover, so institutional screens skip it.
risk_note: Single-site furnace concentration. One unplanned furnace failure or a forced early rebuild at Gavasad takes out essentially all revenue for months; separately, natural gas and soda ash are the two largest input lines and a 20-25% gas price move against a 14% OPM would roughly halve operating profit.
liquidity_note: Mainboard (NSE + BSE) but genuinely thin - a Rs 729 cr market cap with ~39% public float and no institutional sponsorship beyond 2% DII means position building has to be measured in weeks, not days.

guidance_source: Document search for a Haldyn Glass management revenue-growth statement returned no Haldyn-specific transcript, presentation or MD&A chunk. The company does not appear to hold earnings calls. No guidance exists to cite.

Import-sub 3 - nothing imported is being displaced. Promoter 12 - 59.14% sits squarely in the 55-70% band. Institutional 6 - DII 2.03% with zero FII is one-sided, not the both-sides signal. name: Sigma Advanced Systems Ltd. (formerly Megasoft)
business: Hyderabad-based Tier-1 aerospace and defence player formed by folding Sigma Advanced Systems (founded 1994) into the listed Megasoft shell via an NCLT scheme effective April 2024. It makes missile sub-systems (rear servo systems, amplifiers, end-game packages for LRSAM/MRSAM, INVAR, NGARM, KONKURS — roughly 50% of revenue), avionics displays and flight data recorders, naval power distribution and display systems, plus counter-drone products through its Indrajaal investment. It runs 300,000+ sq ft across 8 sites with ~700 FTEs and a dual India-UK footprint after acquiring UK aero-engine supplier Nasmyth (Oct 2025) and AS Strategic (51%, Apr 2026). Reported order visibility includes a ~£300m 7-year Rolls-Royce long-term agreement and a $104.9m US artillery-shell export order.
import_substitution: Two concrete strands. Nasmyth's 'delegatory approvals' let Sigma transfer UK-origin aero-engine hot-section Class I fabrications and critical airframe sub-assemblies — historically machined in the UK and EU for Rolls-Royce and peers — into Indian plants. Separately, its missile rear servo systems and amplifiers for INVAR and KONKURS are indigenous replacements for Russian-origin ATGM sub-systems previously imported by the Indian Army and BDL. The named-origin link is documented; the rupee value substituted is not disclosed.
moat_note: Defence qualification is the barrier: build-to-spec sub-systems for DRDO and BDL missile programmes carry multi-year qualification and are effectively sole-sourced once designed in, with contracts running up to 8 years. On the aerospace side the moat is Rolls-Royce and EU OEM supplier approvals plus the delegatory authority Nasmyth carries, which a new entrant cannot buy.
why_obscure: Not obscure in trading terms — near 50,000 shareholders, a 15x move in four years and a BSE query on unusual trading in May 2026. It is however genuinely under-researched: no sustained sell-side coverage, and the reverse-merger structure means most screening databases still carry a distorted history from the old software entity.
risk_note: Earnings quality. FY26 reported PAT of ₹268cr includes a ~₹185cr land-sale gain and the Extrovis AG divestment; other income was ₹296cr against ₹492cr of operating revenue, so the headline ROE of 90.6% and P/E of 79 both flatter an underlying operating business running mid-single-digit margins. A further preferential issue of 13.25cr shares at ₹347 was approved in June 2026 — below the then-prevailing ₹550-580 — adding dilution within six months of the merger.
liquidity_note: NSE/BSE mainboard with a ₹13,131cr market cap and heavy retail participation; liquidity is not a constraint, but the free float has been repeatedly reshaped by merger allotments and preferential issues rather than by market buying.

name: Euro Pratik Sales Ltd.
business: An asset-light decorative-surfaces brand, not a manufacturer. It designs and sells decorative wall panels, louvers, charcoal panels and allied interior surfacing under the Euro Pratik and Ostrich brands, and outsources essentially all production to third-party converters in India and abroad. Distribution is through a dealer and architect/interior-designer channel across India. Net block is only Rs 85 cr against Rs 2,803 cr of market value - the asset is the brand and the catalogue. Listed September 2025.
import_substitution: None - domestic demand play, and arguably the opposite. A material part of the decorative panel range is sourced from third-party manufacturers including overseas (China) suppliers rather than made in India, so the company is on the import side of this trade, not the substitution side.
moat_note: Brand and channel, nothing more. The 38% ROCE is an artefact of outsourcing manufacture - it is a high return on a tiny capital base, not evidence of a barrier. Design catalogues are copied within a season, and the dealer relationship is the only thing that is slow to replicate. Treat this as a contestable consumer brand, not a moated building-products franchise.
why_obscure: Listed only in September 2025 with no research franchise yet, DII holding of just 4.48% and FII of 0.55%. That said, 26,366 shareholders after an IPO means it is not undiscovered by retail - it is simply unmodelled by institutions.
risk_note: It controls no plant. Every rupee of the 31% operating margin depends on outsourced converters and, for part of the range, on Chinese supply - so an anti-dumping duty or a safeguard duty on decorative panels, a rupee move, or a converter deciding to sell direct hits the margin immediately with no owned capacity to fall back on. At 32.5x with a Rs 0 CWIP line, there is no capex programme creating an offsetting growth asset.
liquidity_note: NSE/BSE mainboard, Rs 2,803 cr market cap, but promoters hold 73.91% so the genuine free float is barely a quarter of the company. Reasonable screen liquidity, materially less than the market cap implies.
cwip_note: CWIP is nil in Mar 2024, Mar 2025 and Mar 2026. Consistent with the outsourced model - there is nothing being built, which is exactly why the ROCE reads 38%. Fails the heavy-CWIP preference completely.
score_rationale: Import substitution 0 - the company sits on the wrong side of this theme, sourcing rather than substituting. Promoter 11: 73.91% is above the 55-70% productive band, so it is discounted for float scarcity rather than rewarded. Institutional 8 - both present but FII at 0.55% is effectively nil. name: Yash Optics & Lens Ltd.
industry: Ophthalmic devices - spectacle lens surfacing, coating and distribution
business: Founded in 2010 and based in the Mumbai/Vasai belt, Yash Optics & Lens supplies vision-correction products - single-vision lenses, progressive and bifocal lenses, and value-added coatings (anti-reflective, blue-cut, photochromic, hard-coat) - to optical retail chains, independent opticians and lens distributors across India. Its own operations are lens surfacing (RX prescription grinding) and coating lines rather than casting lenses from monomer. Be plain about this: like most of the Indian ophthalmic-lens trade, a meaningful part of what it sells starts as semi-finished blanks or finished stock lenses sourced from Asian suppliers and is then surfaced, coated and branded locally, so the company is a processor-cum-distributor, not a fully vertically integrated lens manufacturer. The Rs 22.4 cr of CWIP at Mar 2026 is a new processing/coating facility under construction.
import_substitution: Partial and unnamed by the company: RX surfacing and hard/AR coating done in India replaces finished coated lenses that Indian opticians would otherwise import from China, Korea and Thailand. But the semi-finished blanks themselves are still largely imported, so the value added onshore is the surfacing and coating step, not the lens substrate. No specific product/origin pair is disclosed in any filing available in the document database.
moat_note: Modest and contestable: spectacle lenses are CDSCO-notified medical devices requiring registration/import licences, and coating lines are capital equipment with meaningful process know-how (adhesion, hard-coat yield). But there is no USFDA, CE MDR or NABL-class accreditation involved, and dozens of unlisted Indian RX labs run the same equipment. The 27.3% OPM is high for the trade and probably reflects mix rather than a barrier.
why_obscure: NSE SME platform, half-yearly reporting only, 1,251 shareholders, zero FII and effectively zero DII, no earnings calls or investor presentations, and no documents at all in the filings database. Ophthalmic lenses also get mentally filed under Lenskart-style retail rather than medical devices.
risk_note: Rs 22.38 cr of CWIP - 54% of the Rs 41.58 cr net block - is being built while H1 FY26 profit fell 31% year on year (Rs 3.12 cr in Sep-2025 against Rs 4.55 cr in Sep-2024). If the new capacity ramps slowly, depreciation and interest land on a business whose 3Y profit CAGR is already only 4%, and ROCE at 12.8% sits just 80 bps above the screen's hard gate - a single weak half pushes it out.
liquidity_note: NSE SME (Emerge) - trades in fixed lot sizes with a wide spread and no institutional participation. A Rs 279 cr market cap with a 26.8% float means exit is genuinely constrained; treat as position-size-limited.
cwip_note: CWIP went Rs 6.27 cr (Mar 2024) to Rs 3.05 cr (Mar 2025) to Rs 22.38 cr (Mar 2026) - a 7.3x step-up in one year and 53.8% of net block. This is the heaviest CWIP-to-net-block ratio in this batch and the clearest capex-cycle signal, but no filing explains what the asset is.
score_rationale: No regulator-conferred barrier beyond routine CDSCO device registration and no clinical dossier, so moat caps at 10/25 despite good margins. Import substitution is generic - onshore surfacing/coating, no named product or origin - so 8/20. Promoter 73.19%, stable and unpledged, but above the 55-70% peak band: 12/15. Effectively zero institutions: 3/15. 1,251 holders, SME board, no coverage or filings: 14/15. ROE only 9.53% with a 4% 3Y profit CAGR pulls financials to 6/10. Total 53.
warnings: ROCE 12.8% clears the 12% gate by only 80 bps and ROE 9.53% is well below the double-digit comfort level.

name: Oriana Power Ltd.
industry: Solar EPC and BOOT/Open-Access Independent Power Producer
business: Noida-based, incorporated 2013, running two verticals: (i) turnkey EPC for on-site rooftop and ground-mounted solar and (ii) BOOT/BOO ownership of captive and open-access solar farms sold to C&I offtakers. The IPP book is what converts EPC margin into an annuity and is the reason OPM is 23% rather than the high-single-digit typical of pure solar EPC. FY26 revenue Rs 1,813 cr equivalent (H1 Rs 781 cr + H2 Rs 1,032 cr) with Rs 252 cr PAT. This is explicitly NOT a manufacturer — it buys modules, inverters and structures.
import_substitution: None — domestic demand play. Oriana is a buyer of solar equipment, not a maker of it; to the extent its projects use ALMM-compliant Indian modules, the import substitution accrues to its suppliers (Waaree, Premier, Vikram, Emmvee), not to Oriana.
moat_note: The only defensible barrier is on the IPP side: open-access connectivity approvals, state open-access regulatory clearances and signed long-tenor C&I PPAs are genuinely hard to replicate and are asset-specific. The EPC vertical has no barrier at all — it is a competitively bid contracting business, and per the brief's rule solar EPC contractors are scored accordingly. The 39.6% ROCE is a function of a fast-growing asset base, not of pricing power.
why_obscure: 15,186 holders, no BSE line, SME-to-mainboard migration history, and no earnings-call or investor-presentation footprint in the filings database — I searched and found nothing filed under Oriana. risk_note: This is the classic policy-driven contracting story the sector is full of: 138% 3Y sales CAGR on a business whose EPC leg is re-bid every project, funded with CWIP of Rs 146 cr against Rs 313 cr net block and D/E 0.68. Sterling & Wilson's Q1 FY27 commentary that 'the domestic solar EPC market remained a bit slow for a second consecutive quarter... high domestic module prices, which deferred new project awards' is the direct read-across risk — a two-quarter award drought would strand the capex and the working capital simultaneously.
liquidity_note: NSE-only, Rs 2,469 cr mcap, 15,186 holders — reasonable retail liquidity but a 41.4% public float with almost no institutional ownership means the price is set entirely by retail flow, which is why it trades at 9.8x on 39.6% ROE.
cwip_note: CWIP Mar 2024 Rs 52 cr -> Mar 2025 Rs 50 cr -> Mar 2026 Rs 146 cr, i.e. 46.6% of net block — the second-heaviest ratio in this batch. These are BOOT/open-access solar assets under construction, so unlike a factory the revenue conversion is contractually visible once commissioned; the risk is commissioning delay and grid-connectivity timing, not demand.
score_rationale: Moat 8: deliberately low. Per the brief's rule, a solar EPC contractor gets an assembly-grade moat score; the only credit above the floor is for the BOOT/open-access IPP assets, where connectivity approvals and signed C&I PPAs are a genuine, if asset-specific, barrier. High ROCE here reflects growth, not a barrier. Import-sub 3: none — it buys equipment. Promoter 12: 57.98%, in band, flat, no disclosed pledge, but nearer the bottom of the sweet spot. Institutional 5: FII 0.32 + DII 0.32 = 0.64%. Undercovered 8: 15,186 holders and no filings-database footprint, but a Rs 2,469 cr NSE mainboard name is not obscure. Financials 9: 39.6% ROE, D/E 0.68, 188% 3Y profit CAGR. Lowest total of the eight — included for CWIP intensity and business-model diversity, not because it is the best idea here.

name: Aarvi Encon Ltd.
industry: Third-party inspection, QA/QC and technical engineering services
business: Incorporated in 1987 and headquartered in Mumbai, Aarvi Encon supplies technical manpower and engineering services to oil and gas, refining, petrochemical, power, chemical and infrastructure clients in India and the Gulf, with subsidiaries serving overseas deployments. Alongside the staffing business it runs a dedicated inspection services line for the oil and gas industry - vendor and shop inspection, expediting, site QA/QC, welding and NDT supervision - staffed by certified inspectors. It is a pure services business: net block is Rs 17 cr and there is no manufacturing. The staffing mix is why operating margin is only 3.5% even though ROCE is 14.4%.
import_substitution: None - domestic and GCC services demand play. Aarvi displaces expatriate and foreign inspection agencies on Indian and Gulf project sites rather than any imported product.
moat_note: Thin. The barriers are client vendor-registration and empanelment with PSU refiners and EPC majors, and the certified-inspector bench (ASNT/CSWIP/welding-inspector qualifications) needed to sign off on third-party inspection reports. Neither is a regulator-conferred accreditation of the ISO/IEC 17025 or NABL kind, capital intensity is near zero, and the 3.5% operating margin is itself the clearest evidence that pricing power is limited.
why_obscure: A 3.5% operating margin makes it screen as a low-quality staffing company, so institutions ignore it - FII and DII are both effectively zero despite a mainboard listing. It trades at 11.7x with 8,726 holders, has no earnings call and no documents at all in the filings database, and its inspection vertical is not separately disclosed.
risk_note: Margin fragility. At 3.5% operating margin on a revenue base of roughly Rs 500 cr scale, a 100 bps squeeze between client bill rates and engineer wages removes close to a quarter of operating profit. That squeeze is a live risk given oil and gas capex cyclicality, wage inflation for certified inspectors, and PSU-client payment cycles that push working capital.
liquidity_note: Mainboard on both NSE (AARVI) and BSE (544850), Rs 231 cr market cap with a 26.65% float - modest but genuinely tradeable, and the second-most liquid name in this batch after 3B BlackBio.

name: Urban Enviro Waste Management Ltd.
business: Incorporated 2011, Urban Enviro provides municipal solid waste management to urban local bodies - door-to-door collection, transportation, segregation and disposal - handling roughly 2,000 metric tonnes of waste per day. Portfolio of 36 projects of which 18 are completed, with 10 active projects concentrated in Maharashtra. Recent awards include a Rs 14.58 cr three-year contract with Nagar Palika Parishad Kichha (Uttarakhand) and a Rs 1.64 cr contract with Municipal Council Mul. FY26 sales Rs 182 cr.
import_substitution: None - domestic services play. Collection vehicles, compactors and segregation equipment are procured, not manufactured; there is no imported product being displaced.
moat_note: Municipal concession contracts are the barrier and they are the real thing as far as they go: MSW collection and transport contracts under the Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 are awarded by ULBs on 3-7 year tenure with pre-qualification on fleet, tonnage handled and past ULB completion certificates, and the incumbent controls the routes, the vehicles and the sanitation workforce in that town - re-tendering an incumbent is politically and operationally painful. Against that: it is still competitive tendering, the tenure is short, and there is no processing or landfill asset to entrench the position. Contestable, not conferred.
why_obscure: NSE SME, 1,698 shareholders, zero FII and 0.07% DII. Half-yearly reporting. Municipal sanitation contracting is unglamorous and the listed 'waste' peer group is dominated by Antony Waste and the e-waste names, so a Rs 125 cr collection-and-transport operator gets no attention. It is also the smallest market cap in this batch, barely clearing the Rs 120 cr floor.
risk_note: Government receivable risk plus leverage, together: debtor days rose from 105 to 130 on FY26 sales of Rs 182 cr, implying roughly Rs 65 cr of ULB receivables against Rs 43 cr of equity and Rs 34 cr of borrowings. Municipal councils are among the slowest payers in India and several of these are small-town bodies (Kichha, Mul). A single ULB withholding payment on a multi-crore contract, against 0.79x D/E, forces either a fresh borrowing or a working-capital squeeze - and with half-yearly reporting the deterioration would not surface for six months.
liquidity_note: NSE SME with the largest public float percentage in this batch at 48.74%, but on a Rs 125 cr cap that is still only about Rs 61 cr, held by 1,698 people with essentially no institutional participation. High float share does not equal liquidity at this size; SME lot trading applies.
cwip_note: CWIP went Rs 0 cr (Mar 2024) to Rs 0 cr (Mar 2025) to Rs 7 cr (Mar 2026), which is 26.9% of the Rs 26 cr net block - a genuine step-up in fleet or facility investment beginning in FY26, consistent with the new Uttarakhand and Maharashtra contract wins. Note the asset base is small relative to Rs 182 cr of revenue: Rs 26 cr net block turns over 7x. That is why ROCE reads 33.2% and ROE 37.8% - this is an asset-light, contract-labour-and-fleet service model, and those return figures rest on a small denominator plus 0.79x leverage, not on any structural pricing advantage. Read them with that discount.

name: Baheti Recycling Industries Ltd.
business: Baheti Recycling melts and refines aluminium scrap into aluminium alloy ingots and deoxidant products, operating out of Jamnagar, Gujarat - the country's densest non-ferrous scrap-processing cluster and its main scrap import gateway. Output goes to auto-component casters and to steel mills as a deoxidiser. The company does not disclose named customers in public filings and none are asserted here.
import_substitution: Weak, and arguably inverted. The alloy ingot output does displace imported primary and secondary aluminium ingots, but the feedstock is imported aluminium scrap - largely from OECD sources and the Gulf - so the company is net long on an imported input, not substituting one.
moat_note: Effectively none. This is a melting spread on bought-in scrap: the barrier is scrap-sourcing relationships and segregation labour, both of which India has in abundance at Jamnagar. Per the scoring rubric, beneficiation or smelting on bought-in ore/scrap sits below 8. A 21.7% ROCE here is not a franchise signal.
why_obscure: NSE SME with only 1,035 shareholders, no earnings call, no coverage, and a business description ('recycling') that gets it screened as an ESG/waste name rather than as a metals spread business.
risk_note: Feedstock supply and leverage together. Borrowings are Rs 229 cr against a Rs 93 cr net worth (2.46x) financing a scrap inventory book, against an 8% operating margin - so a two-to-three point compression in the scrap-to-ingot spread would eat the entire interest cover. On top of that, sector management (CMR Green, July 2026 call) has publicly flagged the risk of an EU aluminium scrap export ban; India has applied for exemption but the outcome is unresolved, and a feedstock ban would be existential for a Jamnagar importer.
liquidity_note: NSE SME (Emerge). 1,035 shareholders and lot-size trading make this the least liquid name in the batch alongside Rajputana. Rs 831 cr of market cap on a thousand holders is a warning in itself.
cwip_note: CWIP Rs 8 cr (FY24) -> Rs 2 cr (FY25) -> Rs 6 cr (FY26) against a Rs 34 cr net block, i.e. 17.6% - genuinely heavy relative to fixed assets. But note the fixed asset base is tiny in absolute terms: the capital in this business sits in working capital (Rs 229 cr of borrowings), not in plant. Expanding the net block by a fifth changes very little about the earnings engine.
guidance_source: Document search for Baheti Recycling management revenue commentary returned no Baheti-specific filing; results were dominated by CMR Green Technologies, Hindalco and Vedanta Aluminium. As an NSE SME the company does not hold earnings calls. No guidance to cite.

warnings: CLASSIC RECYCLER ROE ILLUSION: 35.4% ROE and 21.7% ROCE are produced on a Rs 34 cr net block by turning a Rs 229 cr debt-funded working capital book. This is leverage and inventory velocity, not asset quality. A single bad aluminium price move reverses it.

name: Worth Peripherals Ltd.
business: Incorporated 1996; makes corrugated sheets and boxes from two plants in Madhya Pradesh, the main one an eight-acre, 180,000 sq ft site at Indore plus a second unit for board conversion, fitments and partitions. Runs EMBA 175 QS Ultima (2015) and EMBA 245 QS Ultima (2020) flexo-folder-gluers, the latter among the first twenty of that model installed worldwide, targeting output from 3,200 to 4,500 MT per month. Product mix roughly 80% singlewall, 20% doublewall. ISO 9001:2015 certified and SEDEX-audited. FY26 consolidated revenue Rs 304.91 cr, PAT Rs 18.53 cr. End-markets are FMCG, personal care, beverage, chemical and pharmaceutical; no customers are publicly named.
import_substitution: None — domestic demand play. Corrugated packaging is freight-uneconomic to import.
moat_note: Thin, and stated as such. The EMBA high-speed flexo-folder-gluer installed base is genuinely rare in India and, with SEDEX social audit compliance, opens the door to multinational FMCG vendor panels that a typical local corrugator cannot enter. But the product is a box: there is no regulatory approval, no qualification cycle and no switching cost, and 12.9% ROCE with 8.1% ROE against a 1% three-year sales CAGR is exactly what commodity converting looks like.
why_obscure: 6,060 shareholders, no FII, no DII, no earnings calls, no investor presentations, and no entries at all in the filings-document database searched. Recently moved onto the BSE mainboard (scrip 544577) from the SME segment, so it has not yet accumulated a following.
risk_note: The Rs 79 cr of CWIP — equal to 99% of the entire existing Rs 80 cr net block — is going into Worth Wellness Private Limited, a subsidiary in an unrelated 'wellness' line with no revenue yet and an acknowledged possibility of execution delay. That is a bet of one full company's worth of assets, funded off a Rs 172 cr reserve base, on a business outside corrugated packaging, at a company whose core three-year profit CAGR is already minus 7%.
liquidity_note: Small-cap on BSE (544577) with an NSE symbol, 6,060 shareholders, zero institutional ownership and a Rs 247 cr market cap — thin. Recently mainboard, so no SME lot-size constraint, but daily traded value is small.
cwip_note: The most extreme CWIP-to-net-block ratio in this sweep: Rs 1 cr in Mar 2024, Rs 1 cr in Mar 2025, Rs 79 cr in Mar 2026 against a Rs 80 cr net block — the company is building a second company's worth of assets in a single year. score_rationale: Cleanest balance sheet here — D/E 0.22, nil promoter encumbrance confirmed by filing, promoters buying in the open market — attached to the sweep's largest capex signal at Rs 79 cr of CWIP on a Rs 80 cr net block. Scored low on moat and financials because the core business is commodity corrugated converting with 8.1% ROE, a 1% three-year sales CAGR and a negative profit CAGR, and the entire capex is being pointed at an unrelated venture.

name: Bombay Super Hybrid Seeds Ltd.
industry: Hybrid and varietal field-crop and vegetable seeds
business: Gujarat-based producer, processor and marketer of hybrid and GM seeds with a range of over 150 products across field crops and vegetable crops including groundnut, chickpea, coriander, sesame and maize. Seed is multiplied through contract growers, then graded, treated and packed in-house. Net block is only Rs 10 cr - almost the entire balance sheet is seed inventory and grower advances rather than plant. No named institutional customers; the buyer is the farmer through a dealer channel.
import_substitution: None - domestic demand play. Indian seed is already domestically produced; nothing imported is displaced.
moat_note: Weak, and it should be scored that way. State seed licences and variety notification are procedural, not scarce. Most of the named portfolio - groundnut, chickpea, coriander, sesame - is self-pollinated, so farmers can save and re-sow seed, which destroys the annual repeat-purchase economics that make a real hybrid seed company; and Bt cotton pricing is capped by government order. This is closer to seed multiplication and trade than to protected germplasm.
why_obscure: Recent SME-platform listing (BSE 544757), 16,418 holders, zero institutional ownership, no concall corpus - a Trendlyne document search returned no Bombay Super Hybrid Seeds documents whatsoever.
risk_note: Rs 108 cr of borrowings (D/E 0.89) financing seed inventory against a net block of just Rs 10 cr, in a year when kharif 2026 sowing declined on erratic and delayed monsoon. Unsold seed is a wasting asset - germination falls with each season carried - so a bad monsoon converts inventory straight into a write-down while the debt stays.
liquidity_note: SME-platform listing with a 26% float and no institutional holders: exit is the binding constraint, not entry. Rs 945 cr of market cap on a stock that trades in bursts.

business: Arfin India makes consumables for the steel and aluminium industries from plants at Chhatral and Sanand in Gujarat: aluminium deoxidants (notch bar, cubes, shots) used to kill oxygen in liquid steel, aluminium wire rod, cored wire for ladle metallurgy, and ferro and master alloys. Customer names are not disclosed in public filings and none are asserted here; the end market is Indian integrated and secondary steel mills.
import_substitution: Moderate. Cored wire and calcium/aluminium ladle-treatment consumables for steelmaking are otherwise sourced substantially from China, and aluminium deoxidant supply has historically leaned on imports at the margin. The product category and origin are identifiable, but Arfin does not publish displaced-import volumes, and the aluminium input itself is bought-in scrap and metal.
moat_note: Steel-mill vendor approval. Deoxidant and cored-wire suppliers are qualified per mill and per grade because an off-spec addition ruins a heat, and that creates a real switching cost once approved. Against that, the business is a conversion spread on bought-in aluminium with a 7% operating margin, and the ROE of 9.45% says the approvals are not translating into pricing power.
why_obscure: 13,548 shareholders, no earnings call, no coverage, and a product set (deox, cored wire, master alloys) that sits invisibly inside the steel supply chain rather than in any recognised sector bucket.
risk_note: Valuation against a thin margin. A trailing PE of 76 on roughly Rs 18 cr of TTM profit prices in a re-rating that a 7% operating margin and a 9.45% ROE do not currently support; and the March 2025 quarter (Rs 0.53 cr PAT versus a Rs 2.5-3 cr run rate) shows how quickly the spread can collapse when aluminium moves against the order book. Rs 129 cr of borrowings against Rs 170 cr of equity leaves limited room for a bad quarter.
liquidity_note: Mainboard NSE listing at Rs 1,405 cr with 13,548 holders - the most tradeable name in this batch after Diffusion, though a low absolute share price (Rs 83.6) means volume statistics flatter the true depth.
cwip_note: CWIP Rs 0 cr (FY24) -> Rs 4 cr (FY25) -> Rs 0 cr (FY26) on a Rs 74 cr net block. The FY25 project was completed and capitalised; there is no visible expansion cycle running into FY27. This is NOT a heavy-CWIP candidate.
guidance_source: Document search for Arfin India management revenue-growth commentary returned no Arfin-specific transcript, presentation or MD&A chunk; results were dominated by CMR Green, Hindalco, Alufluoride and Vedanta Aluminium. No guidance to cite.
score_rationale: Moat 8 - mill-level vendor qualification is genuine but it is a spread on bought-in aluminium, and the rubric caps that category; the 7% OPM and sub-10% ROE argue against anything higher. Import-sub 10 - generic band; the product categories (cored wire, deoxidants) and origin (China) are identifiable but the company quantifies nothing. Promoter 12 - 69.77% sits at the top of the 55-70% peak. Institutional 3 - FII 0.79% and no DII is effectively no institutional participation. Undercovered 8 - 13,548 holders is mid-range.
