It is a real moat but an ordinary one: it is relationship-based, not IP-based or regulator-conferred, it does not travel outside the therapies where the field force is strong, and a competitor with money can rent the same kind of field force. Nothing here is externally verified — no regulator, rating agency or customer filing was located that speaks to Jenburkt's position, and this pass could not reach Trendlyne's news and filings endpoints (see verify_comment).
import_substitution: Weak and only indirect. Domestic branded formulations displace imported branded equivalents at the margin, but Jenburkt is not substituting an import in any structural sense — it formulates, it does not make the actives. The board screens for import substitution and this name does not really deliver it; it earns its place on operating quality and under-coverage instead, and the score reflects that (s_import_sub 12/20, not higher).
risk_note: Promoter holding is 46.62% — comfortably over the 40% gate but low enough that it is worth watching, and it has drifted down about 0.01pp a quarter for six straight quarters (46.68% to 46.62%), which is noise rather than a trend but is a trend in one direction. The Rs 46 cr of CWIP is roughly 2.4x the existing net block, so the company is roughly tripling its fixed asset base in one go — the return on that capex is unproven and, until it runs, it is a drag on the ROCE that makes this name attractive. Quarterly margin is lumpy (17.3% in Dec-25 against 31.9% in Mar-26 and 17.0% in Jun-26), so any single quarter read alone will mislead. Growth is genuinely slow: 4.7% compound sales growth over nine years.
why_obscure: 7,103 shareholders and effectively no institutional footprint at all — FII 0.00%, DII 0.12%. A profitable, dividend-paying, debt-free pharma company at Rs 454 cr that no institution owns is exactly what this board exists to surface.
verify_comment: Graded from Screener's nine-year standalone accounts only. No external source was checked: Trendlyne's news, corporate-events, insider/SAST and pledge endpoints were rate-limited and timing out throughout this run, so pledging, insider activity and any auditor change are UNCHECKED for this row. The margin and cash-conversion record is from the company's own audited filings, which is why nothing here is graded 'verified'.
data_note: Screener standalone. Consolidated returned no data for this symbol. FY26 figures as reported; TTM sales Rs 169 cr, TTM PAT Rs 33 cr.
penalty_detail: -2 for CWIP at 2.4x net block with unproven returns.

name: Patel Chem Specialities
theme_detail: Cellulose-based pharmaceutical excipients — the inactive half of a tablet.
business: Makes cellulose-derived pharmaceutical excipients — the super-disintegrant and binder class (croscarmellose sodium, sodium starch glycolate and adjacent grades) that goes into solid oral dosage forms. Sales Rs 42 cr (FY21) to Rs 137 cr (FY26), a genuine 27% compound rate. Recently listed: equity capital went Rs 1 cr to Rs 25 cr across FY25-FY26 as the issue landed, and Rs 15 cr of CWIP sits against Rs 30 cr of net block.
moat_note: The import-substitution case here is the strongest in this week's microcap batch, and it is a category fact rather than a company claim: India's pharmaceutical excipient supply for this class has historically been dominated by DFE Pharma, JRS and the former FMC BioPolymer line, and domestic capacity in super-disintegrants is thin. A qualified excipient supplier also enjoys a real switching cost — the excipient is named in the customer's drug master file, so changing supplier mid-product means a regulatory refiling, the same mechanism that defends contract testing labs. What is NOT established is that Patel Chem specifically occupies that position rather than competing on price at the commodity end of it. No customer filing, regulator listing or rating-agency note was located naming the company, and the margin trend argues against a strong position: OPM fell from 15% to 12% and ROCE from 39% to 22% in the year the capacity expanded, which is what price-taking looks like, not pricing power. Graded company-stated: the category is real, this company's place in it is its own account.
import_substitution: Direct and structural, at the category level. Pharmaceutical excipients of this class are substantially imported into India, and every tonne made domestically displaces one. This is the clearest import-substitution story of the twenty names read this week, which is why s_import_sub is 16/20 — the four points withheld are because the company's own share of that substitution is unquantified in anything checkable.
risk_note: The quality metrics that put this name on the screen are already deteriorating: ROCE 39% (FY24) to 35% (FY25) to 22% (FY26), and OPM 15% to 12% over the last year, both coinciding with the post-IPO capital landing and the capacity going in. Half-year margin is still falling (14% in Sep-25 to 11% in Mar-26). Cash conversion is acceptable but not strong — CFO Rs 11 cr against operating profit Rs 17 cr in FY26, and free cash flow has been negative in four of the last five years because of continuous capex. Rs 15 cr of CWIP against Rs 30 cr of net block means another 50% expansion is still to be absorbed. FII holding fell from 8.19% to 6.41% in the most recent two disclosures.
why_obscure: 1,089 shareholders. A 2025-vintage listing that no domestic institution beyond 1.7% has looked at.
verify_comment: Screener standalone accounts only, six years. The excipient-import claim is checked against general industry structure, not against a document naming this company — that is the gap between company-stated and verified here. Trendlyne news, insider/SAST and pledge endpoints were unreachable this run, so pledging and insider activity are UNCHECKED.
data_note: Screener standalone; consolidated returned no data. FY21 cash-flow line in Screener is corrupt (investing outflow shown as Rs -1,978 cr against a Rs 18 cr balance sheet) and has been ignored.
penalty_detail: -4 ROCE almost halved and OPM fell in the year capacity landed; -3 continuous negative FCF with a further 50% of net block still in CWIP.

name: Emkay Tools
theme_detail: Cutting tools — taps and thread-cutting tooling.
business: Cutting-tool manufacturer in the Emkay group's tap and thread-cutting line. Screener carries only two years — FY25 and FY26 — so there is no cycle in the record at all. Sales Rs 117 cr to Rs 144 cr, operating profit Rs 61 cr to Rs 80 cr, zero borrowings, Rs 77 cr of investments against Rs 16 cr of net block, and free cash flow of Rs 61 cr in FY26. Note this is a different listed entity from Emkay Taps & Cutting Tools Ltd (EMKAYTOOLS), which is a Rs 100 cr company; the screen row belongs to this one.
moat_note: The claim implicit in these accounts is a very strong one — a 56% operating margin — and it is the reason the row is here and the reason it cannot be graded above company-stated. For context, Kennametal India, the listed benchmark in Indian cutting tools and a subsidiary of a global tooling major, runs mid-teens operating margins; a 56% margin is roughly four times the sector norm. High-precision tap manufacture is a genuinely defensible niche — thread geometry, coating and heat-treatment know-how are hard to copy and the tools are consumables bought on performance rather than price — so a premium is credible. A premium of this size is not credible without an explanation, and two years of disclosure does not contain one. It could be a genuinely differentiated export-grade product line; it could equally be an artefact of how cost sits between entities in a group that has more than one listed vehicle in the same business. This pass could not distinguish those, and says so rather than guessing. Zero borrowings, Rs 77 cr of investments and CFO at 106% of operating profit are at least consistent with the profit being real cash rather than accounting.
import_substitution: Plausible and category-real. India imports high-end taps and thread-cutting tooling from German and Japanese makers, and a domestic producer at export-grade quality substitutes those directly. Nothing checkable establishes that Emkay Tools competes at that end rather than the commodity end, so 12/20.
risk_note: Two years of accounts. There is no downturn, no cycle and no pre-listing history in anything visible, so every quality metric on this row is unfalsifiable from the record. Inventory stands at 380 days (489 in FY25) and the cash conversion cycle at 331 days — enormous even for a consumables business that must hold a wide catalogue, and the single largest thing that could be hiding a problem. The 56% margin is unexplained (see moat_note) and if it normalises toward sector levels the earnings base falls by more than half. There is no institutional holder at all and only 669 shareholders, so the price is set by a very thin float. Promoter at 74.99% is one basis point under the 75% maximum, which means no promoter buying headroom remains.
why_obscure: 669 shareholders and zero institutional ownership on a Rs 1,126 cr market cap — the largest company on this week's microcap batch by a wide margin and among the least examined.
verify_comment: Two years of Screener standalone accounts and nothing else. The margin claim that defines this row is UNVERIFIED and the row says so. Trendlyne's overview, news, insider/SAST and pledge endpoints were rate-limited and timing out throughout this run, so related-party transactions, pledging and insider activity — the three things that would most efficiently explain or discredit a 56% margin — are all UNCHECKED. This row should be revisited first next week.
data_note: Screener standalone; get_company_overview returns blank for ETL and only get_full_analysis with financial_type=standalone yields data. Face value Rs 1.
penalty_detail: -4 only two years of accounts, no cycle in the record; -3 operating margin roughly 4x the listed sector benchmark with no explanation located; -1 inventory at 380 days.

name: Automobile Corporation of Goa
theme_detail: Bus bodybuilding and pressed sheet-metal components.
business: Bus bodybuilder and pressed sheet-metal component maker at Honda, Goa, with Tata Motors as promoter at 48.98%. Ten years of accounts on Screener including a full cycle: sales Rs 489 cr (FY18), collapsing to Rs 116 cr in FY21 with a Rs 13 cr loss as bus demand stopped during COVID, then recovering to Rs 934 cr in FY26. Borrowings were cut from Rs 86 cr to Rs 10 cr during FY26 and the interest line has been zero throughout the record.
moat_note: No moat is claimed. What exists is a real but double-edged structural position: ACGL is one of India's larger bus bodybuilders and its promoter is also, in substance, its principal customer. Bus bodybuilding does carry genuine entry barriers — bus body code AIS-052 compliance, homologation of each variant, and the paint and jig capital needed to build at rate — which is why the organised segment is small and why an established builder is not casually displaced. But a captive relationship with a 49% shareholder is a contract and a concentration, not a franchise, and it means the margin is set in a negotiation rather than a market. The evidence that the business is well run is nonetheless unusually strong for this board: operating cash flow of Rs 136 cr in FY26 against Rs 86 cr of operating profit (186%), free cash flow of Rs 99 cr, the working capital cycle cut to two days, and a dividend paid in every profitable year of the record at 24-61% payout. The FY21 loss is what makes the rest credible — this is the only microcap added this week whose record contains a genuine downturn.
import_substitution: Real and structural. Bus bodies built in India on Indian chassis displace imported bus bodies and completely-built-unit coach imports, and the domestic bodybuilding industry exists substantially because of that substitution. Scored 13/20 rather than higher because the substitution is long-settled rather than something ACGL is currently driving.
risk_note: Customer concentration is the dominant risk and is structural: the promoter at 48.98% is also the principal customer, so a change in Tata Motors' bus volumes or its sourcing policy moves this company directly, and the FY21 collapse from Rs 489 cr to Rs 116 cr of revenue shows exactly how far that can go. Operating margin is only 9% even at record revenue, so this is a volume business with thin absolute buffer. The most recent quarter (Jun-26) shows margin back down to 5% on Rs 249 cr of sales, against 9% the quarter before, so the trailing figures are flattering. Promoter holding slipped from 49.77% to 48.98% in the March 2026 quarter — small, but the first movement in the record and worth watching given it takes the stake below the halfway mark. Operating cash flow has been negative in four of the last ten years, so the excellent FY26 figure is not a steady state. CWIP jumped from Rs 1 cr to Rs 25 cr.
why_obscure: 11,916 shareholders and effectively zero institutional ownership — FII 0.01%, no DII line at all — on a Rs 1,100 cr company that is a listed Tata Motors subsidiary with Rs 934 cr of revenue. That combination is the most striking under-coverage found in this week's microcap batch.
verify_comment: Screener standalone, ten years. The Tata Motors promoter holding of 48.98% is confirmed from the published shareholding pattern, which is an exchange filing rather than the company's marketing — but it verifies ownership, not a moat, so the row is graded 'none claimed' rather than 'verified'. No moat claim was located to test. Trendlyne news, corporate-events and insider/SAST endpoints were rate-limited and unreachable throughout this run, so pledging, insider activity and any auditor change are UNCHECKED.
data_note: Screener standalone; consolidated returned no data. Entered this week's batch as a replacement after four names in the original worklist turned out to be already on the board.
penalty_detail: -3 the promoter is also the principal customer, and FY21 showed revenue can fall 76% when that customer stops; -1 promoter slipped below 50% for the first time in the record.

name: Silkflex Polymers (India)
theme_detail: Water-based and solvent adhesives for footwear, furniture and packaging.
business: Manufactures polymer adhesives — water-based and solvent systems sold into footwear, furniture and packaging converters. Seven years of accounts: sales Rs 21 cr (FY20) to Rs 110 cr (FY26) with operating margin climbing 4% to 20% across that span. FY26 was a step-change capex year: net block went Rs 16 cr to Rs 66 cr with Rs 6 cr still in CWIP, funded by borrowings rising Rs 36 cr to Rs 62 cr.
moat_note: Adhesive formulation carries a modest but genuine switching cost — the adhesive is qualified into the customer's line speed, cure time and substrate, and a footwear or furniture converter does not re-qualify a bonding system casually. That is the extent of it. Silkflex is a small formulator in a market where Pidilite, Henkel and Jubilant sit above it, and no claim of a proprietary chemistry, patent or exclusive position was found in anything reachable. The margin record does show something: 4% to 20% operating margin over six years while revenue grew five-fold is not the shape of a price-taker, and unlike most of this week's batch it converted — CFO was Rs 29 cr against Rs 22 cr of operating profit in FY26 (146%). But FY25 CFO was Rs -30 cr, so one good year of conversion after one bad one is not yet a record. Graded company-stated: the margin expansion is the company's own reported figure and no external source speaks to its position.
import_substitution: Moderate and category-level. Specialty adhesive systems for footwear and furniture are partly imported, particularly at the high-performance end, and a domestic formulator displaces them. Nothing establishes Silkflex specifically at that end. 12/20.
risk_note: The balance sheet changed shape entirely in one year and the new shape is unproven: net block quadrupled to Rs 66 cr and borrowings rose 72% to Rs 62 cr, against Rs 48 cr of net worth, so this is now a leveraged company running a plant that has not completed a full year. Operating cash flow is violently lumpy — Rs -30 cr in FY25, Rs +29 cr in FY26 — and free cash flow has been negative in six of the last seven years. Inventory sits at 136 days and the cash conversion cycle at 133. The shareholder register is the second-thinnest in this batch at 443 and has fallen from 484, meaning the float is concentrating rather than broadening. There is no FII and the DII holding of 8.94% has been static for five quarters.
why_obscure: 443 shareholders. Effectively a private company with a listing.
verify_comment: Screener standalone, seven years. No external source checked. Trendlyne classifies this as Diversified Consumer Services / Furniture-Furnishing by end-market; it is treated as chemicals here because the company manufactures the polymer system rather than the furniture, and that reclassification is a judgement made in this pass. Pledging, insider activity and news are UNCHECKED — Trendlyne's endpoints were unreachable all run.
data_note: Screener standalone; consolidated returned no data.
penalty_detail: -5 borrowings up 72% to fund a 4x increase in net block that has not yet run a full year; -3 operating cash flow swung from Rs -30 cr to Rs +29 cr in consecutive years, so conversion is not yet a record.

name: G V Electricals
business: Heavy electrical equipment maker, listed 2026. Four years of accounts: sales Rs 104 cr (FY23) to Rs 156 cr (FY26), with operating margin moving 4.2%, 6%, 7%, 12%. Equity capital went from Rs 0.04 cr to Rs 8 cr on listing. Borrowings doubled to Rs 16 cr in FY26.
moat_note: No moat claimed and none evident. This is a small electrical equipment fabricator whose reported returns rest on a very small capital base — Rs 78 cr of total assets carrying Rs 156 cr of sales — rather than on any defended position. The 40.8% ROCE that put it on the screen is a turnover artefact of that leverage, not pricing power. The margin doubling from 6% to 12% across two years is the one thing that would need explaining if it were durable, and there is no explanation available and no cash to corroborate it.
import_substitution: Category-plausible only: domestically made electrical equipment displaces imports in a broad sense. Nothing specific to this company. 9/20.
risk_note: Operating cash flow was Rs -3 cr in FY26 against Rs 18 cr of operating profit — a conversion rate of 3%, and negative in absolute terms in the year margin supposedly doubled. Free cash flow was Rs -6 cr. Debtor days rose from 86 to 119 and working capital days from 31 to 51, which is where the missing cash went: the reported profit is sitting in receivables. Days payable were 206 in FY23 and 187 in FY24 and are no longer reported, so the company was previously financing itself on its suppliers to an extreme degree. Only four years of accounts, none of them pre-listing. 724 shareholders.
why_obscure: 724 shareholders on a 2026 listing.
verify_comment: Screener standalone, four years. No external source checked. No quarterly results are published in the data source, so the FY26 margin jump cannot be traced through the year. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.
data_note: Screener standalone; consolidated returned no data. No quarterly series available. FY25 EPS of Rs 11,365 is pre-split.
penalty_detail: -6 CFO/operating-profit of 3% and negative free cash flow in the year margin doubled; -2 debtor days 86 to 119; -2 four years of accounts and no quarterly series.

name: Gallard Steel
business: Castings and forgings producer, listed 2025-26. Six years of accounts: sales Rs 9 cr (FY21) to Rs 57 cr (FY26), with operating margin stepping from 9% to 19% in FY24 and holding there. Reserves jumped Rs 8.5 cr to Rs 45 cr in FY26 on the issue proceeds; borrowings are modest at Rs 12 cr.
moat_note: No moat claimed, none found. A 19% operating margin is high for castings — Bhagwati Autocast, a longer-established foundry added to this board in the same batch, runs 14% — which suggests either a specialised product mix or a margin that has not been tested through a cycle. Six years of accounts, four of them pre-scale, cannot distinguish those. Note that the screen caught this name at ROCE 23.33% but the current Screener figure is already 20.75%, so the quality metric that qualified it is softening in real time.
import_substitution: Ordinary category plausibility for castings; nothing specific established. 10/20.
risk_note: Cash conversion is poor and getting worse: CFO Rs 1.46 cr against Rs 11 cr of operating profit in FY26, a rate of 33%, down from 49% and against free cash flow that has been negative in four of six years. Debtor days sit at 112 and have not improved in three years. The shareholder register is the thinnest of the twenty names read this week — 392, down from 637 in four months — so the float is actively concentrating and the price is set by almost nobody. ROCE has already fallen from 26.9% to 20.8% in one year. P/E of 27 is the second-highest in this batch on the shortest record.
why_obscure: 392 shareholders — the thinnest register on this week's batch, and falling.
verify_comment: Screener standalone, six years. No external source checked. Only two quarterly datapoints are published, so the margin cannot be traced within the year. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.
data_note: Screener standalone. The screen row used ROCE 23.33%; Screener's current figure is 20.75% and the lower figure is carried here.
penalty_detail: -4 CFO/operating-profit 33% and negative FCF in four of six years; -3 shareholder register down 637 to 392, extreme float concentration; -2 ROCE already down 26.9% to 20.8%.

name: Happy Steels
business: Auto parts and equipment maker. Six years of accounts and the top line has barely moved in them: sales Rs 77 cr (FY21), Rs 88 cr, Rs 94 cr, Rs 81 cr, Rs 82 cr, Rs 95 cr (FY26) — a compound rate of 4.1% over five years. Operating margin is where the whole story sits, moving 5.8%, 3.2%, 5.5%, 12.0%, 9.9%, 14.2%. Equity capital went Rs 1.5 cr to Rs 10.5 cr in FY26 on a bonus or restructuring, and reserves fell from Rs 31.4 cr to Rs 29.5 cr in the same year despite Rs 7.1 cr of profit.
moat_note: No moat claimed and nothing in the record suggests one. Revenue has been flat for six years, which rules out the market-share gain that usually accompanies a real advantage, and the margin series oscillates rather than trends — 12.0% in FY24, back to 9.9% in FY25, up to 14.2% in FY26. A business whose margin moves 4 percentage points in either direction year to year is a price-taker whose input costs happen to move. This is the lowest-quality gate-passer added to the microcap board this week on the gate that matters most: ROCE of 15.86% clears the 12% floor but sits below where this board usually looks, and it was 8.91% as recently as FY25.
import_substitution: Category-plausible for auto components, nothing specific established. 10/20.
risk_note: Working capital is the problem and it is getting worse rather than better: inventory days went 180, 187, 138, 251, 259, 303 and the cash conversion cycle stands at 312 days, up from 161 in FY23. The company finances ten months of stock. Borrowings of Rs 47 cr exceed net worth of Rs 40 cr, and interest of Rs 2.62 cr consumes 20% of operating profit. Reserves FELL in FY26 despite a Rs 7.1 cr profit, which the available data does not explain and which is the single item most worth chasing on this row. Screener publishes no quarterly series and no cash-flow data at all before FY24, so four of the six years cannot be checked for cash. Only 454 shareholders — joint-thinnest register in this batch. ROCE at 15.9% is barely above the board's floor and has been below it inside the record.
why_obscure: 454 shareholders, though a domestic institution holds 12.00%, so someone has looked.
verify_comment: Screener standalone, six years, with cash-flow data only from FY24 and no quarterly series. The FY26 fall in reserves alongside a reported profit is UNEXPLAINED by anything in the available data and is flagged rather than resolved. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.
data_note: Screener standalone; consolidated returned no data. Cash-flow rows show 0.00 for FY21-FY23, which is absent data rather than zero cash flow.
penalty_detail: -4 cash conversion cycle of 312 days and inventory at 303 days, both worsening; -3 borrowings exceed net worth and interest takes 20% of operating profit; -3 reserves fell in FY26 despite a reported Rs 7.1 cr profit, unexplained.

name: Susan Electricals India
business: Wire and cable manufacturer, listed 2026. Six years of accounts: sales Rs 49 cr (FY21) to Rs 269 cr (FY26), with revenue doubling in the final year alone. Operating margin moved 1.8%, 2.2%, 1.7%, 3.5%, 9%, 12% — a step-change from commodity economics to something far better, all of it in the last two years.
moat_note: No moat claimed and the sector does not offer one — wire and cable is a conversion business priced off the copper or aluminium input, which is exactly what the FY21-FY24 margins of 1.7% to 3.5% describe. The question this row turns on is what changed in FY25-FY26 to take margin to 12%, and nothing reachable answers it. A genuine move up the value chain into specialty or LSZH cable would do it; so would a change in what is being reported. The cash flow argues for scepticism: operating cash flow has been negative in all three of FY24, FY25 and FY26 — Rs -5 cr, Rs -18 cr, Rs -10 cr — precisely the years margin expanded. A margin improvement that never reaches the bank account is the single most common way a screen like this one gets fooled.
import_substitution: Category-plausible: domestically drawn wire and cable substitutes imports at the margin. Nothing specific. 9/20.
risk_note: Growth is entirely debt-funded and the cash has never arrived. Borrowings went Rs 25 cr to Rs 45 cr to Rs 67 cr across FY24-FY26 while cumulative operating cash flow over those three years was Rs -33 cr; free cash flow was Rs -10 cr, Rs -20 cr and Rs -14 cr. Inventory days rose from 42 to 93 to 83 and the cash conversion cycle from 63 to 135 to 115 days. The ROE of 64.6% is arithmetic, not quality — it is a Rs 18 cr profit on a Rs 39 cr equity base that was Rs 6 cr two years ago. The Jun-25 quarter was a loss (Rs -0.42 cr) as recently as four quarters ago, so the earnings series is not stable. Interest cost of Rs 7 cr already consumes 22% of operating profit.
why_obscure: 1,247 shareholders on a 2026 listing.
verify_comment: Screener standalone, six years. No external source checked. The margin step-change is the central unexplained fact and this row does not pretend to have explained it. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.
data_note: Screener standalone; consolidated returned no data.
penalty_detail: -6 operating cash flow negative in all three years of the margin expansion, cumulative Rs -33 cr; -2 borrowings up 168% over the same period; -2 CCC 63 to 115 days.

name: Parmeshwar Metal
theme_detail: Copper conversion. Trendlyne classifies this as Consumer Durables / Other Electrical Equipment; the accounts describe a metals conversion business and it is filed accordingly here.
business: Copper conversion — nine years of accounts showing sales of Rs 213 cr (FY19) rising to Rs 1,973 cr (FY26) carried on a total asset base of just Rs 140 cr. Operating margin across the entire record has been 1.0% to 2.2%. This is a throughput business: metal in, metal out, a conversion fee in between.
moat_note: No moat is claimed and none exists, and the important thing this row records is why the screen was wrong to be impressed. The 43.5% ROCE that ranked Parmeshwar second in this week's worklist is arithmetic: Rs 43 cr of operating profit on Rs 140 cr of assets looks like a superb return until you notice the Rs 1,973 cr of revenue it took to generate it, at a 2.2% margin. Asset turns of 14x will produce a high ROCE on almost any margin, and a 2% margin means the business has no pricing power whatever — a 2% move in the copper spread wipes out the entire profit. This is the clearest example in this week's batch of the high-ROCE-low-quality trap the pre-score is prone to, and it is worth keeping on the board as that example. Cash conversion in FY26 was genuinely good (CFO Rs 22 cr, 76% of operating profit) after four poor years, which is the one point in its favour.
import_substitution: Weak. Domestic copper conversion displaces imported copper products in a broad sense, but a converter working on a 2% spread is not substituting anything at a technology level. 8/20.
risk_note: A 2.2% operating margin is the whole risk: the business has no buffer against a copper price move, a customer default or a working-capital squeeze, and Rs 1,973 cr of revenue passing through a Rs 140 cr balance sheet means small percentage errors are large absolute ones. FY26 margin at 2.2% is itself the best in the record (FY24 was 1.0%), so the current earnings are cycle-peak on the only metric that matters. Only 477 shareholders and the register is shrinking fast — 721 to 633 to 477 across three disclosures. Institutional holders have left almost entirely: FII 1.93% to 0.00% and DII 4.07% to 0.03% over the same three disclosures. Free cash flow was negative in four of the last six years.
why_obscure: 477 shareholders and both institutional categories at effectively zero after exiting.
verify_comment: Screener standalone, nine years. No external source checked. Kept on the board deliberately as a worked example of a high ROCE that is a turnover artefact rather than a quality signal. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.
data_note: Screener standalone; consolidated returned no data. EPS series is not comparable across the FY24 equity restructuring.
penalty_detail: -4 operating margin of 2.2% leaves no buffer against a copper-spread move; -2 both institutional categories exited to near-zero and the shareholder register fell 721 to 477.

name: Automotive Stampings & Assemblies
theme_detail: Tier-1 sheet-metal stampings and welded assemblies.
business: Tier-1 supplier of sheet-metal stampings, welded assemblies and modules to vehicle makers, with a ten-year record on Screener and a promoter holding 75%. Sales Rs 331 cr (FY18) to Rs 891 cr (FY26), TTM Rs 971 cr. The defining feature of the record is the turnaround: losses in FY18, FY19, FY20 and FY21 totalling roughly Rs 107 cr drove reserves to Rs -105 cr, and FY26 is the first year since 2017 that the company has had positive reserves at all (Rs 20 cr).
moat_note: No moat claimed. Tier-1 stamping carries a genuine, well-understood and strictly time-limited switching cost: the press tooling is dedicated to the customer's platform and paid for around the part, so the supplier is locked in for the life of that model and has no protection at all when the platform is re-sourced. That is a contract, not a moat, and it is why stamping runs at 6-7% operating margin worldwide. The reason to hold this row is not the moat but that it is the only genuine Tier-1 automotive supplier the microcap screen surfaced this week, with real scale (Rs 971 cr TTM revenue) and a professional promoter at the 75% ceiling. Operating cash flow of Rs 59 cr in FY26 at 101% of operating profit is the strongest absolute cash generation in the batch.
import_substitution: Real at the category level — domestically stamped body and structural parts displace imported pressings and are a standard localisation target for vehicle makers building in India. Nothing establishes a specific substituted import. 12/20.
risk_note: The 128% ROE on this row is an arithmetic artefact and must not be read as a quality signal: it is Rs 28 cr of profit against an equity base of Rs 36 cr that was NEGATIVE Rs 7 cr twelve months earlier. As reserves normalise, the ratio will collapse toward the mid-teens without anything about the business changing. Related and more consequential: the effective tax rate has been 0% for eight straight years on carried-forward losses, and that shield is now exhausting — the Jun-26 quarter carried a 25.08% charge, the first normal rate in the record. Reported profit growth from here faces a roughly 25% headwind that has nothing to do with operations. Borrowings are Rs 124 cr against Rs 36 cr of equity. At 32,616 shareholders this is the least under-covered name added this week; it clears the 40,000 gate but the register is falling (36,175 to 32,616 in five quarters), which is the direction that keeps it eligible rather than any distinction.
why_obscure: It is not, comparatively — 32,616 shareholders is inside the gate but four times the batch median. It earns its place on being a real Tier-1 supplier at Rs 793 cr with no institutional coverage (FII 0.09%, DII 0.00%) rather than on obscurity, and s_undercovered of 5/15 says so.

data_note: Screener standalone. ROE of 128% is reported as-is from the source and is disclaimed in risk_note; it reflects a near-zero equity base, not operating quality.

name: ANB Metal Cast
business: Aluminium casting and alloy producer. Five years of accounts: sales Rs 51 cr (FY22) to Rs 225 cr (FY26), operating margin from 1.3% to 14%. Reserves jumped Rs 25 cr to Rs 87 cr in FY26 as the issue landed; borrowings rose to Rs 47 cr alongside.
moat_note: No moat claimed. Secondary aluminium alloying is a scrap-spread business and the FY22-FY23 margins of 1.3% and 3.8% are what that looks like unaided; the move to 14% over three years is the claim the row turns on and nothing reachable explains it. The cash flow contradicts it outright — see risk_note. Aluminium alloy production does have a genuine input advantage when built around a secured scrap supply, which is the most plausible benign explanation, but no evidence for it was located.
import_substitution: Genuine at the category level: India imports primary and alloyed aluminium, and domestic secondary alloy displaces it directly. This is a real substitution channel and scores 11/20 on that basis, held down because the company's own contribution is unquantified.
risk_note: The cash flow is the problem and it is severe: FY26 operating cash flow was Rs -38 cr against Rs 32 cr of operating profit, a conversion rate of MINUS 114%, and free cash flow was Rs -44 cr. Operating cash flow has been negative in four of the five reported years. The entire FY26 expansion was funded by Rs 55 cr of financing inflows. Working capital is deteriorating in every component: inventory days 85 to 138, debtor days 81 to 110, cash conversion cycle 104 to 202 days in a single year. Only 624 shareholders. Five years of accounts, none pre-listing.

name: IC Electricals Company
business: Electronic components maker, listed 2026. Three years of accounts: sales Rs 99 cr, Rs 121 cr, Rs 144 cr with operating margin rising 13%, 16%, 19%. Fixed assets are almost nil at Rs 3 cr against Rs 191 cr of total assets, so essentially the entire balance sheet is working capital.
moat_note: No moat claimed and the balance-sheet shape argues against one existing. A manufacturer with Rs 3 cr of net block supporting Rs 144 cr of sales is not manufacturing much — it is holding inventory and extending credit, which is a distribution or assembly economics, and inventory days of 402 confirm it. Margin has improved for three straight years, but with only three years visible and none of them pre-listing, there is no way to know whether 19% is a level or a peak.
import_substitution: Category-plausible for electronic components, which India imports heavily. But a business with almost no fixed assets is more likely sourcing than substituting, and that ambiguity is exactly what cannot be resolved here. 9/20.
risk_note: Operating cash flow has been negative in every one of the three reported years — Rs -2 cr, Rs -8 cr, Rs -11 cr — and has got worse each year while margin improved. The cash conversion cycle is 349 days against inventory of 402 days, meaning the company finances more than a year of stock. Interest of Rs 8 cr consumes 30% of operating profit and borrowings have risen to Rs 74 cr against Rs 65 cr of net worth. Promoter holding of 60.94% is the lowest but one in this batch. name: Medico Remedies
business: Generic pharmaceutical formulations — tablets, capsules and liquids — sold substantially into export markets. Ten years of accounts: sales Rs 61 cr (FY18) to Rs 206 cr (FY26), TTM Rs 238 cr, so growth is real and sustained at about 16% compound. ROCE has improved steadily from 8% (FY19) to 23% (FY26).
moat_note: No moat claimed and the margin says there isn't one. Operating margin has never exceeded 10% in ten years and is 8% on the latest full year — that is contract-manufacturing and commodity-generic economics, where the customer specifies the product and the price is the variable. The improvement in ROCE from 8% to 23% is genuine but is asset-turn and scale, not pricing power: the fixed asset base has been flat at Rs 20-22 cr since FY23 while revenue nearly doubled. The quarterly margin series is the tell — 16.13%, 7.37%, 5.19%, 7.38%, 12.59%, 4.76% across the last six quarters, a range of more than 11 percentage points with no seasonal pattern, which is what order-mix volatility looks like in a business with no price-setting power.
import_substitution: Weak in the direction this board screens for. Medico is an exporter of Indian generics rather than a substituter of imports into India, so it strengthens the trade balance without displacing an import. Scored 10/20 on that distinction being worth something but not what the thesis asks for.
risk_note: Promoter holding fell from 63.79% to 61.38% between March and September 2025, a reduction of 2.41 percentage points, which crosses this board's 2-point flag threshold. It has been flat at 61.38% for three disclosures since. Receivables are the structural weakness: debtor days have risen 94, 125, 138, 145 across four years and now exceed four and a half months, and cash conversion has fallen to 43-64% of operating profit over the last three years against 104-111% in FY22-FY23. Free cash flow has been roughly break-even or negative for most of the record. Borrowings have started rising again, Rs 8 cr to Rs 19 cr over two years. No dividend has ever been paid in the ten-year record despite consistent profitability.
why_obscure: 15,863 shareholders with essentially no institutional holder — FII 0.08%, DII 0.00%. Well inside the coverage gate but the least obscure pharma name added this week.

name: Anawil Wire and Engineering
business: Wire and engineering products manufacturer. Four years of accounts: sales Rs 26 cr (FY23) to Rs 143 cr (FY26). Reported operating margin across the whole record is 50%, 42%, 38%, 43%. FY26 was a transforming capex year — net block Rs 59 cr to Rs 136 cr, borrowings Rs 55 cr to Rs 128 cr, total assets Rs 114 cr to Rs 292 cr.
moat_note: DEBUNKED. The claim carried by these accounts is a 43% operating margin in wire drawing, and it does not survive comparison with the listed comparable set. Rajratan Global Wire, the best-regarded specialist in Indian wire with a genuine niche in bead wire and a near-duopoly position in tyre bead, runs mid-teens operating margins. D P Wires runs low single digits. Excellent Wires and the rest of the small-cap wire cohort sit between. Anawil reports two to eight times the margin of every one of them, in the same product category, at a fraction of the scale, with four years of history and no disclosed technology, patent, certification or customer relationship that would explain it. That is not a moat claim that has been checked and found weak; it is a claim that is inconsistent with the economics of the industry it operates in. Two further facts point the same way: inventory stands at 409 days, so the margin is embedded in stock that has not been sold, and cash conversion has never exceeded 47% of operating profit in any year. A high margin held in inventory rather than converted to cash is the standard signature of the problem this grade exists to record.
import_substitution: Nominally category-plausible for specialty wire, but since the underlying margin claim is debunked there is no basis for crediting a technology-led substitution story. 7/20.
risk_note: Beyond the margin question: FY26 free cash flow was Rs -75 cr, borrowings rose 133% to Rs 128 cr in one year, and the company now carries Rs 128 cr of debt against Rs 90 cr of net worth to run a plant that has not completed a full year. Inventory days of 409 and payable days of 376 mean the company is financing more than a year of stock on its suppliers, an arrangement that unwinds violently if supplier terms tighten. Screener publishes no quarterly series for this name, so nothing can be traced within the year. Four years of accounts, none pre-listing. Market capitalisation of Rs 1,163 cr on Rs 37 cr of profit and a P/E of 31.7 leaves no margin for the margin being wrong.

name: GTV Engineering
business: Industrial machinery maker with a ten-year record on Screener. Sales Rs 50 cr (FY18) rising to Rs 120 cr (FY24) and then FALLING to Rs 102 cr in both FY25 and FY26. Operating margin over the same period: 2.7%, 2.2%, 2.0%, 2.4%, 1.9%, 2.7%, 4.5%, 16%, 18%.
moat_note: DEBUNKED. The implied claim is that a business which earned 2-4% operating margins for seven consecutive years discovered an eight-fold margin improvement in FY25. What makes it not survive checking is that the improvement arrived while revenue FELL 15%, from Rs 120 cr to Rs 102 cr, and has stayed flat there for two years. Genuine pricing power or a genuine mix shift into a defended niche shows up as margin and revenue moving together, or at worst margin rising while revenue holds. Margin octupling on shrinking revenue is more consistent with the company having exited its volume business and retained a small high-margin remainder — in which case the 30% ROCE describes a Rs 102 cr rump, not a franchise — or with a change in what is being recognised. Three corroborating facts point away from a franchise: cash conversion is 42% of operating profit and 39% the year before, against 100%+ in the low-margin years; the quarterly margin series is wildly unstable (8.2%, 23.7%, 28.5%, 17.6%, 14.8%, 27.6%, 12.4%, 17.8%), which is not what a structural improvement looks like; and the promoter has sold into it.
import_substitution: Nominally category-plausible for domestically built machinery. With the margin claim debunked there is nothing on which to build a technology-substitution case. 9/20.
risk_note: Promoter holding fell from 64.44% to 57.88% across the FY26 disclosures, a drop of 6.56 percentage points, concentrated in the June and December 2025 quarters — the same period in which the new margin level was being reported. The shareholder register went 2,121 to 4,862 to 9,503 and has since fallen back to 7,870, a churn pattern consistent with a promoter placement being distributed and then partly exiting. Quarterly margin swings between 8% and 28% with no seasonal logic. Cash conversion is 42% of operating profit. Revenue has not grown in two years. Rs 10 cr of the Rs 93 cr balance sheet sits in investments rather than the business.
why_obscure: 7,870 shareholders and effectively no institutional holder, though the register quadrupled and then shrank within eighteen months, so this is churn rather than settled under-coverage.
verify_comment: The DEBUNKED grade rests on facts internal to Screener's own ten-year series — margin octupling on falling revenue, cash conversion collapsing as margin rose, and the promoter reducing 6.56pp over the same two quarters. No external source was checked and Trendlyne's insider/SAST endpoint, which would show exactly how the promoter stake was reduced, was unreachable this run. That is the first check to run next week.
data_note: Screener standalone. Equity capital rose Rs 3 cr to Rs 9 cr in FY26 (face value Rs 2), so per-share figures are not comparable across that year.
penalty_detail: -5 promoter reduced 6.56pp in the two quarters the new margin level was reported; -2 cash conversion fell to 42% as margin rose; -2 revenue down 15% and flat for two years.

name: De Neers Tools
business: Hand tools — spanners, wrenches and the branded mechanic's-tool range. Five reporting periods on Screener: sales Rs 60 cr (FY22, nine months) to Rs 158 cr (FY26), with operating margin rising 12% to 21%. Fixed assets are Rs 2 cr against Rs 196 cr of total assets, so this is a brand-and-inventory business rather than a manufacturing one.
moat_note: DEBUNKED. The claim a branded hand-tool business makes is brand pricing power, and the 21% operating margin is offered as the evidence. It does not survive two checks. First, the margin has never become cash: operating cash flow was Rs -49 cr, Rs -25 cr, Rs -17 cr, Rs +20 cr and Rs -14 cr across the five reported periods, so in four of five the business consumed cash while reporting rising profit, and the cash conversion cycle stands at 489 DAYS — the company holds and finances more than sixteen months of working capital to produce a 21% margin. A brand that had genuine pricing power would collect faster, not slower. Second, and decisively, the people best placed to judge the brand have been selling it: promoter holding fell from 62.38% to 42.80% across four disclosures between September 2024 and July 2026, a reduction of 19.58 percentage points, or very nearly a third of the promoter's stake, while the margin was being reported as improving. Rs 2 cr of net block also makes clear that De Neers is largely sourcing and branding rather than making, which caps how deep any moat could be.
import_substitution: Weak to negative. A business with Rs 2 cr of fixed assets against Rs 158 cr of sales is buying tools rather than making them; whether the source is domestic or imported is not disclosed anywhere reachable, and if imported, this row runs against the board's thesis rather than with it. 6/20 and it should probably be lower.
risk_note: Promoter holding at 42.80% is only 2.80 percentage points above the board's 40% gate, and the trajectory — 62.38%, 47.54%, 46.25%, 42.80% — points at it. If the next disclosure continues at anything like this rate the company fails the skin-in-the-game gate outright. Inventory days of 436 and a cash conversion cycle of 489 days on Rs 73 cr of borrowings is a financing structure with very little slack. Free cash flow has been negative in four of five reported periods, cumulatively about Rs -91 cr. The P/E of 7.31 is the lowest in this batch and is better read as the market pricing these facts than as value.
why_obscure: 941 shareholders — but the register has been churning (635, 602, 1,224, 1,052, 1,020, 941) rather than sitting undiscovered.

Trendlyne's insider/SAST endpoint, which would show whether the reduction was an open-market sale, a pledge invocation or a placement, was unreachable this run — that distinction matters and is the first thing to check next week.

name: Aptus Pharma
business: Pharmaceuticals, listed 2025. Four years of accounts and they are small: sales Rs 13.9 cr (FY23) to Rs 46.6 cr (FY26), net profit Rs 4.62 cr. The market capitalisation is Rs 498 cr, which is 107.9 times those earnings and roughly eleven times revenue.
moat_note: DEBUNKED. The claim is a 16-20% operating margin pharma business growing at 90% a year, and the row is priced at 108x earnings on it. It fails the only test this pass can apply and fails it completely: operating cash flow has been negative in every single reported year — Rs -0.18 cr, Rs -2.17 cr, Rs -1.84 cr and Rs -6.86 cr — and the FY26 figure is negative against Rs 7.45 cr of reported operating profit, a conversion rate of minus 76%. Four years of a company that has never, in any year of its existence as a reporting entity, turned its stated profit into cash. The working capital tells the same story: inventory at 232 days, receivables at 147 days and a cash conversion cycle of 240 days, all deteriorating. The corroborating fact is the ownership: FII holding went from 10.03% to 0.00% and DII from 2.80% to 0.00% between the September and December 2025 disclosures — every institutional holder exited completely in a single quarter, and none has returned in the two disclosures since.

Financing inflows of Rs 9.04 cr in FY26 exceeded net profit and funded the working capital the operations did not. Free cash flow was Rs -9.05 cr in FY26 and negative in all four years. The complete and simultaneous exit of both institutional holders in the December 2025 quarter is the most direct adverse signal available on any row added this week. Four years of accounts, none pre-listing.

No allegation is made about the accounts; what is recorded is that reported profit has never converted to cash and that both institutional holders exited in full in one quarter. Trendlyne news and insider/SAST endpoints were unreachable this run.

name: Speciality Medicines
business: Pharmaceuticals. Five years of accounts with a discontinuity in them: sales fell Rs 40 cr (FY22) to Rs 23 cr (FY23) and then rose to Rs 75 cr (FY26) at a much higher margin, so the pre-FY23 and post-FY23 businesses are not obviously the same business. Fixed assets are Rs 2 cr against Rs 95 cr of total assets.
moat_note: DEBUNKED. The returns that put this name on the screen are not produced by operations. The effective tax rate was 36% in FY24, then 1% in FY25 and MINUS 0% in FY26 — a company reporting Rs 9 cr and then Rs 13 cr of pre-tax profit and paying essentially no tax on either. Net profit rose from Rs 3 cr to Rs 9 cr to Rs 13 cr, but pre-tax profit rose from Rs 5 cr to Rs 9 cr to Rs 13 cr: a material part of the earnings growth that produced the 25.6% ROE is the tax line going to zero, not the business improving. There may be a legitimate explanation — a tax-holiday unit under section 80-IC/80-IE, or a MAT credit being drawn down — and nothing reachable in this pass discloses one, which is precisely the problem: the single largest driver of the reported return is unexplained. Alongside that, operating cash flow has been negative in every year since FY23 (Rs -4 cr, -5 cr, -6 cr, -1 cr) and working capital days have gone from -3 to 221. A moat claim resting on returns that come from the tax line and never reach the bank account does not survive checking.

risk_note: Promoter holding is 43.43%, the lowest of any name added this week and only 3.43 percentage points above the board's 40% gate. Only one shareholding disclosure is available in the data source, so whether that figure is stable or falling cannot be determined — a material gap on a company this close to the gate. The zero tax charge is unexplained (see moat_note) and if it normalises to 25% the reported profit falls by a quarter with no operational change. The FY22-FY23 revenue halving from Rs 40 cr to Rs 23 cr suggests a business discontinuity that the record does not describe. Operating cash flow negative for four straight years. 757 shareholders.

No allegation is made; what is recorded is that the return metrics which qualified this company for the screen are driven by an unexplained zero tax charge. name: Ahmedabad Steelcraft
business: Iron and steel intermediate products. The ten-year record contains two entirely different companies. From FY18 to FY24 the entity reported Rs 9 cr, Rs 10 cr, Rs 7 cr, Rs 2 cr, Rs 1 cr, Rs 2 cr and Rs 1 cr of sales, with an operating loss in every one of those seven years — FY24 showed an operating margin of MINUS 609%. Then FY25 reported Rs 172 cr of sales and FY26 Rs 221 cr, at 7% and 11% margins. Total assets went from Rs 23 cr to Rs 220 cr over the same two years, of which Rs 215 cr is 'other assets' and Rs 4 cr is fixed assets.
moat_note: DEBUNKED, and it is the clearest case in this week's batch. The 22.2% ROCE that put this name on the screen is generated by a business that did not exist two years ago and is not visible in the balance sheet. A company reporting Rs 221 cr of revenue on Rs 4 cr of fixed assets and Rs 0 of inventory is not manufacturing iron and steel products — inventory days are recorded as zero for the entire record, which for a steel intermediate producer is not a low number, it is an impossible one. What the balance sheet does show is Rs 215 cr of receivables and other current assets, against debtor days of 349 — that is, on average the company waits eleven and a half months to be paid. The cash flow confirms it: operating cash flow was MINUS Rs 77 cr in FY25 and MINUS Rs 22 cr in FY26, so across the entire two-year transformation the business has consumed Rs 99 cr of cash while reporting Rs 30 cr of profit. Any moat claim resting on a 22% ROCE produced this way does not survive the first check.
import_substitution: Nothing established, and with Rs 4 cr of fixed assets against Rs 221 cr of sales there is no manufacturing base on which a substitution claim could rest. 5/20 on bare category membership.
risk_note: Seven consecutive loss years to FY24 followed by an unexplained Rs 172 cr revenue step in FY25 is the central fact and it is not explained by any capex — fixed assets were Rs 0 cr in FY24 and Rs 4 cr in FY26. Working capital days peaked at 1,296 in FY22 and stand at 211. Debtor days of 349 mean the reported profit is entirely uncollected. The quarterly series is already reversing: Rs 64.7 cr of sales at 16.2% margin in Sep-25 against Rs 38.7 cr at 5.4% in Jun-26, the weakest quarter since the transformation began. Other liabilities rose from Rs 0 cr to Rs 84 cr in two years, so the receivables are being funded by payables, an arrangement that unwinds without warning. The effective tax rate was 0% in Sep-24, 7.9% in Dec-24 and 15.8% in Mar-26 against a 25% norm.
why_obscure: 3,138 shareholders and no institutional holder of any kind.

No allegation is made about the accounts and none can be from this evidence; what is recorded is that the return metrics which qualified this company for the screen are not supported by its balance sheet or its cash flow. Trendlyne news and insider/SAST endpoints were unreachable this run and are the obvious next check.

name: National Aluminium Company
theme_detail: Integrated bauxite-alumina-aluminium, Navratna CPSE under the Ministry of Mines.
business: Fully integrated aluminium producer: it owns the Panchpatmali bauxite mine in Odisha, the Damanjodi alumina refinery, the Angul smelter and captive coal-fired power to run it. Ten years of accounts. FY26 sales Rs 17,843 cr with a 44% operating margin, operating cash flow Rs 6,438 cr and free cash flow Rs 4,413 cr, against borrowings of Rs 60 cr against Rs 21,603 cr of net worth — effectively debt-free at scale. Dividend payout has been 36-82% in every profitable year of the record.
moat_note: The moat is captive raw material and captive power, and it is structural rather than commercial. An aluminium smelter's cost position is set almost entirely by what it pays for alumina and electricity; NALCO mines its own bauxite under a long-dated lease, refines its own alumina and generates its own power, which places it in the low-cost part of the global cost curve and is the reason a 44% operating margin is achievable in a commodity. That advantage cannot be replicated by a competitor with capital alone — it needs a bauxite lease, and those are granted by the state, not bought. What is VERIFIED here is the ownership and the conferred status: the exchange-filed shareholding pattern shows the President of India holding 51.28%, and NALCO's Navratna designation is conferred by the Department of Public Enterprises, both sources outside the company. What is NOT verified is the cost-curve position itself, which rests on the company's own disclosure and on general industry knowledge — that part is company-stated, and the split is recorded here deliberately rather than letting the 'verified' grade cover more than it earned.
import_substitution: Direct and large. India is a net importer of aluminium and of downstream aluminium products; NALCO's metal displaces those imports and its alumina is exported, so it works on both sides of the trade balance. Aluminium is also on the government's critical-minerals list, which makes domestic primary capacity a policy objective and not merely a commercial one. Scored 16/20 — held back from higher only because the substitution is long-established rather than something NALCO is currently expanding.
risk_note: The 44% operating margin and 39.6% ROCE that place this row at the top of the moat board are cycle-peak figures, and the record proves how far they move: operating margin was 6% in FY20, 32% in FY22, 16% in FY23 and is 44% now, tracking the LME aluminium price rather than anything NALCO controls. A reader who anchors on the current ROCE will be anchoring on the top of a commodity cycle. Capital work in progress has grown from Rs 566 cr to Rs 6,395 cr across the record — a very large expansion whose returns are unproven and which, in a state-owned enterprise, is directed partly by policy rather than purely by return on capital. That is the standing risk with a PSU: the controlling shareholder has objectives beyond the share price, and dividend policy, capex and pricing can all reflect them. Inventory days of 261 and a 152-day cash conversion cycle are high even for a mining-to-metal chain.
verify_comment: The 'verified' grade covers exactly two things and no more: Government of India promoter holding of 51.28%, from the exchange-filed shareholding pattern, and Navratna CPSE status, conferred by the Department of Public Enterprises. Both are sources that are not the company, which is what CRITERIA.md requires. The cost-curve and integration claims are the company's own and are treated as company-stated inside the moat note. Trendlyne's news, corporate-events and insider/SAST endpoints were rate-limited and unreachable throughout this run, so pledging and insider activity are UNCHECKED.

name: Force Motors
theme_detail: Light commercial vehicles and contract engine/axle manufacture for German OEMs.
business: Builds the Traveller light commercial vehicle range, the Gurkha off-road SUV and agricultural tractors, and separately manufactures engines and axles on contract for Mercedes-Benz India and BMW India. Ten years of accounts containing a genuine cycle: losses of Rs 124 cr (FY21) and Rs 91 cr (FY22) with ROCE at -5%, recovering to Rs 1,212 cr of profit and 36% ROCE in FY26. Borrowings have been repaid entirely — Rs 1,069 cr in FY22 to Rs 0 in FY26 — while operating cash flow ran at 116% of operating profit and free cash flow reached Rs 761 cr.
moat_note: The strongest non-state moat evidence in this week's moat-board batch, and it is worth being precise about what it is. Force Motors manufactures engines and axles to Mercedes-Benz and BMW specification in India. A German premium OEM does not qualify an engine line casually: it requires process capability the supplier must build over years, it is audited continuously, and once a powertrain programme is running the OEM cannot re-source it inside a model cycle without re-homologating the vehicle. That is a deep and time-limited switching cost, and it is also an implicit third-party endorsement of Force's process quality that no marketing claim could substitute for. Crucially, though, the arrangement is disclosed by FORCE, not by Daimler or BMW in their own filings, and this pass located no customer filing or contract award to confirm scope or duration — so it is graded company-stated, not verified, and upgrading it would need exactly that customer-side document. The vehicle business is a weaker moat: Traveller has a long-held position in the 10-26 seat passenger van niche where scale economics deter entrants, but it competes directly with Mahindra and Ashok Leyland and has no structural protection.
import_substitution: Direct and exactly what this board screens for. Engines and axles for German premium vehicles assembled in India were previously imported as completely-knocked-down kits; building them locally substitutes that import content directly and is the reason the arrangement exists. The Traveller and Gurkha ranges are entirely domestically designed and built. Scored 16/20.
risk_note: Other income of Rs 322 cr in FY26 is 22% of operating profit and is extremely lumpy — the Dec-25 quarter alone carried Rs 241 cr against Rs 374 cr of operating profit, and the Mar-25 quarter Rs 418 cr. Anyone reading the profit line without stripping this out will badly misjudge the trend, and nothing reachable explains what it is. The record contains two consecutive loss years (FY21, FY22) with ROCE at -5% and -3%, so the current 36% is a cycle-high on a business that has demonstrably gone negative. The shareholder register nearly doubled in twelve months, from 56,164 to 94,439, which usually means retail crowding into a stock that has already re-rated. Dividend payout is only 5% despite Rs 1,212 cr of profit and no debt, so cash is accumulating without a stated use. Force is dependent on two German customers for the contract-manufacturing half of the story and discloses no concentration figure.
verify_comment: Screener consolidated, ten years. The Mercedes-Benz and BMW engine arrangement — the load-bearing moat claim on this row — is taken from Force Motors' own disclosure and is UNVERIFIED against any customer filing or contract award; that is precisely why the grade is company-stated. Trendlyne endpoints were unreachable this run, so pledging, insider activity and news are UNCHECKED.

name: Sharda Motor Industries
business: Makes exhaust systems and emission-control aftertreatment — catalytic converters, diesel particulate filters and selective catalytic reduction hardware — for passenger and commercial vehicle makers. Ten years of accounts: sales Rs 1,155 cr (FY18) to Rs 3,397 cr (FY26), TTM Rs 3,652 cr. The balance sheet is unusually clean for an auto component maker: Rs 49 cr of borrowings against Rs 1,313 cr of net worth and Rs 1,136 cr held in investments, with the cash conversion cycle at MINUS 30 days.
moat_note: Emission aftertreatment is a better business than 'exhaust systems' sounds, and the reason is regulatory. A catalytic converter or SCR system is calibrated and homologated to a specific engine-and-vehicle combination; the certification is granted against that combination, so changing supplier means re-certifying the vehicle. That is a real switching cost and it renews with each emission-norm step rather than eroding — BS-VI raised the technical content per vehicle sharply, and the next tightening will do so again. The financial evidence is consistent with a supplier that has pricing power rather than one being squeezed: ROCE has run 38%, 40%, 41%, 38%, 36% across five years, operating cash flow has been 94-141% of operating profit in four of the last five, and the working capital cycle is negative, which means customers and suppliers fund the business rather than the other way round. What is missing is any external confirmation of position — no OEM filing, regulator listing or rating-agency note naming Sharda was located, and the company makes no 'largest in India' claim this pass could test. Hence company-stated.
import_substitution: Genuine. BS-VI aftertreatment hardware and the substrate/washcoat technology behind it were substantially imported before Indian localisation, and building it here displaces that directly. Scored 15/20; the catalyst substrates and precious-metal loading at the heart of the system are still largely imported, so the substitution is partial rather than complete.
risk_note: The margin is drifting the wrong way and the most recent quarter is the weakest in two years: operating margin went 14% (FY25) to 12% (FY26), and the Jun-26 quarter came in at 10% against 15% two years earlier. ROCE has likewise eased from 41% to 36%. Other income of Rs 108 cr is 26% of operating profit, which is what a Rs 1,136 cr investment book throws off — real cash, but it means a quarter of the reported earnings is treasury rather than operations, and it will move with rates. The customer base is Indian vehicle OEMs and no concentration figure is disclosed in anything reachable; a single platform loss would be material at this scale. This is also a business whose entire product exists because of the internal combustion engine — a genuine electric-vehicle transition removes the addressable market rather than shrinking it, and nothing on the balance sheet yet indicates a hedge against that.
verify_comment: Screener consolidated, ten years. No external source located that speaks to Sharda's competitive position, so the moat rests on the financial record plus general knowledge of how emission homologation works — company-stated, not verified. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.

name: Tata Motors (Commercial Vehicles)
business: India's largest commercial vehicle maker, now a standalone listed entity following the demerger that separated the CV business from the passenger vehicle business (TMPV). Only two reporting periods exist in the record and the first is a ten-month stub: FY25 (10m) sales Rs 58,217 cr and FY26 sales Rs 83,855 cr, TTM Rs 87,197 cr. FY26 generated Rs 14,981 cr of operating cash flow against Rs 7,617 cr of operating profit — 209% conversion — Rs 12,878 cr of free cash flow, and borrowings were cut from Rs 9,925 cr to Rs 5,615 cr. The cash conversion cycle is MINUS 54 days.
moat_note: The commercial vehicle moat is the dealer and service network, and it is one of the few genuinely durable moats in Indian manufacturing. A fleet operator does not buy a truck on price; it buys on uptime, which means it buys the certainty that a part and a mechanic exist within reach of wherever the vehicle breaks down. That network takes decades and enormous fixed investment to build, it cannot be rented, and it is why the Indian CV market has stayed a duopoly for forty years despite repeated well-funded attempts to enter it. Tata Motors' network is the largest of the two. The financial signature is consistent: a MINUS 54 day cash conversion cycle and 209% cash conversion mean the business is funded by its own dealers and suppliers, which only a supplier with real bargaining power achieves. The claim is graded company-stated because market-share and network figures come from the company and industry bodies rather than from a regulator or a customer filing, and because there is almost no listed history to test any of it against.
import_substitution: Settled rather than active. Indian commercial vehicles are almost entirely built in India, with deep local supply chains; Tata Motors is a reason that is true rather than a company currently displacing imports. Scored 14/20 on the scale and depth of the domestic supply chain it anchors.
risk_note: The single largest problem with this row is that there is no record to read. Two reporting periods exist, one of which is a ten-month stub created by the demerger, so there is no cycle, no downturn and no comparable prior-year in anything Screener carries — and the commercial vehicle cycle is the most violent in Indian autos, with peak-to-trough volume falls of 40-50% within living memory. Every ratio on this row is a single good year. Second, other income is deeply negative and unexplained: MINUS Rs 2,533 cr on a TTM basis, with a MINUS Rs 1,865 cr hit in the Sep-25 quarter that turned it into a Rs 867 cr loss, and MINUS Rs 981 cr in Dec-25. Charges of that size swamp the operating result and nothing reachable in this pass explains them; until they are understood the earnings series should not be extrapolated. Operating margin is 9% on the full year, so this is a thin-margin volume business whose returns depend on the cycle staying favourable. The promoter stake of 42.56% is the Tata Sons holding and has not moved since the demerger.
verify_comment: Screener consolidated. Only FY25 (10-month) and FY26 exist post-demerger. The dealer-network moat is argued from industry structure and the company's own disclosure, not from an external document, hence company-stated. The negative other-income entries are flagged as UNEXPLAINED rather than interpreted. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED. This row should be revisited once a full comparable year exists.

name: Acutaas Chemicals
theme_detail: Advanced pharmaceutical intermediates and specialty chemicals. Formerly Ami Organics.
business: Makes advanced pharmaceutical intermediates — the last few synthetic steps before an active ingredient — plus specialty chemicals and electrolyte additives. Ten years of accounts: sales Rs 188 cr (FY18) to Rs 1,339 cr (FY26), TTM Rs 1,462 cr, a 24% compound rate. Operating margin has run 16-24% for most of the record and then jumped to 36% in FY26, with the Mar-26 quarter at 42%.
moat_note: Advanced intermediates carry a genuine and well-understood switching cost: the intermediate and its manufacturing site are named in the customer's drug master file, so a formulator changing supplier mid-product triggers a regulatory refiling. That locks a qualified supplier in for the life of a molecule and is why the good businesses in this category earn 20%+ margins durably. Acutaas has the shape of one — margins in the high teens to low twenties for eight years, growth at 24% compound, and a customer base of regulated-market pharma companies. What this pass cannot explain, and therefore will not credit, is the FY26 step: operating margin went from 20% in the Sep-24 quarter to 42% in the Mar-26 quarter, roughly doubling in six quarters, and no product launch, contract or mix shift disclosed in anything reachable accounts for a move that size. It may be a genuine high-value molecule reaching scale, which is exactly how this business is supposed to work. It may also not persist. The moat is credited at 15/25 on the eight-year record rather than on the last four quarters, and the row says so.
import_substitution: The strongest on this week's moat board and a matter of explicit national policy rather than commercial preference. Indian formulators have historically bought advanced intermediates from China; reducing that dependence is the stated purpose of the PLI scheme for bulk drugs and key starting materials. Every tonne Acutaas makes displaces a Chinese import into a supply chain the government has designated as strategically exposed. Scored 17/20.
risk_note: Free cash flow has been NEGATIVE in every one of the eight years in the record — cumulatively about Rs 400 cr — because capital expenditure has consistently exceeded operating cash flow, and Rs 332 cr sits in capital work in progress against Rs 745 cr of net block, so another large tranche is still to be absorbed. Operating cash flow at 84% of operating profit is respectable but the cash conversion cycle has widened every year, from 11 days (FY17) to 149 days (FY26). Promoter holding is 32.66%, the lowest of anything added to either board this week, and it fell from 35.96% in the March 2025 quarter; on the microcap board that would fail the skin-in-the-game gate outright, and while the moat board has no promoter gate for good reasons, a third-owned promoter is a materially different governance position from a two-thirds-owned one. The P/E of 67 prices the FY26 margin as permanent. Offsetting all of this, institutional ownership is 41% combined, the highest of any name added this week, so the position is at least well scrutinised.
verify_comment: Screener consolidated, ten years. The DMF-based switching cost is argued from how pharmaceutical regulation works, not from a document naming Acutaas, and no customer filing was located — company-stated. The FY26 margin doubling is recorded as UNEXPLAINED rather than credited. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.

name: Jamna Auto Industries
theme_detail: Leaf and parabolic suspension springs for commercial vehicles.
business: Makes leaf springs, parabolic springs and lift axles for commercial vehicles, supplying the Indian truck and bus makers. Ten years of accounts including a full cycle: sales fell from Rs 2,135 cr (FY19) to Rs 1,129 cr (FY20) and Rs 1,079 cr (FY21) as the CV market collapsed, then recovered to Rs 2,612 cr in FY26 at a 15% operating margin, the best in the record. FY26 generated Rs 510 cr of operating cash flow against Rs 396 cr of operating profit and borrowings were cut from Rs 358 cr to Rs 12 cr.
moat_note: Suspension springs have a moat that is mostly geographic and partly technical, and the geographic half is the durable one. A leaf spring is heavy, bulky and low in value density, so freight and duty make importing one uneconomic against local supply — the addressable competitor set is therefore domestic, and the domestic segment has consolidated to a small number of players. On top of that, the spring is validated to a specific chassis and load rating, so it is qualified per platform in the ordinary Tier-1 way. Jamna's scale within that consolidated segment is real and its customer list covers essentially every Indian CV maker. The company does publish a market-share figure; this pass located no independent source for it and does not repeat it, which is the difference between company-stated and verified. The financial record supports a business with pricing power at the margin: operating margin has been 10-15% through a cycle that halved its revenue, and cash conversion has been 120% and 153% in the last two years.
import_substitution: Real but structurally settled — CV suspension components are domestic because economics make them so, not because of a substitution programme. 14/20.
risk_note: The dividend was cut to ZERO in FY26 after eight consecutive years at 27-47% payout, and that happened in the company's best-ever profit year, which is the single most notable and least explained fact on this row. Cash did not vanish — borrowings were repaid from Rs 358 cr to Rs 12 cr and Rs 245 cr went into investing — so the most likely reading is deleveraging plus capex, but a board that stops a long-standing dividend in a record year is signalling something, and nothing reachable in this pass says what. Beyond that, this is a pure commercial-vehicle cycle play and the record shows exactly what that means: revenue halved in FY20 and ROCE fell from 49% to 15% in one year. Promoter holding is 49.84% and has drifted just under the halfway mark. Capital work in progress swings hard — Rs 56 cr, Rs 121 cr, Rs 275 cr, Rs 108 cr across four years — so the capex programme is lumpy and hard to read.

The FY26 dividend suspension is flagged as UNEXPLAINED. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.

name: Jyoti CNC Automation
theme_detail: CNC machine tools — turning centres, machining centres, multi-tasking machines.
business: Builds CNC machine tools — turning centres, vertical and horizontal machining centres and multi-tasking machines — from a plant in Rajkot, with a European subsidiary. Eight years of accounts containing a deep trough: losses in FY20, FY21, FY22 and FY23 totalling about Rs 180 cr with ROCE at or below zero, then a sharp turn to Rs 336 cr of profit and 21% ROCE by FY26 on sales of Rs 2,093 cr.
moat_note: Machine tool building is one of the genuinely hard things to do in manufacturing and India does very little of it — the spindle, the way system, the thermal stability and the control integration are accumulated engineering rather than purchasable capability, and the customer's own process capability depends on the machine, so switching is slow and conservative. Jyoti is one of a very small number of Indian firms operating at this level. That much is structural and is why the moat scores 14/25 rather than lower. What holds it below the leaders on this board is that the financial evidence does not corroborate a strong position: a 25% operating margin sitting on a 359-day cash conversion cycle with 453 days of inventory is not what pricing power looks like, it is what building large machines to order against long lead times looks like, and the cash has not followed the profit. The company's aerospace and defence customer exposure is its own disclosure and no contract award or qualification document was located to support it, so the strategic credit is partial.
import_substitution: Among the clearest categories on this board. India imports the large majority of its CNC machine tools from Japan, Taiwan, Germany and South Korea, and machine-tool capacity is upstream of every other manufacturing ambition the country has — you cannot localise aerospace or defence components without the machines that cut them. A domestic builder at this level substitutes directly and at a strategically meaningful point in the chain. Scored 17/20.
risk_note: The cash record is the reason this row scores where it does rather than higher. Operating cash flow was MINUS Rs 48 cr (FY24) and MINUS Rs 105 cr (FY25) before recovering to Rs 54 cr in FY26 — that is 34% of operating profit, after 1% and minus 4% — and free cash flow has been negative in five of the eight reported years, at MINUS Rs 269 cr in FY26. Inventory stands at 453 days and the cash conversion cycle at 359, both worse than three years ago. Borrowings rose from Rs 497 cr to Rs 853 cr in FY26. No dividend has ever been paid. The P/E of 69.9 is the highest of the fifteen names added to the moat board this week and it is being paid for a business that has not yet demonstrated it can turn its reported margin into cash across a full cycle — and this company's last cycle produced four consecutive loss years.
