name: GlaxoSmithKline Pharmaceuticals
theme_detail: Indian arm of GSK plc — branded formulations and vaccines.
business: The Indian listed arm of GSK plc, which holds 75.00%. Sells branded prescription formulations and vaccines into the domestic market. Ten years of accounts: sales Rs 2,871 cr (FY18) to Rs 3,822 cr (FY26) — a compound rate of 3.6%, so this is not a growth business — but operating margin has climbed steadily from 18% to 34% and ROCE from 22% to 61% over the same period. Operating cash flow has been 92-133% of operating profit in every single year of the record, and the working capital cycle is MINUS 91 days.
moat_note: The moat is real, unusually strong on the numbers, and — the point that matters for a reader — not owned by the entity you would be buying. A 61% ROCE with a minus 91-day working capital cycle is produced by a portfolio of long-established prescription brands and vaccines that distributors pay for before the company pays its own suppliers. That is textbook brand pricing power in pharmaceuticals. But the portfolio originates with GSK plc, is licensed to the Indian entity, and the parent holds 75% and decides which products the Indian arm gets, on what royalty and transfer-pricing terms. The listed company is a distribution and formulation channel for a moat that belongs to someone else, and the 3.6% nine-year growth rate is what that looks like from the minority holder's seat. Graded company-stated: nothing external was checked, and the 75.00% parent holding — which IS verifiable from the exchange filing — establishes control, not competitive advantage.
import_substitution: The weakest of the fifteen moat-board names added this week, and this row will not pretend otherwise. GSK India substantially formulates and distributes products originated by its parent, with meaningful imported content in the vaccine range in particular. On the specific question this board screens for — does this company replace an import — the honest answer is that it is closer to being an import channel than an import substituter. Scored 7/20, and it is on the board for moat quality and strategic category rather than for substitution. Note qualifies_as carries only 'manufacturer' for this reason: 'import-substitution' would be wrong.
risk_note: Dividend payout has been 85-99% of earnings in every recent year — 93% in FY26 — which means essentially nothing is reinvested and the 3.6% nine-year sales growth rate is structural, not a phase. A P/E of 46.7 on a business growing at low single digits requires the margin to keep expanding, and margin expansion from 34% has limited room. The deeper risk is the ownership structure: at 75.00% the parent sits exactly at the maximum permitted promoter holding, controls the product pipeline, sets the royalty, and has in the past restructured Indian subsidiaries in ways minority holders did not choose. The FY22 accounts contain Rs 1,401 cr of other income that made that year's profit meaningless as a comparison, and FY20's tax rate of 70% did the same in the other direction — this series needs reading year by year rather than as a trend.

name: LG Electronics India
theme_detail: Home appliances and consumer electronics manufactured in India.
business: The Indian arm of LG Electronics of Korea, which holds 85.00%, listed in late 2025. Manufactures and sells refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, televisions and other home appliances, largely from plants at Noida and Pune. Seven years of accounts: sales Rs 15,710 cr (FY20) to Rs 24,605 cr (FY26), TTM Rs 25,575 cr. Operating cash flow has been 77-122% of operating profit and the balance sheet carries almost no debt.
moat_note: Brand and distribution in Indian home appliances is a genuine moat — LG has been at or near the top of the refrigerator and washing machine market for two decades, and appliance buying is a low-frequency, high-consideration purchase where brand trust and after-sales service reach do most of the work. The service network across small-town India is the part a new entrant cannot buy. The financial evidence is consistent: a ROCE that ran 35%, 27%, 36%, 47%, 57% before easing to 32%, on a balance sheet with essentially no debt. As with GSK, the qualification is ownership: the brand is the Korean parent's, licensed to the listed entity, and at 85.00% the parent holds the maximum the listing permits, leaving minority holders with a 15% float in a moat they do not control. Graded company-stated; no external source on competitive position was checked.
import_substitution: Genuine and policy-backed. LG manufactures the large majority of what it sells in India domestically rather than importing finished goods, and appliance and electronics localisation is directly supported by the PLI scheme for white goods and for air conditioners specifically. Each washing machine or refrigerator built at Noida is one not imported from China or Korea. Scored 15/20; component-level localisation — compressors, panels, semiconductors — remains substantially incomplete, so the substitution is at assembly depth rather than throughout the chain.
risk_note: Earnings went backwards in FY26 and the trend within the year is worse than the annual figure suggests: net profit fell from Rs 2,203 cr to Rs 1,685 cr, a 24% decline, operating margin fell from 13% to 10%, and the Dec-25 quarter came in at 4.8% margin — the weakest in the seven-year record. A P/E of 60.4 is being paid for that. The 85% promoter holding is the structural issue: the parent controls the product roadmap, the royalty, the transfer price on imported components and the allocation of regional manufacturing, and a 15% float means the market price is set on very little stock. No dividend has been paid since listing, and the pre-listing record shows payouts of 87-193% in FY21-FY24, so the distribution policy has changed entirely with no stated replacement. Screener's consolidated page for this company returns no financial data at all — only standalone is usable — which is a data-quality limitation on any analysis of it, including this one. There is less than a year of listed history.

name: SPR Auto Technologies (Shriram Pistons & Rings)
theme_detail: Pistons, piston rings and engine valves.
business: Makes pistons, piston rings and engine valves for two-wheeler, passenger vehicle, commercial vehicle and stationary engine applications, and has expanded into precision plastic components and electric drivetrain parts through acquisitions. Ten years of accounts: sales Rs 1,729 cr (FY18) to Rs 4,459 cr (FY26), TTM Rs 4,970 cr, with operating margin improving from 11-17% to a steady 20-21% over the last four years. Operating cash flow has been 83-108% of operating profit in every year of the last decade.
moat_note: Pistons and rings are a proper Tier-1 moat of the qualification kind. The part is designed against a specific engine's bore, thermal profile and ring pack, validated over thousands of hours, and an engine maker changing piston supplier is re-validating the engine — so the supplier is held for the life of that engine family, which in commercial and two-wheeler applications can run fifteen years. The segment has also consolidated globally to a handful of players, and Shriram Pistons is the largest Indian one. The evidence is a decade of 83-108% cash conversion and margin that expanded rather than compressed through the 2021-23 input cost shock. What the row cannot say is that any of this is externally confirmed: no customer filing, no rating-agency note and no market-share document was located, and the company's own position claims are not repeated here. The deeper qualification is that the whole moat is attached to the internal combustion engine.
import_substitution: Real. High-precision pistons and rings were historically imported into India, and the domestic capability that replaced them is the business Shriram Pistons is in. Scored 14/20.
risk_note: FY26 transformed the balance sheet and the transformation is unproven: borrowings rose from Rs 508 cr to Rs 1,968 cr — a 287% increase against Rs 2,901 cr of net worth — fixed assets went from Rs 1,203 cr to Rs 2,976 cr, and the investing outflow was Rs 1,815 cr, funded by Rs 1,252 cr of new financing. That is an acquisition-scale deployment and there is one year of post-deal reporting to judge it by. Interest cost has already risen from Rs 34 cr to Rs 62 cr and Rs 34 cr in the Jun-26 quarter alone, and operating margin slipped from 21% to 18% in the two most recent quarters. Promoter holding fell from 43.75% to 41.55% in the August 2026 disclosure, a 2.20 percentage point reduction and the first movement in the record. The strategic risk is unavoidable and long-dated: pistons, rings and valves exist because of the internal combustion engine, and while India's two-wheeler and CV transition will be slower than Europe's, the terminal value of this product line is genuinely uncertain in a way a fastener or a bearing business is not.
verify_comment: Screener consolidated, ten years. No external source on competitive position was checked; company position claims are not repeated. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run, so the mechanism of the 2.20pp promoter reduction is UNCHECKED — that is the first thing to look at next week.
data_note: Screener consolidated under symbol SHRIPISTON; the company is now named SPR Auto Technologies Ltd. Enumerated in the mid-tier moat screen on 2026-08-23.

warnings: promoter 41.55% — down 2.20pp from 43.75% in the Aug-2026 disclosure, as of 2026-08-23

name: RPG Life Sciences
theme_detail: Niche APIs and branded domestic formulations.
business: Part of the RPG group. Two businesses: niche active pharmaceutical ingredients — the immunosuppressant and oncology end, where volumes are small and the chemistry is demanding — and a branded domestic formulations arm sold through its own field force. Screener carries only two years of consolidated accounts: FY25 sales Rs 653 cr and FY26 Rs 708 cr, TTM Rs 734 cr. Promoter holding is 72.95%, unchanged across six consecutive disclosures, with a 34% dividend payout.
moat_note: The moat here is small-market chemistry, and it is genuine but narrow. Immunosuppressants and oncology APIs address patient populations measured in thousands rather than millions, which means the total profit pool is too small to attract a large competitor, while the synthesis is difficult enough to deter a small one — and the API and its site are named in the customer's regulatory filing, so a qualified supplier is hard to displace. That combination produces durable 20%+ margins in a narrow lane and is why the segment is attractive. The branded formulations arm has the ordinary prescriber-relationship moat of Indian branded generics: real, replicable with money. Nothing external was located to confirm RPG's specific position in either, and with only two years of consolidated accounts on Screener there is very little record to test the claim against — a material limitation on this row and the reason the moat is credited at 13/25 rather than higher.
import_substitution: Genuine at the category level. Immunosuppressant and oncology APIs are a real import-substitution target for India — they were historically sourced from Europe and China, and domestic capability in them is exactly what the bulk-drug policy is trying to build. Scored 14/20; RPG's own contribution to that substitution is not quantified in anything checkable.
risk_note: FY26 was a materially worse year than the headline suggests and the reason is a one-off in the prior year. Reported net profit fell from Rs 183 cr to Rs 115 cr, a 37% decline, but FY25 contained Rs 95 cr of other income concentrated in the Mar-25 quarter (Rs 115 cr in that quarter alone against Rs 25 cr of operating profit). Strip it out and the underlying business went from roughly Rs 100 cr to Rs 115 cr — a very different and much less alarming picture, but it means neither year's reported figure should be used at face value, and the P/E of 37.3 is calculated on the depressed one. Separately, the operating margin genuinely did fall, from 25% to 21%, and cash conversion weakened from 81% to 63% of operating profit with free cash flow turning negative at MINUS Rs 9 cr. Inventory days rose from 159 to 179 and the cash conversion cycle from 72 to 99. Only two years of consolidated data exist in the source, so no cycle can be observed at all.
verify_comment: Screener consolidated, and only two years are available — the shortest record of any moat-board name added this week, which limits what can be concluded. No external source on competitive position was checked. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.

name: Lloyds Metals & Energy
theme_detail: Captive iron ore mining at Surjagarh plus integrated steel.
business: Mines iron ore at Surjagarh in Gadchiroli, Maharashtra, and is building an integrated steel complex around it. The transformation is recent and enormous: sales went from Rs 692 cr (FY22) to Rs 3,353 cr, Rs 6,522 cr, Rs 6,721 cr and then Rs 17,113 cr in FY26, with TTM at Rs 22,084 cr. Total assets grew from Rs 8,911 cr to Rs 41,650 cr in a single year.
moat_note: The moat is a mining lease, and mining leases are the most durable kind of moat there is — the Surjagarh deposit exists in one place, the lease was granted by the state, and no amount of competitor capital creates a second one. That is why a company with no particular processing advantage earns a 36% operating margin: it is selling ore it owns rather than ore it buys. To the extent this row is a moat-board name at all, that is the reason, and it is a good one. Everything built on top of the mine is a different question. The downstream integration is being funded by an extraordinary amount of debt against a single, geographically concentrated, security-sensitive asset, and the returns on it are entirely prospective. Graded company-stated: the mining lease itself is a matter of public record, but this pass did not retrieve the lease document or a ministry allocation notice, and the cost and reserve claims are the company's own.
import_substitution: Partial. India both imports and exports iron ore depending on grade and cycle, and domestic ore feeding a domestic steel plant substitutes imported ore and imported steel at the margin. Scored 11/20 — real but not the reason to hold this row.
risk_note: The balance sheet changed beyond recognition in twelve months and this is the dominant fact about the company. Borrowings went from Rs 1,073 cr to Rs 20,716 cr — a nineteen-fold increase, against Rs 13,871 cr of net worth — capital work in progress from Rs 4,267 cr to Rs 13,946 cr, and free cash flow was MINUS Rs 7,040 cr. Interest cost has already gone from Rs 27 cr to Rs 510 cr and is running at Rs 276 cr in a single quarter. None of the capacity this debt has bought has completed a full year of operation, and the returns on it are entirely unproven. Meanwhile the quality metric that put this name on the screen has been collapsing as the capital base grows: ROCE was 81% (FY23), 78% (FY24), 37% (FY25) and is 27% now. Inventory days of 534 and payable days of 535 mean the working capital is being carried on suppliers to an extreme degree. Institutional ownership is remarkably thin for a company of this size — FII 1.85% and DII 2.18%, against 20%+ for most large caps — which is itself a signal worth weighing. Promoter holding fell 1.81pp from 63.44% to 61.63%. Finally, and not visible in any ratio: Gadchiroli is a district with a long history of left-wing insurgency, and a single-site mining operation there carries a security and continuity risk that a diversified miner does not.
verify_comment: Screener consolidated. Screener's series for this company has gaps — it jumps from FY2013 to FY2020 — so the long record is not continuous. The mining lease is public record but was NOT retrieved in this pass; reserve, grade and cost claims are the company's own. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.
data_note: Screener consolidated, with a gap between FY2013 and FY2020. Enumerated in the large-tier moat screen on 2026-08-23.
penalty_detail: -7 borrowings up nineteen-fold to Rs 20,716 cr against Rs 13,871 cr of net worth, funding Rs 13,946 cr of CWIP with returns entirely unproven; -3 ROCE collapsing 81% to 27% as the capital base grows; -2 free cash flow MINUS Rs 7,040 cr and inventory at 534 days; -1 single-site concentration in a security-sensitive district.

name: Precision Wires India
theme_detail: Enamelled copper winding wire and continuously transposed conductor.
business: Draws and enamels copper winding wire and makes continuously transposed conductor, sold to transformer, motor and electrical machine manufacturers. Ten years of accounts: sales Rs 1,408 cr (FY18) to Rs 5,410 cr (FY26), TTM Rs 6,127 cr. The number that governs everything on this row is the operating margin, which has been between 3.5% and 6% in every one of those ten years and is 4.7% now.
moat_note: There is no pricing-power moat here and the margin says so plainly. Winding wire is a copper conversion business: the copper price passes through to the customer and the company earns a conversion spread of four to five percent, which is what a price-taker earns. The 32.9% ROCE that ranked this name into the small-tier batch is a TURNOVER artefact — Rs 5,410 cr of revenue turning over a small net capital base will produce a high ROCE on almost any margin — and reading it as a quality signal is the same error the microcap board records against Parmeshwar Metal this week. What genuine advantage exists is qualification-based and shallow: winding wire is specified into a transformer or motor design and approved per customer, so an incumbent is not casually displaced, and continuously transposed conductor for large power transformers is a more demanding product with fewer qualified suppliers. That is worth something — 9/25 — and no more.
import_substitution: Genuine at the category level and improving in importance. Enamelled winding wire and CTC for power transformers, and increasingly for electric vehicle traction motors, are categories where domestic supply displaces imports and where demand is being pulled by the transmission build-out and by EV localisation. Scored 13/20.
risk_note: The FY26 balance sheet expanded aggressively and the funding was debt: borrowings rose from Rs 62 cr to Rs 293 cr, capital work in progress from Rs 30 cr to Rs 183 cr and net block from Rs 218 cr to Rs 316 cr, with free cash flow turning negative at MINUS Rs 7 cr despite operating cash flow of Rs 273 cr. The dividend, paid at 23-50% payout for nine consecutive years, was cut to ZERO in FY26. Promoter holding fell from 57.93% to 56.61% across the Sep-25 and Dec-25 disclosures. A P/E of 45.9 on a business earning a 4.7% conversion spread prices in a great deal of the capacity that has not yet run. Separately and importantly for anyone re-checking this row: Screener's CONSOLIDATED page for PRECWIRE is broken — it returns only FY2015 and FY2016 data and reports a P/E of 473, ROCE of 16.9% and ROE of 8.88%, none of which are current. Everything on this row is taken from the standalone page.
verify_comment: Screener STANDALONE, ten years. The consolidated page for this symbol is stale and internally inconsistent (FY2015-16 data only, P/E 473) and must not be used. No external source on competitive position was checked. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run: pledging, insider activity and news UNCHECKED.
data_note: Screener standalone. Consolidated is broken for this symbol — see verify_comment. Enumerated in the small-tier moat screen on 2026-08-23.
penalty_detail: -3 the 32.9% ROCE is a turnover artefact on a 4.7% conversion spread, not pricing power; -2 borrowings up 373% and CWIP up six-fold to fund unproven capacity, FCF negative; -1 dividend cut to zero after nine years and promoter down 1.32pp.
warnings: dividend payout fell from 23% (FY25) to 0% (FY26) — as of 2026-08-23

name: Glenmark Pharmaceuticals
theme_detail: Generic and specialty pharmaceuticals with an innovation arm.
business: Generic and specialty pharmaceuticals across India, the US, Europe and emerging markets, with an innovation arm pursuing novel biologics. Ten years of accounts: sales Rs 9,074 cr (FY18) to Rs 16,983 cr (FY26). The record includes a Rs 1,434 cr loss in FY24 and operating cash flow of MINUS Rs 265 cr (FY24) and MINUS Rs 828 cr (FY25) before a Rs 3,445 cr recovery in FY26.
moat_note: DEBUNKED, and the thing being debunked is specifically the metric that qualified this company for the moat board. Glenmark entered the large-tier batch on a 39.8% ROCE. That figure is not produced by the operating business. The ten-year ROCE series reads 21%, 15%, 15%, 14%, 15%, 16%, 10%, 12%, 19% and then 40% — the jump happens entirely in FY26, and the FY26 accounts show where it came from: the Sep-25 quarter reported Rs 6,047 cr of sales against Rs 3,264 cr the quarter before and Rs 3,901 cr the quarter after, at a 39% operating margin against 18-22% either side. That is a one-off recognition — a licensing or milestone event in the innovation arm — not a change in how the business earns. Strip that quarter back to trend and the underlying enterprise is a mid-teens-ROCE generics company, which is a perfectly respectable thing to be and is not a moat-board company by this board's own quality floor. The corroborating oddity is 'other income' of MINUS Rs 1,805 cr in FY26 and MINUS Rs 259 cr in FY25 — charges large enough to swamp the operating result, unexplained by anything reachable in this pass. A moat claim resting on a single quarter's licensing recognition does not survive checking, and the row records that rather than carrying a flattering number forward.
import_substitution: Ordinary for an Indian generics manufacturer: it makes formulations and some intermediates domestically and exports the majority. This displaces imports into India only weakly, and the company is better described as an exporter. Scored 10/20.
risk_note: Beyond the ROCE question: FY24 was a Rs 1,434 cr loss year with a tax charge of 430% of pre-tax profit, and operating cash flow was negative in both FY24 and FY25 — cumulatively about MINUS Rs 1,093 cr — so this is a business that consumed cash for two consecutive years very recently. Free cash flow was MINUS Rs 1,162 cr and MINUS Rs 1,576 cr in those years. Borrowings have moved violently, Rs 4,608 cr to Rs 1,231 cr to Rs 2,473 cr to Rs 594 cr across four years, which reflects asset sales rather than operating deleveraging. Inventory sits at 264 days. The innovation arm is the source of both the FY26 upside and much of the prior volatility, and its value is genuinely hard to assess from the outside — it is a binary pipeline, not an earnings stream. Promoter holding of 46.65% is stable.
verify_comment: DEBUNKED on facts internal to Screener's own ten-year series: the ROCE step is isolated to FY26 and traceable to a single quarter's revenue recognition, against a ten-year history in the 10-21% range. No allegation about the accounts is made or supported. The negative other-income entries are recorded as UNEXPLAINED. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run: news and corporate events, which would identify the licensing event directly, are UNCHECKED and are the first thing to look at next week.
data_note: Screener consolidated, ten years. Enumerated in the large-tier moat screen on 2026-08-23. The row is kept on the board as a worked example of a quality metric produced by a one-off rather than by operations.
penalty_detail: -8 the 39.8% ROCE that qualified this row is produced by a single quarter's one-off recognition against a ten-year 10-21% range; -4 operating cash flow negative in FY24 and FY25, cumulatively about MINUS Rs 1,093 cr, with a Rs 1,434 cr loss in FY24; -2 other income of MINUS Rs 1,805 cr in FY26, unexplained.

name: Ram Ratna Wires
business: Enamelled copper winding wire, the same product category as Precision Wires India, sold to transformer, motor and appliance manufacturers. Ten years of accounts: sales Rs 1,138 cr (FY18) to Rs 5,177 cr (FY26), TTM Rs 6,047 cr. Operating margin across the entire decade has been between 4.0% and 6.0% and is 5% now.
moat_note: No moat is claimed and none is present. Like Precision Wires, this is a copper conversion business earning a five percent spread on a pass-through input, and the 23.6% ROCE that ranked it into the small-tier batch is a function of asset turns rather than of anything defensible — Rs 5,177 cr of revenue on a Rs 1,994 cr balance sheet will do that at almost any margin. Winding wire is qualified into a customer's motor or transformer design, which gives an incumbent some stickiness, and that is the whole of it. Of the two winding-wire names read this week Ram Ratna is the weaker: the same margin, a worse cash record and a promoter who has been reducing. This row is on the board to make the comparison visible rather than because it belongs among moat companies.
import_substitution: Category-genuine, as for the sector: domestic winding wire displaces imports into transformer and motor manufacturing. Scored 13/20 on the category, not on anything specific to this company.
risk_note: FY26 broke the cash record badly. Operating cash flow was MINUS Rs 93 cr against Rs 261 cr of operating profit — a conversion rate of minus 18%, after five straight years of 75-160% — and free cash flow was MINUS Rs 264 cr, the worst in the decade. It was funded with debt: borrowings rose from Rs 305 cr to Rs 675 cr, a 121% increase, while other liabilities rose from Rs 512 cr to Rs 739 cr. Interest cost is now Rs 86 cr against Rs 261 cr of operating profit, so a third of the operating profit is going to lenders. Promoter holding fell from 72.98% to 68.84% in the September 2025 quarter — a 4.14 percentage point reduction, the largest of any moat-board name added this week — and has since recovered only to 69.30%. Institutional ownership is negligible at 1.09% combined. A P/E of 34.4 on a five-percent-margin conversion business that just consumed Rs 264 cr of cash is the least defensible valuation on this week's moat board.
verify_comment: Screener consolidated, ten years. No external source checked; no moat claim exists to test. Trendlyne endpoints unreachable this run, so the mechanism of the 4.14pp promoter reduction is UNCHECKED and is the priority check next week.
data_note: Screener consolidated, ten years. Enumerated in the small-tier moat screen on 2026-08-23. Directly comparable with Precision Wires India (PRECWIRE), added in the same batch.
penalty_detail: -4 operating cash flow MINUS Rs 93 cr against Rs 261 cr of operating profit and free cash flow MINUS Rs 264 cr, after five years of positive conversion; -2 borrowings up 121% and interest now a third of operating profit; -2 promoter down 4.14pp.
warnings: promoter 69.30% — down 4.14pp from 72.98% in the Sep-2025 quarter, as of 2026-08-23

name: Hindusthan Insulators & Industries
theme_detail: Electro-porcelain high-tension insulators, 33 kV to 1,200 kV.
business: Electro-porcelain high-tension insulators for power transmission and distribution, substations, transformers and railway electrification, across a 33 kV-1,200 kV voltage range, plus overhead conductors. Renamed from Hindusthan Urban Infrastructure in February 2026 and part of the 70-year-old Hindusthan Group. Total operating income grew at a 20% CAGR over FY24-FY26 to Rs 339 crore, with an order book of Rs 611 crore as at 30 June 2026 — about a year of revenue visibility, against which CARE expects FY27 income to nearly double. A Rs 210 crore capex to double capacity is running to December 2026, funded from the sale of its stake in Hindusthan Speciality Chemicals and group funds rather than external debt.
moat_note: Confirmed against an independent source rather than the company's own page, which is what moved this off the candidates queue. CARE Ratings, in its 22 July 2026 press release, credits the company's "prominent position in the domestic insulator industry" and states that "HIIL is among the top players in high-voltage insulator manufacturing in India in terms of manufacturing capacity and product profile" — the agency's words, in the strengths section of a live rating. The economic shape of the moat is qualification-based: high-voltage porcelain insulators are type-tested (CPRI, ERDA, CESI Italy, EDF France, Hydro Quebec) and specified into transmission projects, and PGCIL and government T&D entities are the customer base, so an incumbent with six decades of approvals is not displaced quickly. Honest limits: the same agencies flag high competitive intensity in insulators and conductors, top-10 client concentration is 38% of sales, and the company is a downstream supplier whose fortunes track the T&D capex cycle rather than setting their own terms.
import_substitution: Specific and independently recorded, which is rare on this board. ICRA's rationale on the same issuer names the "extension of the safeguard duty on import of insulators" as a rating strength — a tariff wall documented by a third party rather than a Make-in-India gesture claimed by the company. Domestic HT insulator capacity displaces imported units into the national grid build-out; the company still imports 10-15% of raw material, so the substitution is at the product level, not the input level.
risk_note: FY26 closed in a net loss of Rs 7.87 crore, on a one-time exceptional loss of Rs 47 crore from selling the stake in subsidiary Hindusthan Speciality Chemicals; gross cash accruals were still over Rs 50 crore, so this is an accounting event rather than an operating collapse, but the reported ROE of 8.3% flatters what the P&L actually printed. Working capital is heavy — gross current assets 282 days in FY26, a 4-6 month inventory holding period, and a moderate sanctioned limit that leaves the company leaning on promoter-group entities, which had Rs 71.17 crore of interest-bearing unsecured loans outstanding at 31 March 2026. The margin turnaround is very recent: PBILDT margin was 2-5% through FY23-FY25 and only exceeded 20% in H2FY26, so one good half-year is carrying the FY27 doubling thesis. Alumina is 35-40% of raw material cost and the order book is fixed-price. Liquidity in the stock is the quiet problem: 2,167 shareholders and no FII, with DII at 0.55%.
verify_comment: Moat confirmed independently: CARE Ratings press release, 22 July 2026, read in full from the primary PDF (careratings.com), not from a search summary. Import-substitution leg confirmed separately from ICRA's rationale on the same issuer. Financials from Screener standalone, 31 August 2026. Not checked: whether the FY27 doubling implied by the order book is being delivered — the H1FY27 result is the thing to read next.

Surfaced by the weekly discovery pipeline as a new listing on 2026-08-31 and promoted after the independent-source pass the same day. Note the exchange feed's small-cap guess was wrong — market cap is about Rs 1,002 crore, not the sub-500 crore the sweep assumed.

name: Tempsens Instruments (India)
theme_detail: Contact and non-contact temperature sensors, electrical heaters, specialised cables.
business: Thermal engineering: thermocouples, RTDs, infrared pyrometers, online thermal imagers, temperature and pressure gauges, electrical heating solutions and specialised cables, sold into steel, power, glass, cement, chemicals and defence, with a balanced mix of project and MRO revenue. Revenue from operations compounded 27.2% from Rs 274.81 crore in FY24 to Rs 444.88 crore in FY26, with PAT compounding faster at 31.8%. Listed on NSE and BSE on 28 August 2026 from a Rs 650 crore issue at Rs 300 — Rs 95 crore fresh and Rs 555 crore offer for sale.
moat_note:
The only sole-Indian-manufacturer claim among the twenty candidates that survived independent checking, and read in the primary document rather than in coverage of it. The Frost & Sullivan section of the RHP states that "Tempsens is the only Indian manufacturer of Non-contact temperature sensors in the market as of March 31, 2026", that "There are currently no other domestic manufacturers in this segment, making the country largely dependent on imports", and that in FY2026 "it is the only manufacturer of pyrometers and online thermal imagers in India". Criterion 4 is met as squarely as this board ever sees it.

The size of that monopoly is the thing to hold onto, and it is smaller than the claim sounds. F&S puts the entire Indian non-contact segment at INR 2.2 billion — about Rs 220 crore — of which Tempsens holds 21.3%, so roughly Rs 47 crore, around a tenth of its Rs 444.88 crore of FY26 revenue. Being the only domestic maker has not made it the main supplier: about 79% of that segment is still imported. Read correctly this is a beachhead with a long runway, not a toll gate. The other 90% of the business — contact sensors, heaters, specialised cables — is the ordinary competitive part, where the 10.5% share that makes it "largest" sits against WIKA and Endress+Hauser (global brands still hold 59% of the overall market, down from 75% in FY2018) and Indian rivals Radix and Pyroelectric. F&S was commissioned by the issuer, which is why this is graded on a named third party rather than an arm's-length one.
import_substitution: The best-evidenced import-substitution case among the 31-Aug-2026 additions, and it is structural rather than rhetorical: F&S records that the absence of any other domestic manufacturer leaves the country "largely dependent on imports" for non-contact sensors, and that by indigenising the product Tempsens "has reduced reliance on foreign suppliers". The runway is quantified by the same report — about 79% of the non-contact segment is still imported, and across the whole temperature-sensor market the share held by global brands has fallen from 75% in FY2018 to 59% in FY2026 while organised Indian players rose from 15% to 31%. This is a company positioned in the direction the market is already moving, which is also why the substitution is not proprietary to it.
risk_note: Three trading days of history at the time of writing — every price-derived figure here is provisional, and the P/E of 70.8 prices a business whose public record is one listing week long. The issue structure deserves attention: Rs 555 crore of the Rs 650 crore went to selling shareholders and only Rs 95 crore to the company, so the promoter group and early holders monetised at listing while the balance sheet gained comparatively little. This is also not an undiscovered company by this board's standards and never will be: 156,649 shareholders, FII 3.27% and DII 10.92% at the August 2026 disclosure, versus the 25,000-holder line the v3 screen used to define obscurity. It is here on the moat, explicitly not on obscurity. The moat evidence rests on a single commissioned report with no rating-agency corroboration yet — the first CRISIL/ICRA/CARE rationale on the post-IPO entity is the check that would either harden or puncture it.

Reading the source changed the record: it supplied the INR 2.2 billion segment size and the ~79% import share that the earlier note lacked, and the moat score was cut accordingly. Financials and shareholding from Screener, 31 August 2026. Still not checked, and still the priority: no credit-rating rationale on the post-IPO entity was found, so nothing arm's-length has tested the share figures.

name: PPAP Automotive
theme_detail: PVC/TPO extruded profiles and automotive body sealing systems.
business: Automotive body sealing systems — extruded PVC/TPO and rubber weatherstrips — and injection-moulded interior and exterior parts, supplied to Maruti Suzuki, Honda, Toyota and their tier-1s from five plants (Noida, Surajpur, Chennai, Pathredi, Viramgam). The rubber sealing business runs through PPAP Tokai India Rubber, a joint venture with Tokai Kogyo of Japan, whose technical collaboration dates to 1989; sealing and moulded parts together are about 94% of revenue.
moat_note: Independently corroborated, but in a narrower form than the company's own materials claim. CRISIL, in its 16 January 2026 rationale, calls PPAP "one of the largest players in the PVC/TPO-based profiles segment for the auto industry" and credits it with a "leadership position in the polyvinyl chloride (PVC)/thermos plastic olefins (TPO) auto component industry" — an agency asserting leadership in a defined product niche. What CRISIL does not do is extend that to body sealing systems generally, which is how the company frames it, so the moat recorded here is the narrower PVC/TPO profile one. The durable part is tooling: a sealing profile is cut into model-specific dies and qualified for the life of a vehicle programme, so share is won at model launch and held for years. The fragile part is on the other side of the same fact — CRISIL puts the top two customers at about 68% of FY25 revenue, which is the same dependence read from the customer's side, and notes limited ability to pass through input costs.
import_substitution: Category-genuine rather than company-specific: domestic extrusion and moulding under a Japanese technical tie-up localises components that would otherwise be imported into Indian OEM assembly. Nothing in the independent record quantifies it, and the company makes no import-substitution claim of its own; scored on the category.
risk_note: The financials are the reason this scores where it does rather than higher. ROE is negative at -4.66% and ROCE is 3.64%, so the P/E of 87.9 sits on a base that is not currently earning its cost of capital; operating margin was 10.4% in FY25 with CRISIL explicitly noting limited pricing pass-through. Customer concentration is the structural exposure — roughly 68% of FY25 revenue from two customers, so a single model programme ending at Maruti or Honda moves the whole P&L, and the model-life tooling that creates the stickiness also means share is only contestable at launch, in both directions. Promoter holding has drifted down 0.7 points over eight quarters to 64.31%. The credit itself is fine — CRISIL A-/Stable, A2+, reaffirmed — which is the tension worth holding: a sound balance sheet attached to a currently unprofitable equity.

name: Sukhjit Starch & Chemicals
theme_detail: Maize starch and derivatives — dextrose, sorbitol, liquid glucose, maltodextrin.
business: Maize wet-milling: starch and its derivatives — dextrose monohydrate and anhydrous, sorbitol, liquid glucose, high-maltose syrup, maltodextrin, modified and pregel starches — plus the co-product stream of maize gluten, germ, oil and bran, from four plants at Phagwara, Nizamabad, Malda and Gurplah. Incorporated in 1943; sells into food, pharma, paper, textiles and animal feed.
moat_note:
Promoted because a top-tier agency says it independently, and the primary rationale — read directly, not through a summary — says more than the queue had recorded. CRISIL, rating the company A+/Negative and A1, states that the ratings reflect "the strong market position of SSCL as a leading manufacturer of starch and its derivatives in the domestic maize processing industry", and puts numbers behind it: 1,600 TPD of capacity and a "near double-digit market share" of the domestic maize processing industry. That share figure is the closest thing to criterion 3 in this batch that did not come from the company itself. CRISIL also records a genuine structural strength the original note missed — a "diversified and reputed clientele" with the top five customers at only 15% of revenue, which is unusually low for a small-cap processor and the opposite of PPAP's position on the same board.

What it still is not: a monopoly, or anything with pricing power. Starch is commodity wet-milling with competitors at scale (Gujarat Ambuja Exports, Sanstar, Gulshan Polyols), margins are set by the maize-to-starch spread, and CRISIL's own weaknesses are "operating margin susceptible to volatility in raw materials prices" and "modest debt protection metrics". Eight decades of operation and near-10% share of a commodity industry is a leadership position, recorded as such, and not evidence of defensibility.
import_substitution: None specific to the company. Starch derivatives are overwhelmingly domestically produced for a domestic market and the company makes no import-substitution claim; scored on the category alone.
risk_note: The returns are the problem and they are not marginal: ROE of 1.47% and ROCE of 5.88% mean an eighty-year-old asset base is earning next to nothing on shareholder funds, and a P/E of 14.5 on that is not obviously cheap. CRISIL's FY25 figures show the shape — Rs 1,487 crore of operating income converting to a PAT margin of 2.66%, with interest coverage of 3.56x and gearing of 0.49x, which CRISIL calls a healthy capital structure but modest debt protection. The outlook was revised to Negative from Stable while the A+ was reaffirmed: the direction of travel on the credit is down, which is the single most important fact in the independent record and cuts directly against the leadership framing. Input exposure is unhedgeable in the ordinary sense — maize is the raw material, its price is set by the crop, and the starch spread absorbs the difference. Institutional ownership is exactly zero on both FII and DII, and shareholder count has fallen from 10,495 to 9,638 over four quarters.

name: Foods & Inns
theme_detail: Mango and tropical fruit pulp, purees, spray-dried powders.
business: Tropical fruit and vegetable processing — mango pulp above all, plus purees, concentrates, spray-dried powders and frozen products — sold to global food and beverage brands, with mango pulp about 78% of FY22 sales. Processed over 300,000 MT of fruit and vegetables in FY2022-23 on a turnover above USD 110 million, from plants including Valsad and Sinnar. Government-recognised export house; over 50 years in the trade.
moat_note: The weakest of the five promoted names, and included because a rating agency does say it rather than only the company. Brickwork Ratings describes Foods & Inns as "one leading names in the fruit pulp industry with three" plants and "one of the largest exporters of Mango pulp in the country"; CRISIL, separately, credits an "established market position" and geographical diversification. That is third-party, but it is hedged wording from a lower-tier agency, and "one of the largest" is a scale statement, not a defensibility one. The real economics are seasonal agri-processing: the moat, such as it is, sits in long-standing relationships with international beverage buyers who audit and approve a processing site, and in owning capacity near the Alphonso and Totapuri catchments during a short crushing window. There is no technology barrier, no licence, and no pricing power — the fruit price sets the year.
import_substitution: None — this is an export business, not an import replacement, and no claim is made. Scored at the floor for the category.
risk_note: Promoter holding is 25.39% and has fallen 3.4 points over the period shown, which is by a distance the lowest promoter stake among the names promoted in this pass and leaves control thin for a family-origin processor. Institutional presence is nominal — FII 0.01%, DII 1.13% — so the register is 73% public with 22,041 holders and falling. The business itself is exposed at both ends: mango is a single-crop, single-season input whose price and availability swing with the monsoon, and the customer side is concentrated in a handful of international beverage buyers. CRISIL's rating is BBB/Stable with A3+ on the short-term facilities — investment grade but at its lower boundary — and both agencies name large working capital as a weakness, which is inherent to buying a year's fruit in a few weeks. ROE of 5.01% on that working-capital load is the summary.
